# PART 5 — TASK 2: DEFINE RETENTION METRICS CORRECTLY

Different types of retention must be treated independently.

Implement multiple retention measurement definitions.

## 5.1 Customer relationship retention

Measures whether the overall customer relationship remains active.

For a customer with multiple qualifying subscriptions, determine active customer status according to the approved Phase 5 customer-level business definition.

A customer remains active when at least one qualifying subscription or service continues, if that is the approved business policy.

Do not treat cancellation of one subscription as customer churn when other qualifying subscriptions remain active.

## 5.2 Subscription retention

Measures whether the original subscription remains in its qualifying active state.

A customer can have high customer retention while individual subscriptions are being cancelled or replaced.

Calculate separately.

## 5.3 Product engagement retention

Measures whether customers continue using the product or service during a period.

Use the activity definition from Phase 6.

Examples:

- At least one qualifying login.
- At least one meaningful usage event.
- At least one qualifying service interaction.

Do not treat engagement inactivity as equivalent to subscription termination.

## 5.4 Paid subscription retention

Measures the percentage of cohort members whose qualifying paid relationship remains active.

Use reliable billing and subscription history.

Distinguish trial customers from paid customers.

## 5.5 Revenue retention

Where reliable recurring revenue information exists, calculate cohort revenue retention separately.

Potential measures:

- Starting recurring revenue.
- Remaining recurring revenue.
- Contraction.
- Churned recurring revenue.
- Expansion.
- Gross revenue retention.
- Net revenue retention.

Do not combine different currencies without approved conversion.

Do not double-count invoice amounts and payments.

Do not claim revenue retention is available when the subscription pricing model or historical revenue data is insufficient.

## 5.6 Retention metric registry

Each metric must define:

- Metric ID.
- Metric name.
- Business definition.
- Numerator.
- Denominator.
- Entity scope.
- Activity definition.
- Observation period.
- Censoring policy.
- Reactivation policy.
- Currency handling where applicable.
- Metric version.

Do not use one generic retention field for every measurement type.

---

# PART 6 — TASK 3: IMPLEMENT COHORT PERIOD CALCULATIONS

## 6.1 Calendar-month cohort analysis

For each customer acquisition cohort, calculate retention across:

- Month 0.
- Month 1.
- Month 2.
- Month 3.
- Month 4.
- Month 5.
- Month 6.
- Month 7.
- Month 8.
- Month 9.
- Month 10.
- Month 11.
- Month 12.

Support longer historical periods if data is available.

Month 0 represents the acquisition cohort baseline and should show 100% of the eligible starting cohort where the metric definition supports it.

For cohort retention, subsequent columns represent months since acquisition, not calendar month names.

## 6.2 Cohort matrix structure

The result should resemble:

| Acquisition cohort | Month 0 | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 | Month 4 |
| ------------------ | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |
| Jan 2025           | 100%    | 85%     | 76%     | 69%     | 63%     |
| Feb 2025           | 100%    | 88%     | 79%     | 71%     | —       |
| Mar 2025           | 100%    | 82%     | 74%     | —       | —       |
| Apr 2025           | 100%    | 90%     | —       | —       | —       |

All values above are illustrative, not real results.

The implementation must calculate the actual percentages from verified customer history.

## 6.3 Retention formula

For cohort C and period k:

`Retention(C, k) = Retained eligible cohort entities at period k / Original eligible cohort size × 100`

The original cohort denominator must remain fixed.

Do not silently replace it with the number of customers remaining in the previous period.

## 6.4 Retained entity definition

For each period, determine whether the entity satisfies the selected activity or subscription status definition.

Provide distinct metrics for:

- Active at period end.
- Active at any time during period.
- Continuously retained through period end.
- Reactivated during period.

Do not confuse these definitions.

## 6.5 Standard periodic retention

Calculate whether an entity meets the activity or relationship condition during each individual period.

A customer may be retained in Month 1, inactive in Month 2 and active again in Month 3.

Preserve that actual sequence.

## 6.6 Continuous retention

Calculate the population that has remained continuously retained according to the specified definition.

A confirmed churn event should affect continuous retention even if the customer later reactivates, unless an explicit alternative policy is approved.

## 6.7 Reactivation-aware retention

Optionally calculate active-at-period-end retention that allows customers to return after inactivity or churn.

Report reactivation separately.

Do not erase the original churn event.

## 6.8 Elapsed-period retention

In addition to calendar-month cohorts, support exact elapsed periods:

- First 7 days.
- First 30 days.
- First 60 days.
- First 90 days.
- First 180 days.
- First 365 days.

Use consistent window boundaries anchored to each customer's acquisition timestamp.

Keep elapsed-day retention separate from calendar-month cohort retention.

## 6.9 Calendar boundary handling

Use a documented timezone and month-boundary convention.

Avoid treating all months as exactly 30 days.

Use calendar arithmetic for calendar-month retention and elapsed durations for exact 30-day analysis.

# PART 7 — TASK 4: BUILD THE RETENTION TABLE GENERATION ENGINE

Create a reusable cohort table calculation service.

## 7.1 Input requirements

Require:

- Cohort policy version.
- Cohort dataset version.
- Retention metric definition.
- Entity scope.
- Start period.
- End period.
- Period granularity.
- Source dataset versions.
- Historical observation coverage.

## 7.2 Output requirements

For each cohort and period, calculate:

- Cohort ID.
- Cohort acquisition period.
- Original cohort size.
- Period index.
- Period start.
- Period end.
- Observed population.
- Active population.
- Retained population.
- Churned population.
- Reactivated population.
- Censored population.
- Eligible denominator.
- Retention rate.
- Churn rate.
- Coverage status.

Store raw counts as well as percentages.

Never store only percentages.

## 7.3 Fixed cohort denominator

The original eligible acquisition cohort is the baseline denominator.

Do not recalculate the original cohort size for every subsequent month.

## 7.4 Period calculations

For every cohort-period cell:

- Calculate the eligible observation count.
- Calculate retained entities.
- Calculate churned entities.
- Determine whether the period is mature.
- Calculate retention only where valid.
- Mark unavailable periods explicitly.

## 7.5 Cohort table consistency

Ensure:

- Month 0 matches the policy-defined baseline.
- Counts are nonnegative.
- Retained count does not exceed the relevant denominator.
- Rates remain within valid percentage bounds.
- Incomplete future periods are not treated as zero retention.
- Censored observations are reported separately.

# PART 8 — TASK 5: RIGHT-CENSORING AND INCOMPLETE COHORTS

This is a mandatory requirement.

Recent acquisition cohorts often have not had enough time to complete their later observation periods.

Do not interpret missing future periods as failed retention.

## 8.1 Observation coverage

Record:

- Earliest reliable source date.
- Latest reliable source date.
- Latest synchronization time.
- Source update delay.
- Customer lifecycle coverage.
- Subscription lifecycle coverage.
- Activity coverage.

## 8.2 Immature cohort periods

Suppose an April 2026 cohort is being analyzed in May 2026.

Its Month 3 retention has not yet been observed.

The Month 3 value must be marked:

- NOT_MATURED.
- UNAVAILABLE.
- CENSORED.

Do not write 0%.

## 8.3 Right censoring

A period is censored when the observation window is not fully available or the required source information is incomplete.

Examples:

- Observation date has not arrived.
- Source data ends early.
- Subscription history is incomplete.
- Activity source synchronization is delayed.
- Historical source coverage is unavailable.

## 8.4 Denominator policies

Implement clearly documented options:

### Fixed cohort denominator

All original eligible cohort entities remain in the denominator.

Use this for the primary retention table.

### Observable denominator

Only entities with verified observable outcomes are included for supported secondary analyses.

Report this separately.

Do not switch denominator policies silently between cohort periods.

## 8.5 Censoring report

For every cohort-period pair, record:

- Original cohort size.
- Observable population.
- Censored population.
- Excluded records.
- Coverage percentage.
- Retention calculation eligibility.

## 8.6 Survival analysis boundary

The primary Phase 9 output is cohort retention tables and heatmaps.

If survival analysis such as Kaplan–Meier is added, implement it as a separately labelled statistical view using appropriate event-time and censoring definitions.

Do not treat ordinary retention percentages and survival probabilities as interchangeable.

# PART 9 — TASK 6: CUSTOMER-LEVEL AND SUBSCRIPTION-LEVEL COHORTS

Maintain distinct cohort scopes.

## 9.1 Customer-level acquisition cohorts

Group customers by their verified initial acquisition date.

Measure:

- Customer relationship retention.
- Product engagement retention.
- Paid customer retention.
- Customer churn.
- Reactivation.
- Customer revenue retention where supported.

## 9.2 Subscription-level acquisition cohorts

Group subscriptions by verified activation or start date.

Measure:

- Active subscription retention.
- Subscription churn.
- Voluntary subscription churn.
- Involuntary subscription churn.
- Renewal behavior.
- Subscription reactivation.
- Subscription revenue retention where supported.

## 9.3 Multiple subscriptions

Example:

Customer CUST-001:

- SUB-001 acquired in January.
- SUB-002 acquired in March.
- SUB-003 acquired in May.

The customer remains in the original January customer cohort.

Each subscription belongs to its own subscription cohort.

Do not move the original customer into the latest subscription acquisition cohort.

## 9.4 Customer-level retention aggregation

Apply the approved Phase 5 customer relationship policy.

If any qualifying service remains active, customer-level retention may remain positive.

Document how:

- Trial subscriptions.
- Free subscriptions.
- Paid subscriptions.
- Paused subscriptions.
- Suspended subscriptions.
- Terminated subscriptions.
- Reactivated subscriptions.

Affect the definition.

## 9.5 Cohort conflict reporting

Identify:

- Customers without verified acquisition dates.
- Subscriptions with invalid start dates.
- Conflicting customer mappings.
- Ambiguous customer relationships.
- Incorrect source event history.

Do not force unresolved records into a cohort.

# PART 10 — TASK 7: CUSTOMER CHURN AND COHORT COMPARISON

Extend the Phase 8 churn analytics engine.

## 10.1 Cohort churn

For each cohort-period calculate:

- Churned customers.
- Retained customers.
- Censored customers.
- Unknown outcomes.
- Excluded customers.
- Churn rate.

Use the approved Phase 5 churn events and the cohort retention definition.

## 10.2 Voluntary and involuntary churn

Measure separately:

- Voluntary churn by cohort.
- Involuntary churn by cohort.
- Other churn by cohort.
- Unknown churn by cohort.

Do not assume all lost retention is voluntary churn.

## 10.3 Cumulative churn

Calculate cumulative churn as of each completed period according to the approved event definition.

Clearly distinguish:

- Churn during the period.
- Cumulative churn since acquisition.
- Current inactive population.
- Permanently terminated relationships according to the business policy.

Do not count the same churn event multiple times.

## 10.4 Period churn

Calculate:

- Period-specific churn.
- Period-specific churn rate.
- Cumulative churn.
- Retention comparison.

Document the denominators and observation rules.

## 10.5 Cohort churn comparison

Allow comparisons between:

- Acquisition months.
- Acquisition quarters.
- Acquisition channels.
- Customer segments.
- Subscription plans.
- Contract types.
- Billing frequencies.

Use appropriate sample sizes.

Do not rank small cohorts as if their percentages were equally reliable as large cohorts.

# PART 14 — TASK 11: REACTIVATION AND CUSTOMER RETURN ANALYSIS

Implement explicit reactivation analysis.

## 14.1 Reactivation detection

Identify customers who:

- Churned historically.
- Later became active again.
- Started a new qualifying subscription.
- Resumed a qualifying customer relationship.

Use verified source events.

## 14.2 Reactivation measurements

Calculate:

- Reactivated customer count.
- Reactivation rate.
- Time from churn to reactivation.
- Reactivation by original acquisition cohort.
- Reactivation by churn type.
- Reactivation by customer segment.
- Reactivation by previous subscription type.

## 14.3 Retention treatment

Preserve two distinct views:

**Original acquisition retention**

Measures the customer's relationship with the business according to the original cohort policy.

**Current active relationship**

Measures whether the customer is currently active, including qualifying reactivations.

Do not erase the historical churn event when a customer returns.

## 14.4 Subscription replacement

If a customer cancels an old subscription and starts a new one:

- Preserve the original subscription churn event.
- Preserve the new subscription lifecycle.
- Keep the original customer cohort.
- Record subscription-level cohort membership separately.

Do not count the replacement subscription as proof that the old subscription never churned.

# PART 15 — TASK 12: REVENUE COHORT RETENTION

Implement only where historical recurring revenue is sufficiently reliable.

## 15.1 Starting cohort revenue

Calculate qualifying recurring revenue at cohort entry.

Define the period and currency.

## 15.2 Period revenue

Calculate eligible recurring revenue for the cohort at subsequent periods.

Consider:

- Churned subscriptions.
- Contractions.
- Upgrades.
- Downgrades.
- Additional subscriptions.
- Expansion revenue.

## 15.3 Gross revenue retention

Where the input data supports it:

`GRR = (Starting recurring revenue - Churned recurring revenue - Contraction) / Starting recurring revenue × 100`

Define the exact treatment of price adjustments, currency conversion and excluded items.

## 15.4 Net revenue retention

Where supported:

`NRR = (Starting recurring revenue - Churned recurring revenue - Contraction + Expansion) / Starting recurring revenue × 100`

Do not invent expansion revenue.

## 15.5 Revenue retention requirements

- Keep revenue metrics separate from customer retention.
- Preserve customer and subscription scopes.
- Use consistent revenue periods.
- Use Decimal-compatible financial calculations.
- Keep different currencies separate unless an approved conversion source and historical exchange rates are available.
- Prevent invoice/payment double-counting.
- Document revenue recognition assumptions.

If the project does not have adequate recurring revenue history, mark this feature as BLOCKED or unavailable.

# PART 16 — TASK 13: ADVANCED STATISTICAL COHORT ANALYSIS

Extend the EDA statistical infrastructure where appropriate.

## 16.1 Cohort sample sizes

Always report cohort population sizes.

Do not display only percentages.

## 16.2 Confidence intervals

Where suitable, calculate confidence intervals for retention estimates.

Use a documented method appropriate to the binomial proportion and sample characteristics.

Clearly label uncertainty.

Do not display confidence intervals as guarantees.

## 16.3 Cohort comparison tests

When comparing cohort retention, use statistically appropriate methods.

Evaluate:

- Proportion tests.
- Chi-square tests.
- Fisher's exact test for suitable sparse cases.
- Survival analysis where censoring requires it.
- Other justified statistical comparisons.

Account for repeated observations and overlapping windows.

Do not treat every cohort-period cell as an independent sample when it shares the same customers.

## 16.4 Survival analysis

Optionally implement Kaplan–Meier retention/survival curves if event-time and censoring data are sufficient.

Define:

- Time origin.
- Event.
- Censoring time.
- Inclusion criteria.
- Event type.
- Interpretation.

If competing risks between voluntary and involuntary churn are analyzed, use an appropriate competing-risk methodology rather than treating all event causes as ordinary independent outcomes.

## 16.5 Statistical limitations

Document:

- Small cohorts.
- Unequal observation coverage.
- Late-arriving data.
- Right censoring.
- Missing acquisition dates.
- Repeated customers.
- Multiple subscriptions.
- Cohort composition differences.

Do not claim causality from retention differences between cohorts.

## Five essential completion checks

Before allowing the coding agent to finish Phase 9, verify:

1. Stable acquisition cohorts: A customer remains in the original acquisition cohort even when acquiring additional subscriptions.
2. Correct retention denominator: The original cohort population remains the denominator.
3. Censoring: An unobserved future period is never displayed as zero retention.
4. Separate retention metrics: Customer retention, subscription retention and engagement retention are measured independently.
5. Historical evidence: Every retention result can be traced to actual customer or subscription lifecycle records.

My recommendation: Make monthly acquisition-cohort retention the primary Phase 9 deliverable. Keep customer retention and subscription retention as separate heatmap views, and make engagement retention a third view. This will give you a much clearer understanding of whether customers are leaving the business, individual subscriptions are ending, or customers are simply becoming less active.




# Phase 10 — Survival Analysis & Time-to-Churn Intelligence



Advanced statistical analysis

Step 10 of 20



Phase 10 builds directly on Phase 5's verified churn events, Phase 7's historical Feature Store, Phase 8's EDA and Phase 9's cohort membership, retention tables and censoring logic.

The important difference is that Phase 9 measures retention at defined observation periods, while Phase 10 measures how long customers or subscriptions remain free from a qualifying churn event.

The core deliverable is a statistically correct Kaplan–Meier survival analysis engine, with survival curves, confidence intervals, numbers-at-risk tables, censor marks, group comparisons and appropriate handling of voluntary and involuntary churn.

One critical requirement: do not build Kaplan–Meier from the Phase 5 binary 30-day churn label alone. Survival analysis needs verified event times and observation/censoring times from historical lifecycle records. The 30-day labels may be used for comparison or validation, but they cannot replace the underlying time-to-event history.

# PART 3 — UNDERSTAND THE PURPOSE OF SURVIVAL ANALYSIS

Survival analysis studies the time until a defined event occurs.

For this application, the primary event is a verified qualifying customer or subscription churn event.

Define:

- **Time origin:** The approved acquisition or activation event.
- **Event:** The first qualifying churn event under the selected policy.
- **Event time:** Time between the origin and the verified churn event.
- **Censoring time:** Time until reliable observation ends without observing the event.
- **Survival probability:** Probability that the entity remains free from the selected event beyond a given time.

The main statistical function is to estimate:

`S(t) = P(T > t)`

Where:

- `S(t)` is the survival probability at time t.
- `T` is the time until the qualifying event.
- `t` is the elapsed observation time.

Interpretation:

A higher survival probability means a larger proportion of the relevant population remains free from the defined churn event beyond that elapsed time.

Do not describe survival probability as the probability that a customer will never churn.

It is a time-specific estimate under the stated population, event definition and statistical assumptions.

# PART 4 — TASK 1: DEFINE THE SURVIVAL ANALYSIS POLICIES

Create a configurable and versioned survival-analysis policy.

Do not hardcode a single event definition throughout the application.

## 4.1 Primary survival endpoint

The default endpoint should be:

**Time from verified customer acquisition to first qualifying customer-level churn event.**

The endpoint must reuse the approved Phase 5 customer-level churn definition.

## 4.2 Additional supported endpoints

Where source data is adequate, support:

1. Time from subscription activation to subscription termination.
2. Time from customer acquisition to loss of the overall customer relationship.
3. Time from paid subscription activation to paid subscription termination.
4. Time from trial activation to trial termination or conversion, using a separately defined endpoint.
5. Time from first qualifying product activity to meaningful inactivity, as a distinct engagement endpoint.

Do not combine these endpoints into one survival curve.

## 4.3 Survival policy fields

Each policy must define:

- Policy ID.
- Policy name.
- Policy version.
- Endpoint type.
- Entity scope.
- Time origin.
- Event definition.
- Event timestamp field.
- Event cause classification.
- Censoring timestamp.
- Observation cutoff.
- Eligibility conditions.
- Left-truncation handling.
- Reactivation handling.
- Competing event handling.
- Time unit.
- Timezone.
- Tie handling.
- Data completeness requirements.
- Statistical estimator.
- Confidence interval method.
- Approval status.

## 4.4 Policy versioning

When an event definition, time origin, inclusion rule or censoring rule changes:

- Create a new policy version.
- Preserve old analyses.
- Record the reason.
- Record the author.
- Record the timestamp.
- Require appropriate approval.

Do not silently change the meaning of earlier survival curves.

# PART 5 — TASK 2: CONSTRUCT THE TIME-TO-EVENT DATASET

This dataset is the foundation of the survival engine.

Construct a reusable, validated analytical dataset.

## 5.1 Required analytical fields

Each observation must contain:

- Observation ID.
- Customer ID or subscription ID.
- Entity scope.
- Original acquisition cohort ID.
- Segment identifiers where available.
- Time-origin timestamp.
- Event timestamp if observed.
- Censoring timestamp.
- Event indicator.
- Event type.
- Event cause.
- Observed duration.
- Delayed-entry time if applicable.
- Source dataset version.
- Churn policy version.
- Survival policy version.
- Data quality status.
- Exclusion reason.

## 5.2 Event indicator

Use a standard event convention:

- `1` = Qualifying event observed.
- `0` = Right-censored without observing the qualifying event.

Do not use null to represent ordinary right censoring.

Use separate status information to represent invalid or unresolved observations that must not enter the statistical estimator.

## 5.3 Duration

Calculate:

`Observed duration = End of observation - Time origin`

For an event observation:

`Observed duration = Event timestamp - Time origin`

For a right-censored observation:

`Observed duration = Censoring timestamp - Time origin`

Store sufficient precision to reproduce the time difference.

Avoid rounding the duration prematurely.

## 5.4 Event timestamp hierarchy

Use the approved Phase 5 event policy.

Determine whether the event timestamp should represent:

- Cancellation request.
- Cancellation approval.
- Service termination.
- Effective customer relationship termination.
- Another approved qualifying event.

The default should represent the business event defined in Phase 5, not whichever timestamp is easiest to retrieve.

For example, a customer may request cancellation on one date but continue receiving the service until a later effective termination date.

The selected event date must be documented.

## 5.5 Observation cutoff

For every survival-analysis run, record an observation cutoff.

This is the maximum point in time up to which reliable event information is available.

Do not use the system's current date as an automatic substitute for source completeness.

If the latest source data only provides reliable lifecycle information through an earlier date, use that verified coverage boundary.

## 5.6 Censoring time

For a non-event observation, censor at the last reliable observation date permitted by the policy.

Possible sources include:

- Verified subscription status snapshot.
- Verified customer relationship history.
- Last confirmed lifecycle observation.
- Approved source coverage cutoff.

Do not simply use the last login as the censoring date for customer relationship survival.

Product usage and business relationship status are different concepts.

## 5.7 No negative or impossible durations

Reject or quarantine observations where:

- Event precedes time origin.
- Censoring precedes time origin.
- Entry occurs after the event.
- Required dates conflict.
- Dates are unreasonably inconsistent with source history.

Do not silently convert negative durations to zero.

Same-day events must follow an explicit documented boundary rule.

## 5.8 Date precision

Distinguish:

- Exact timestamps.
- Date-only observations.
- Monthly snapshots.
- Approximate or inferred dates.

Do not pretend a monthly snapshot provides an exact termination timestamp.

If the event is only known to have occurred between two observations, classify it as interval-censored.

A standard Kaplan–Meier implementation must not treat interval-censored observations as exact events.

Either exclude them with a clear reason or implement a separately labelled interval-censored estimator if justified.

# PART 6 — TASK 3: CUSTOMER-LEVEL AND SUBSCRIPTION-LEVEL SURVIVAL

These populations require separate analytical definitions.

## 6.1 Customer-level survival

Measure the time from initial customer acquisition until the customer experiences the first qualifying loss of the overall customer relationship.

Reuse Phase 5 customer aggregation rules.

For customers with multiple qualifying subscriptions:

- Reconstruct active subscription states.
- Identify the effective termination of each qualifying subscription.
- Determine when the overall qualifying customer relationship ends.
- Preserve other subscriptions that remain active.
- Use the approved customer-level event date.

Do not mark customer churn when only one of several active qualifying subscriptions ends.

## 6.2 Subscription-level survival

Measure the time between subscription activation and its first qualifying termination.

Each subscription is an independently identified observation, subject to the statistical independence considerations discussed later.

## 6.3 Paid customer survival

Where the billing and subscription data permits it, analyze paid customer relationship survival separately.

Do not mix free or trial customers with paid customers unless the policy explicitly calls for that population.

## 6.4 Engagement survival

Optionally implement a separate time-to-inactivity endpoint.

Define meaningful inactivity through the approved Phase 6 or Phase 5 methodology.

Do not equate product inactivity with subscription cancellation or confirmed customer churn.

## 6.5 Survival endpoint selector

In the application, offer separate endpoint choices:

- Customer relationship survival.
- Subscription survival.
- Paid customer survival.
- Product engagement survival.

Only show endpoints that have validated supporting data.

# PART 7 — TASK 4: HANDLE RIGHT CENSORING CORRECTLY

Right censoring is a foundational requirement.

A customer who has not experienced a verified churn event by the observation cutoff is not automatically known to remain a customer forever.

Their future event time is unknown.

## 7.1 Right-censored observations

Examples:

- Customer acquired in January who remains active at the verified observation cutoff.
- Subscription that is still active when reliable source coverage ends.
- Customer whose historical relationship is known only up to a specific date.

Record:

- Censoring timestamp.
- Observed duration.
- Censoring reason.
- Source coverage reference.
- Censoring policy version.

## 7.2 Administrative censoring

When an observation window ends at a common analysis cutoff, record the administrative censoring reason.

## 7.3 Loss-to-follow-up censoring

If an entity disappears from the dataset before the final analysis cutoff:

- Determine whether the source provides evidence of a real termination.
- Determine whether source coverage was lost.
- Do not assume disappearance means churn.
- Record the reason for censoring or exclusion.

## 7.4 Censoring classifications

Support:

- ADMINISTRATIVE_CENSORING.
- LOSS_TO_FOLLOW_UP.
- SOURCE_COVERAGE_END.
- INCOMPLETE_HISTORY.
- OTHER_APPROVED_REASON.

Use only classifications supported by evidence.

## 7.5 Independent censoring assumption

Kaplan–Meier estimation relies on a non-informative censoring assumption conditional on the analysis being performed.

Document this assumption.

Investigate whether censoring is systematically associated with:

- Customer segment.
- Acquisition channel.
- Subscription plan.
- Payment behavior.
- Customer activity.
- Source system.
- Calendar period.

If censoring is strongly associated with likely churn risk, explicitly report the potential bias.

Do not claim Kaplan–Meier automatically solves informative censoring.

## 7.6 Censoring diagnostics

Report:

- Censoring count.
- Censoring percentage.
- Censoring reason distribution.
- Censoring over time.
- Censoring by cohort.
- Censoring by customer segment.
- Censoring by source.

# PART 8 — TASK 5: HANDLE LEFT TRUNCATION AND DELAYED ENTRY

Support delayed entry when the historical data requires it.

## 8.1 The problem

An entity may have started its customer relationship before the available observation system began recording reliable historical activity.

For example:

- Customer acquired in January 2024.
- Historical system data begins in July 2024.
- Customer is already active in July 2024.

The customer entered the observable risk set in July, not January.

## 8.2 Required handling

Where the required dates are known, preserve:

- Original time origin.
- Delayed-entry time.
- Event or censoring time.

Do not simply treat the customer as newly acquired in July.

## 8.3 Left-truncation method

Implement a statistically appropriate delayed-entry Kaplan–Meier risk-set calculation when this data is available.

At each event time, the risk set must account for observations that entered follow-up before that event time and have not yet experienced an event or been censored.

## 8.4 When delayed entry cannot be reconstructed

When the original acquisition time or entry time is unknown:

- Mark the observation as having incomplete time-origin information.
- Exclude it from the relevant delayed-entry calculation.
- Record the exclusion reason.
- Report the number excluded.

Do not use guessed acquisition dates.

# PART 9 — TASK 6: IMPLEMENT KAPLAN–MEIER ESTIMATION

Implement a genuine Kaplan–Meier estimator using a tested statistical library or a well-tested internal implementation.

Inspect the existing dependencies and choose the approach that best fits the existing stack.

Do not independently write an unverified statistical algorithm merely to avoid using an appropriate library.

## 9.1 Kaplan–Meier estimator

The estimator is:

`S(t) = ∏[1 - d_i / n_i]`

For each event time:

- `d_i` = Number of qualifying events at that time.
- `n_i` = Number of entities at risk immediately before that time.
- `S(t)` = Estimated probability of remaining free from the event beyond time t.

## 9.2 Event-time preparation

Implement:

1. Filter eligible observations.
2. Validate event and censoring status.
3. Calculate observed duration.
4. Account for delayed entry if supported.
5. Sort unique event times.
6. Determine risk set at each event time.
7. Count events.
8. Calculate Kaplan–Meier survival probability.
9. Calculate cumulative event probability.
10. Calculate uncertainty estimates.

## 9.3 Risk-set correctness

The number at risk must be calculated immediately before the relevant event time.

Exclude:

- Entities whose events occurred earlier.
- Entities censored earlier.
- Entities that have not yet entered the risk set.

Handle tied event and censoring times using the selected estimator's documented convention.

Use library behavior that has been validated against deterministic reference examples.

## 9.4 Survival output

For every event time, record:

- Event time.
- Number at risk.
- Number of events.
- Number censored.
- Survival probability.
- Cumulative event probability.
- Standard error.
- Lower confidence bound.
- Upper confidence bound.

## 9.5 Cumulative event probability

For a single event endpoint:

`F(t) = 1 - S(t)`

Clearly label this as cumulative event probability for the relevant endpoint.

Do not automatically use this equation to claim cause-specific cumulative incidence in a competing-risk setting.

## 9.6 Survival curve baseline

The curve must begin at survival probability 1.0 at time zero for a correctly defined eligible starting population.

Do not introduce artificial early event points to improve the visual appearance.

## 9.7 Median survival time

Calculate the median survival time only when the estimated survival curve reaches or crosses 0.5.

If the curve does not reach 0.5 during reliable observation:

- Report MEDIAN_NOT_REACHED.
- Show the available observation horizon.
- Do not invent a median survival time.
- Do not extrapolate beyond the observed evidence.

## 9.8 Percentile survival times

Optionally calculate:

- 25th percentile event time.
- Median event time.
- 75th percentile event time.

Only report identifiable estimates.

Document whether the percentile refers to the time at which survival drops below the corresponding probability threshold.

Implement suitable survival confidence intervals.

## 10.1 Greenwood variance

Use an appropriate Greenwood variance estimator for Kaplan–Meier survival estimates.

The variance calculation must account for event counts and risk-set sizes.

## 10.2 Confidence interval method

Use a statistically appropriate confidence interval method, such as log-minus-log transformed intervals where suitable.

Do not use a simple normal interval that creates impossible survival bounds without justification.

## 10.3 Configurable confidence level

Support commonly used confidence levels:

- 90%.
- 95%.
- 99%.

The default should be 95%.

## 10.4 Confidence interval output

For each reported time point, include:

- Survival estimate.
- Lower bound.
- Upper bound.
- Confidence level.
- Method.

Ensure:

- Bounds stay within valid probability limits.
- Lower bound does not exceed upper bound.
- Uncertainty is correctly represented.
- Small-sample limitations are disclosed.

## 10.5 Confidence bands

Support stepwise confidence bands on survival charts.

Differentiate confidence bands from a smooth trend line.

Do not smooth the primary Kaplan–Meier estimate in a manner that changes its statistical interpretation.

# PART 14 — TASK 11: IMPLEMENT LOG-RANK TESTING

Implement appropriate statistical group comparison.

## 14.1 Primary comparison

Use the standard log-rank test for suitable comparisons between two or more independent survival groups.

It evaluates whether the observed event patterns differ between the groups across follow-up.

## 14.2 Required outputs

For each comparison, store:

- Test name.
- Group identifiers.
- Sample sizes.
- Event counts.
- Censoring counts.
- Observed event counts.
- Expected event counts.
- Test statistic.
- Degrees of freedom.
- P-value.
- Significance threshold.
- Interpretation.
- Assumption checks.

## 14.3 Null and alternative hypotheses

Document:

**Null hypothesis:** The compared groups have the same underlying survival experience under the test's assumptions.

**Alternative hypothesis:** At least one group differs in its survival experience.

Do not interpret a nonsignificant result as proof that groups are identical.

## 14.4 Two-group comparison

Support:

- Group A versus Group B.
- Selected acquisition cohort versus another cohort.
- Selected customer segment versus another segment.

## 14.5 Multiple-group comparison

Support an overall comparison across multiple groups.

If the overall test is significant, allow appropriate pairwise comparisons.

## 14.6 Pairwise testing

When many comparisons are performed:

- Adjust for multiple testing.
- Prefer Holm correction or another documented appropriate method.
- Optionally support Benjamini–Hochberg for exploratory discovery.
- Store raw and adjusted p-values.

Never report multiple uncorrected pairwise tests as though all were independently confirmatory.

## 14.7 Interpretation

Report:

- Whether the observed difference meets the configured statistical threshold.
- The size of the evidence.
- Group sample sizes.
- Event counts.
- Censoring rates.
- Follow-up limitations.

Do not write that a customer segment causes churn merely because its survival curve differs.

---

# PART 15 — TASK 12: SUPPORT ALTERNATIVE COMPARISON METHODS

The standard log-rank test is not appropriate for every survival comparison.

Implement other methods only when their assumptions and data requirements are satisfied.

## 15.1 Weighted log-rank tests

Consider supported weighted log-rank alternatives when differences may occur at different points in follow-up.

Examples include:

- Early differences.
- Late differences.
- Crossing survival curves.

Document the selected weighting method.

Do not select a test simply because it produces a smaller p-value.

## 15.2 Restricted mean survival time

Implement Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) as an alternative comparison.

The RMST through a fixed horizon represents the area under the survival curve over that horizon.

Calculate:

- RMST for group A.
- RMST for group B.
- RMST difference.
- Confidence interval.
- Statistical comparison where supported.

Choose a comparison horizon that is adequately observed in both groups.

Do not extrapolate survival beyond the observed reliable horizon.

## 15.3 Proportional hazards considerations

Log-rank comparisons are commonly most efficient under proportional hazards conditions.

Where proportional hazards are questionable:

- Document the issue.
- Use suitable alternative summaries.
- Consider weighted log-rank tests.
- Consider RMST.
- Avoid forcing a misleading single comparison statistic.

## 15.4 Selection rules

The application must identify the analysis method and explain why it was selected.

Do not automatically choose methods solely based on whichever returns the most favorable result.

# PART 16 — TASK 13: OPTIONAL COX PROPORTIONAL HAZARDS EXTENSION

An optional Cox model may be added if time-to-event data and baseline covariates are adequate.

This is not a substitute for the mandatory Kaplan–Meier engine.

## 16.1 Scope

Where justified, implement a separately labelled adjusted survival analysis.

Potential baseline predictors:

- Acquisition channel.
- Subscription plan.
- Contract type.
- Customer segment.
- Customer tenure at origin where applicable.
- Baseline usage.
- Baseline engagement.
- Baseline support friction.
- Baseline billing behavior.

## 16.2 Predictor timing

All predictors must be available at the survival time origin.

Do not use:

- Future feature values.
- Future churn events.
- Post-churn support tickets.
- Future payment failures.
- Future engagement declines.

This prevents leakage.

## 16.3 Model output

Where implemented, report:

- Hazard ratios.
- Confidence intervals.
- P-values.
- Reference categories.
- Model sample size.
- Event count.
- Covariates.
- Missing-data handling.
- Model convergence status.

Explain that hazard ratios describe relative instantaneous event rates under the model assumptions, not simple differences in churn probabilities.

## 16.4 Proportional hazards diagnostics

Evaluate the proportional hazards assumption using suitable diagnostics, such as Schoenfeld-residual-based checks.

Document:

- Global diagnostic.
- Covariate-specific diagnostics.
- Potential violations.
- Corrective method, if any.
- Remaining limitations.

## 16.5 Other model diagnostics

Where supported, check:

- Linearity for continuous predictors.
- Influential observations.
- Multicollinearity.
- Missing values.
- Sparse categorical groups.
- Model convergence.
- Functional form.

## 16.6 Model boundary

Do not implement a large predictive ML model in this phase.

Do not present a Cox model as a fully verified churn prediction system.

It is an optional inferential extension of the survival analysis functionality.

---

# PART 17 — TASK 14: COMPETING RISKS FOR VOLUNTARY AND INVOLUNTARY CHURN

This requirement is especially important for subscription businesses.

A customer may experience different types of churn.

For example:

- Voluntary: Customer chooses to cancel.
- Involuntary: Subscription is terminated after a qualifying billing or payment failure process.
- Other: Another verified qualifying reason.
- Unknown: Cause cannot be established.

These event causes should not be treated as interchangeable when estimating the probability of a particular cause.

## 17.1 Overall churn endpoint

First, calculate overall customer or subscription survival using all qualifying churn causes as the event.

This produces the time to first qualifying churn of any supported cause.

## 17.2 Cause-specific survival

Provide separate cause-specific hazard or survival views where appropriate.

Clearly explain their interpretation.

When analyzing time to voluntary churn, another type of churn prevents voluntary churn from occurring later within the original relationship.

## 17.3 Critical competing-risk distinction

Do not estimate real-world voluntary or involuntary cumulative incidence by simply treating all other event causes as ordinary right censoring and presenting `1 - Kaplan–Meier` as the cause-specific event probability.

That approach can overestimate actual cause-specific cumulative incidence.

Implement a proper competing-risk framework for cause-specific event probability.

## 17.4 Cumulative incidence function

Where supported, implement the Aalen–Johansen cumulative incidence estimator for:

- Voluntary churn.
- Involuntary churn.
- Other qualifying churn causes.

Return the probability of each event type by elapsed time while accounting for competing events.

## 17.5 Gray's test

Where appropriate, support Gray's test for comparing cumulative incidence functions between groups.

Document its assumptions and limitations.

## 17.6 Cause-specific hazard comparisons

Optionally support cause-specific hazard comparisons using an appropriate event model.

Distinguish cause-specific hazard ratios from cumulative incidence differences.

## 17.7 Competing-risk report

Display:

- Overall churn-free survival.
- Voluntary churn cumulative incidence.
- Involuntary churn cumulative incidence.
- Other churn cumulative incidence.
- Unknown or unresolved event causes.
- Competing event counts.
- Censoring counts.

Do not count one event as multiple competing churn events.

## 17.8 Data readiness

If the available historical data cannot reliably identify event causes, mark cause-specific analysis as BLOCKED or limited.

Do not infer voluntary or involuntary churn from ambiguous status fields.

---

# PART 18 — TASK 15: REACTIVATION AND MULTI-STATE LIFECYCLE HANDLING

Reactivation must not erase a previously observed churn event.

## 18.1 Time-to-first-churn analysis

For primary Kaplan–Meier survival:

- The first qualifying churn event ends the initial event-free relationship.
- Subsequent reactivation does not undo that event.
- The original survival time remains unchanged.

## 18.2 Reactivation analysis

Create a separate reactivation analytics view.

Measure:

- Time from churn to reactivation.
- Reactivated customer population.
- Reactivation by original cohort.
- Reactivation by churn cause.
- Reactivation by customer segment.
- Reactivation by subscription plan.

## 18.3 Recurrent events

If adequate event history exists, optionally implement a separate recurrent-event analysis.

Do not count repeated churn/recovery cycles as independent ordinary Kaplan–Meier observations.

## 18.4 Multi-state extension

Where justified, model distinct states:

- Active.
- Suspended.
- Churned.
- Reactivated.

Define allowed transitions explicitly.

An active-to-churned event is not the same transition as churned-to-reactivated.

## 18.5 Scope boundary

Keep the primary Phase 10 Kaplan–Meier result focused on time to first qualifying churn.

Multi-state and recurrent-event analysis is an additional, separately labelled extension.

A newer cohort may have insufficient follow-up to estimate later survival.

Different acquisition cohorts may be exposed to different business conditions, product changes, marketing strategies and pricing policies.

Document these possible differences.

Do not interpret cohort differences as causal effects of acquisition timing.

## 20.5 Cohort comparison testing

Apply multiple testing correction where many cohorts are compared.

# PART 26 — TASK 23: STATISTICAL VERIFICATION AND REFERENCE VALIDATION

This phase requires stronger statistical testing than ordinary frontend feature work.

Do not test only whether the functions execute.

Verify the numerical correctness of the estimates.

## 26.1 Deterministic example

Create a small artificial dataset with known event and censoring times.

Calculate expected Kaplan–Meier estimates independently.

Verify each event-time step against the reference calculations.

## 26.2 Test scenarios

Create deterministic test datasets for:

1. No events.
2. One event and no censoring.
3. Multiple events.
4. One censored observation.
5. Multiple censored observations.
6. Tied event times.
7. Event and censoring tied in time.
8. Same-day acquisition and churn.
9. Different follow-up durations.
10. No median survival reached.
11. Median survival reached.
12. Delayed-entry observations.
13. Left-truncated observations.
14. Multiple acquisition cohorts.
15. Customer with multiple subscriptions.
16. Voluntary and involuntary competing events.
17. Unknown event causes.
18. Incomplete event dates.
19. Interval-censored records.
20. No usable records.

## 26.3 Numerical verification

Validate:

- Risk-set counts.
- Event counts.
- Censor counts.
- Survival estimates.
- Cumulative event probability.
- Standard errors.
- Confidence interval bounds.
- Median survival.
- Numbers-at-risk table.
- Log-rank statistics.
- P-values.
- RMST differences where implemented.
- Competing-risk cumulative incidence where implemented.

## 26.4 Independent reference calculations

Compare the project's results with a trusted statistical reference implementation or independently calculated known results.

Use numerical tolerances justified by floating-point precision.

Record:

- Reference method.
- Library/version.
- Test dataset.
- Expected values.
- Actual values.
- Tolerance.
- Pass/fail status.

Do not validate an estimator only by comparing it against itself.

## 26.5 Statistical invariants

Test that:

- Survival begins at 1.0 for the eligible baseline population.
- Survival never increases after an event in ordinary Kaplan–Meier estimation.
- Survival remains within [0, 1].
- Cumulative event probability is consistent with 1 minus survival for the single-endpoint analysis.
- Event count is never negative.
- Risk-set count is valid.
- Censor markers do not create events.
- Median survival is not fabricated.
- No estimation occurs beyond reliable observation.
- Delayed entry is reflected in the risk set when enabled.

---

# PART 27 — TASK 24: TEMPORAL AND LEAKAGE TESTING

Temporal correctness must be independently verified.

## 27.1 Future-event mutation test

For an observation with a fixed analysis cutoff:

1. Calculate its survival dataset and curve.
2. Add a qualifying churn event after the observation cutoff.
3. Rebuild the same historical analysis using the original cutoff.
4. Verify that the historical result does not change.

A future event must not become a historical event.

## 27.2 Late-arriving event test

Add an event whose actual timestamp is before the cutoff but whose availability/import timestamp is after the cutoff.

Determine whether it was knowable under the selected analysis policy.

Maintain the distinction between:

- Retrospective corrected history.
- As-known-at-the-time analysis.

Do not silently mix these two views.

## 27.3 Future-feature leakage test

For optional Cox analysis:

- Establish baseline predictors at the origin.
- Add future features after the origin.
- Verify that baseline predictor values remain unchanged.

## 27.4 Cohort consistency

Verify that survival comparisons use the same acquisition cohort IDs and membership policies as Phase 9.

## 27.5 Reproducibility

Run the same analysis using the same immutable inputs and verify equivalent outputs.

# PART 34 — NON-NEGOTIABLE STATISTICAL AND ENGINEERING RULES

1. Never calculate survival from binary 30-day churn labels alone.
2. Never invent customer acquisition dates.
3. Never invent event timestamps.
4. Never treat missing customers as confirmed churn.
5. Never treat right-censored observations as observed events.
6. Never ignore the risk-set calculation.
7. Never display censored observations as churn events.
8. Never pretend interval-censored dates are exact.
9. Never ignore delayed entry when it is required and reconstructable.
10. Never mix customer survival and subscription survival.
11. Never let one cancelled subscription automatically represent customer churn.
12. Never erase a first churn event after reactivation.
13. Never report median survival when the curve does not reach the median threshold.
14. Never extrapolate results beyond reliable follow-up.
15. Never display confidence intervals without a documented method.
16. Never run group tests without checking sample sizes and assumptions.
17. Never interpret a p-value as the size or business importance of a difference.
18. Never interpret a nonsignificant result as proof of equality.
19. Never present cause-specific `1 - Kaplan–Meier` as the real-world cumulative incidence when competing events exist.
20. Never mix cause-specific hazards and cumulative incidence.
21. Never use post-origin features in baseline comparisons.
22. Never make causal claims from observational survival comparisons alone.
23. Never hardcode survival curves.
24. Never fake p-values or statistical significance.
25. Never claim unexecuted tests passed.
26. Never overwrite historical analysis versions.
27. Never break Phases 1–9.
28. Never automatically start the next phase.

# Phase 11 — ML Dataset Preparation & Leakage-Safe Temporal Splitting



Machine learning data engineering

Step 11 of 20



Phase 11 connects the previous nine data and analytics phases to the machine learning development stages. Its responsibility is to transform verified historical records and point-in-time features into reproducible, model-ready datasets.

The most important requirement is that the system must simulate how predictions would actually have been made in the past. A customer’s future cancellation, future payment failure, future usage or future support activity must never accidentally appear in the features used to predict that customer's churn.

The primary split will be chronological:

Train → Validation → Test

The prompt also requires a stricter customer-disjoint evaluation option, because evaluating future predictions for existing customers and evaluating completely unseen customers are two different problems.

# PART 4 — DEFINE THE PRIMARY PREDICTION PROBLEM

Build the primary ML dataset around the verified Phase 5 30-day churn target.

## 4.1 Primary prediction task

At prediction cutoff T, predict whether an eligible customer experiences a qualifying churn event during the following 30 days.

The primary binary target is:

`churn_30d`

Use:

- `1` = A qualifying churn event occurs inside the target window.
- `0` = No qualifying churn event occurs and the entire target observation window is reliably observed.
- `NULL` = Outcome cannot be established because the observation window or label evidence is incomplete.

Only eligible, fully determined target examples may enter the binary supervised training dataset.

Do not treat NULL as 0.

## 4.2 Prediction window

Use the approved Phase 5 target boundary:

`T < churn_event_at <= T + 30 days`

This means:

- Events occurring at or before T belong to historical state, not future churn targets.
- Events strictly after T and at or before T + 30 days may qualify.
- Events after T + 30 days do not count toward this target.

Use the same boundary convention as Phase 5.

## 4.3 Additional horizons

Design the preparation system to support separately configured horizons, where supported by historical labels:

- 7 days.
- 14 days.
- 30 days.
- 60 days.
- 90 days.

The default primary target remains 30-day churn.

Each horizon must have a separate target definition and maturity check.

Do not relabel a 30-day target as a 60-day prediction.

Do not combine different horizons into one ambiguous target column.

## 4.4 Additional prediction tasks

Prepare support for future target types:

- Any churn.
- Voluntary churn.
- Involuntary churn.
- Other qualifying churn.
- Verified churn cause classification.
- Subscription churn.

Use existing Phase 5 label definitions and eligibility semantics.

Do not invent cause labels where evidence is missing.

## 4.5 Prediction scope

Create independently defined datasets for:

1. Customer-level churn prediction.
2. Subscription-level churn prediction.

Do not mix customer rows and subscription rows in the same target population.

## 4.6 Prediction timestamp

Each ML observation represents one entity at one prediction cutoff.

Required uniqueness:

`entity_scope + entity_id + prediction_cutoff + target_policy_version + feature_schema_version`

If the existing architecture requires a more specific unique key, document and implement it.

Do not accidentally create multiple duplicate observations for the same entity and prediction cutoff.

# PART 5 — TASK 1: BUILD POINT-IN-TIME FEATURE SNAPSHOTS

This is one of the most important requirements in Phase 11.

Every feature used for prediction must have been available at the relevant prediction cutoff.

## 5.1 Required timestamp fields

Preserve the distinction between:

- `event_time`: When the underlying business event occurred.
- `available_at`: When the event or data became available to the system.
- `materialized_at`: When a feature value was calculated or stored.
- `prediction_cutoff`: When the hypothetical prediction is made.
- `label_event_time`: When the target event occurs.
- `label_available_at`: When the outcome becomes knowable from the source.

Do not collapse these into one timestamp.

## 5.2 Feature eligibility

A feature is eligible for a prediction at T only when its information was available by T under the selected historical evaluation policy.

The normal point-in-time rule is:

- Underlying event time must be before T.
- Source information availability time must be at or before T.
- Snapshot version must be compatible with the selected historical data policy.
- The feature value must not depend on information after T.

Apply the approved Phase 7 point-in-time retrieval behavior.

## 5.3 Late-arriving data

Handle records that happened before T but were imported after T.

Support two clearly separated analytical modes:

**Mode A — As-known-at-the-time**

Only information available to the system by T is eligible.

This best simulates a real prediction made at that time.

**Mode B — Retrospectively corrected history**

Historical records may be corrected or backfilled after T, but their later availability must remain visible in lineage.

Use this mode only where explicitly configured and appropriate for the intended evaluation.

Do not mix both modes in the same dataset without marking the difference.

## 5.4 Feature snapshot integrity

For each ML observation, preserve:

- Feature group ID.
- Feature schema version.
- Feature definition version.
- Feature snapshot ID.
- Source record versions.
- Prediction cutoff.
- Feature availability boundary.
- Materialization run ID.
- Snapshot revision.

## 5.5 Missing historical snapshots

If the Feature Store lacks an eligible historical snapshot:

- Attempt approved historical backfill from valid Phase 4 records.
- Preserve the same feature definitions.
- Preserve point-in-time rules.
- Record the backfill run.
- Validate the regenerated snapshot.
- Record unresolved features.

Do not substitute the current feature snapshot for a missing historical snapshot.

Do not use a current customer profile to recreate an old historical feature vector.

## 5.6 Snapshot mutation

Test that modifying a future event does not change the features of an earlier prediction cutoff.

Preserve immutable historical feature snapshot versions.
