# PART 6 — TASK 3: IMPLEMENT SAFE PREPROCESSING PIPELINES

Preprocessing must be fitted only on training observations.

Use an integrated pipeline architecture, such as appropriate scikit-learn Pipeline and ColumnTransformer components, when supported by the chosen dependencies.

Do not fit transformations using the complete dataset.

## 6.1 Numeric features

Handle:

- Missing values.
- Infinite values.
- Numeric type conversion.
- Scaling.
- Optional approved transformations.
- Outlier policies.

For Logistic Regression, use an appropriate scaling strategy.

Tree-based algorithms generally do not require standard scaling, but must still receive valid numerical inputs and consistent missing-value treatment.

## 6.2 Categorical features

Handle:

- Missing categories.
- Known categories.
- Unknown categories.
- Rare categories.
- High-cardinality categories.

Use a well-defined encoding policy.

One-hot encoding is an acceptable baseline for appropriate categorical cardinalities.

Do not encode category labels using arbitrary numeric order unless the ordering is meaningful and approved.

## 6.3 Boolean features

Convert using consistent, documented mappings.

Do not mix strings, numbers and booleans unpredictably.

## 6.4 Dates and identifiers

Do not send raw customer identifiers or raw source identifiers into the model.

Use approved date-derived features from Phase 6.

Do not create new time-derived features using future information.

## 6.5 Missing-value behavior

For numeric features:

- Median imputation may be used when justified.
- Mean imputation may be configured where appropriate.

For categorical features:

- Use a suitable missing category or documented imputation strategy.

For each strategy:

- Fit on training data only.
- Save fitted values.
- Apply unchanged to validation and test.
- Record its artifact version.

## 6.6 Unknown categories

The validation and test partitions may contain unseen categories.

Handle them using a deterministic unknown-category policy.

Do not refit the encoder with validation or test categories.

## 6.7 Preprocessing artifact persistence

Persist:

- Transformer pipeline.
- Input schema.
- Output schema.
- Fitted imputation values.
- Scaling parameters.
- Category vocabulary.
- Feature ordering.
- Training dataset version.
- Library versions.
- Artifact checksum.

## 6.8 Model-specific preprocessing

Allow different appropriate pipelines for different algorithms.

For example:

- Logistic Regression: numeric imputation, numeric scaling and categorical encoding.
- Random Forest: numeric imputation and categorical encoding.
- XGBoost: validated numeric and encoded categorical feature representation, unless the supported native categorical workflow is explicitly implemented and tested.
- LightGBM: validated numeric and categorical representation using a documented compatible approach.

Do not compare models on different feature populations without reporting the difference.

## 6.9 Missing-value strategy

If a model library supports missing values natively, this may be used where it is appropriate.

However, comparisons must document whether preprocessing differs between model families.

Never allow missing-value behavior to vary silently.

---

# PART 7 — TASK 4: TRAIN LOGISTIC REGRESSION

Logistic Regression is the primary interpretable baseline.

Implement an actual trainable Logistic Regression classifier.

## 7.1 Objective

Estimate the probability of churn using a logistic function.

The model provides a simple baseline against which more complex models can be compared.

## 7.2 Required configuration

Support configurable:

- Regularization type.
- Regularization strength.
- Solver.
- Maximum iterations.
- Class weighting.
- Tolerance.
- Random state where applicable.

Support suitable regularization options such as L1, L2 or elastic-net only when compatible with the selected solver and library version.

## 7.3 Baseline configuration

Create a reproducible baseline configuration.

Do not use arbitrary parameters without explanation.

The baseline must:

- Fit the training data.
- Predict validation probabilities.
- Generate validation classifications at a configurable threshold.
- Calculate validation metrics.
- Save coefficients and model metadata.

## 7.4 Regularization

Use regularization to reduce overfitting where appropriate.

Evaluate:

- L1.
- L2.
- Other supported choices.

Do not blindly select the configuration that performs best on the final test dataset.

## 7.5 Class imbalance

Support:

- No class weighting as baseline.
- Balanced class weights where appropriate.
- Explicit configurable class weights.

Compare the effects on recall, precision, probability calibration and precision-recall performance.

## 7.6 Feature coefficients

Provide:

- Coefficient value.
- Feature name.
- Sign.
- Magnitude.
- Model configuration.
- Reference category for encoded features.

Explain that coefficient sign and magnitude describe model associations under the model's specification, not causal effects.

## 7.7 Convergence

Detect:

- Convergence warnings.
- Maximum iteration exhaustion.
- Invalid matrices.
- Numerical instability.
- Unsupported parameter combinations.

A model with unresolved convergence problems must not receive an unconditional PASS status.

---

# PART 8 — TASK 5: TRAIN RANDOM FOREST

Implement a genuine Random Forest classifier.

## 8.1 Objective

Capture nonlinear feature relationships and interactions through an ensemble of decision trees.

## 8.2 Required configurable parameters

Support:

- Number of trees.
- Maximum tree depth.
- Minimum samples per split.
- Minimum samples per leaf.
- Maximum features.
- Bootstrap configuration.
- Class weighting.
- Random seed.
- Parallel worker count.
- Split criterion.
- Pruning configuration where justified.

## 8.3 Training workflow

1. Load training feature matrix.
2. Load training labels.
3. Fit the approved preprocessing pipeline.
4. Train the forest.
5. Generate validation probabilities.
6. Calculate validation metrics.
7. Save the trained model.
8. Save configuration and training metadata.

## 8.4 Overfitting controls

Evaluate:

- Tree depth.
- Minimum leaf size.
- Number of trees.
- Feature subsampling.
- Class weighting.

Inspect the difference between training and validation performance.

Do not assume a higher training score means a better model.

## 8.5 Feature importance

Provide:

- Built-in impurity-based importance.
- Permutation importance using validation data where appropriate.

Clearly distinguish these measures.

Impurity importance can favor certain feature types and cardinalities.

Do not present it as a causal explanation.

## 8.6 Out-of-bag estimates

Out-of-bag evaluation may be recorded as a supplementary diagnostic when enabled.

Do not substitute it for chronological validation or the untouched test evaluation.

---

# PART 9 — TASK 6: TRAIN XGBOOST

XGBoost is a mandatory primary model family.

Use the current compatible XGBoost package and API.

Verify the installed version and official documentation before implementation.

## 9.1 Objective

Train a gradient-boosted decision tree model to predict the probability of 30-day churn.

Use an appropriate binary classification objective.

## 9.2 Required configuration

Support configurable:

- Number of boosting rounds.
- Learning rate.
- Maximum tree depth.
- Minimum child weight.
- Subsample.
- Column subsampling.
- L1 regularization.
- L2 regularization.
- Minimum split loss.
- Positive-class weight.
- Tree method.
- Evaluation metrics.
- Random seed.
- Worker count.

## 9.3 Tree method

Use an appropriate method for the installed runtime and hardware.

CPU training should work as the reliable default.

GPU acceleration may be optional when supported and available.

Do not claim GPU usage unless verified.

## 9.4 Class imbalance

Support `scale_pos_weight` or another suitable method where justified.

Calculate candidate weighting based on training-label counts only.

Compare:

- Unweighted baseline.
- Weighted model.

Do not calculate weighting ratios from validation or test labels.

## 9.5 Early stopping

Use the approved validation dataset for early stopping.

Do not use the test dataset for early stopping.

Record:

- Evaluation metric.
- Patience.
- Best iteration.
- Best score.
- Training iterations.
- Stopping reason.

Verify the behavior of the installed XGBoost API.

The model artifact used for prediction must use the intended best iteration, not accidentally include unwanted post-best trees.

## 9.6 Evaluation metric

Select the primary early-stopping metric based on the predefined model objective.

Support suitable probability or ranking metrics.

Do not use accuracy as the only early-stopping criterion for imbalanced churn data.

## 9.7 XGBoost artifacts

Save a native model artifact in an appropriate supported format, such as JSON or UBJ, in addition to the metadata and preprocessing artifacts.

Avoid depending exclusively on an unsafe or non-portable pickle representation.

## 9.8 Version and compatibility

Record:

- XGBoost version.
- Python version.
- Platform.
- Training parameters.
- Feature schema.
- Tree method.
- Best iteration.
- Dependency versions.

---

# PART 10 — TASK 7: OPTIONAL LIGHTGBM IMPLEMENTATION

LightGBM is an optional additional model.

Implement it if:

- The project environment supports it.
- Its dependency installation is compatible.
- It can be tested reliably.
- It provides a meaningful additional model comparison.

Do not make the mandatory primary models depend on LightGBM.

## 10.1 Required behavior

When enabled:

- Train `LGBMClassifier` or another appropriate supported API.
- Use training data for fitting.
- Use validation data for early stopping.
- Record best iteration.
- Calculate the same comparison metrics.
- Save the native model artifact.
- Record library and dependency versions.

## 10.2 Configurable parameters

Support:

- Number of estimators.
- Learning rate.
- Number of leaves.
- Maximum depth.
- Minimum child samples.
- Feature fraction.
- Bagging fraction.
- Bagging frequency.
- L1 regularization.
- L2 regularization.
- Class weighting.
- Positive-class weighting.
- Random seed.
- Worker count.

## 10.3 Validation

Check:

- Sparse categories.
- High-cardinality categorical features.
- Class imbalance.
- Early-stopping behavior.
- Numerical stability.
- Compatibility with preprocessing.

## 10.4 Failure behavior

If LightGBM cannot be installed or verified:

- Mark it BLOCKED or NOT IMPLEMENTED.
- Record the reason.
- Keep the other model families operational.

Do not report an optional model as trained if only its configuration exists.

---

# PART 11 — TASK 8: HYPERPARAMETER OPTIMIZATION

Create a controlled hyperparameter optimization framework.

Model tuning must not compromise the temporal separation established in Phase 11.

## 11.1 Supported approaches

Support appropriate methods such as:

- Manual parameter configuration.
- Randomized search.
- Grid search for small controlled spaces.
- Bayesian optimization such as Optuna, if compatible and justified.

Reuse existing dependencies where possible.

Do not add unnecessary optimization infrastructure.

## 11.2 Search boundaries

Each model needs its own documented search space.

Do not search unlimited parameter combinations.

Define:

- Search parameters.
- Parameter ranges.
- Trial budget.
- Maximum training time where configured.
- Primary scoring metric.
- Early-stopping policy.
- Random seed.
- Search status.

## 11.3 Training-data-only temporal tuning

When using internal cross-validation or backtesting, use chronological or expanding-window folds that are constructed strictly inside the training partition.

Preserve the Phase 11 label-maturity and purging rules for every fold.

Do not use ordinary shuffled K-fold or random stratified folds as the default.

Do not create new temporal folds that ignore target-window overlap.

## 11.4 Validation-based selection

Use the approved validation dataset to evaluate candidate configurations and select the final configuration.

All candidate comparisons must use the same validation population for a fair comparison.

## 11.5 Search metric

The default primary selection metric should be Average Precision / area under the precision-recall curve when the positive churn class is meaningfully imbalanced.

Allow the objective to be configured for other business requirements.

Secondary metrics should be stored.

## 11.6 Avoid validation overfitting

Record:

- Number of trials.
- Search space.
- Candidate configurations.
- Validation scores.
- Selection logic.

Do not endlessly tune against the same validation period.

Where possible, use time-respecting folds within the training period to reduce overfitting to the single validation set.

## 11.7 Search results

Store every completed and failed trial.

Do not delete unsuccessful experiments.

Do not invent a best configuration when all trials fail.

## 11.8 Resource controls

Support:

- Trial limits.
- Time limits.
- Worker limits.
- Cancellation.
- Resource monitoring.
- Failure recovery.

---

# PART 12 — TASK 9: HANDLE CLASS IMBALANCE

Churn datasets may have fewer churn-positive observations than non-churn observations.

Implement explicit class imbalance handling.

## 12.1 Initial diagnosis

Calculate training-only:

- Positive count.
- Negative count.
- Positive percentage.
- Negative percentage.
- Imbalance ratio.

Report validation and test distributions separately for evaluation.

## 12.2 Baseline strategy

Train an unweighted model first.

Establish the natural performance baseline.

## 12.3 Supported techniques

Evaluate suitable approaches:

- Class weights.
- Cost-sensitive learning.
- Positive-class weighting.
- Threshold adjustment.

## 12.4 Optional resampling

Resampling methods may be included as optional experiments:

- Random oversampling.
- Random undersampling.
- SMOTE, when suitable.

However:

- Apply resampling only inside the training partition.
- Perform it inside the training pipeline or training-only folds.
- Never resample validation or test.
- Do not create artificial samples before chronological splitting.
- Preserve original validation and test prevalence.

SMOTE must not be applied blindly to encoded high-cardinality categories or inappropriate mixed feature types.

## 12.5 Strategy comparison

Compare the following where data supports them:

1. Original distribution.
2. Class-weighted approach.
3. Carefully controlled oversampling.
4. Carefully controlled undersampling.

Use the same untouched validation and test populations.

## 12.6 Probability implications

Class weights and resampling can affect probability calibration.

Do not assume weighted output scores are automatically calibrated real-world churn probabilities.

Evaluate calibration separately.

---

# PART 13 — TASK 10: MODEL EVALUATION METRICS

Build a shared evaluation engine.

All model families must use the same approved metrics and target interpretation.

Do not report model quality using accuracy alone.

## 13.1 Core confusion matrix metrics

Calculate:

- True positives.
- False positives.
- True negatives.
- False negatives.
- Accuracy.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- Specificity.
- F1 score.
- Balanced accuracy.
- Matthews correlation coefficient.

Show the classification threshold associated with these metrics.

## 13.2 Ranking metrics

Calculate:

- ROC-AUC.
- Average Precision.
- Precision-recall AUC using a clearly documented implementation where available.

Display the baseline prevalence for the precision-recall analysis.

For imbalanced churn prediction, Average Precision should normally be the default primary comparison metric unless an explicitly approved business objective requires another criterion.

## 13.3 Probability metrics

Calculate:

- Log loss.
- Brier score.

Use the probabilities produced by the model.

Check for:

- Invalid probabilities.
- NaNs.
- Infinite outputs.
- Incorrect class ordering.

## 13.4 Threshold-independent metrics

Report metrics that assess ranking or probability quality independently of an arbitrary class threshold.

## 13.5 Threshold-dependent metrics

Report metrics at:

- 0.50 default threshold.
- Selected validation threshold.
- Other approved operational threshold candidates.

Do not present threshold-dependent metrics without showing the threshold.

## 13.6 Calibration metrics

Evaluate whether predicted probabilities correspond to observed event frequencies.

Include:

- Brier score.
- Reliability diagram.
- Calibration table.
- Predicted-versus-observed churn frequency.
- Calibration slope/intercept where statistically appropriate.

Use a suitable binning strategy.

Show bin counts and uncertainty.

## 13.7 Lift and gain

Support:

- Lift at top 5%.
- Lift at top 10%.
- Lift at top 20%.
- Cumulative gain.
- Capture rate among the highest-risk customers.

Use the actual validation and test populations.

Do not invent business gains.

## 13.8 Confidence intervals

Where feasible, calculate uncertainty intervals for selected evaluation metrics.

Account for repeated observations from the same customer.

Do not automatically use an independent-row bootstrap if repeated entity observations make observations dependent.

Use a suitable entity-clustered or time-aware uncertainty method where justified.

Record the method and assumptions.

## 13.9 Comparison fairness

Every model comparison must use:

- The same target.
- The same prediction horizon.
- The same entity scope.
- The same validation population.
- The same metric definitions.
- The same class interpretation.

Where model-specific preprocessing differs, clearly document it.

---

# PART 14 — TASK 11: MODEL TRAINING, VALIDATION AND TEST PROTOCOL

This is one of the most important controls.

## 14.1 Training partition

Use only training data to fit model parameters.

The training partition is the only source used for learning the initial model parameters.

## 14.2 Validation partition

Use validation for:

- Hyperparameter selection.
- Early stopping.
- Model comparison.
- Calibration decisions under a documented protocol.
- Threshold selection.
- Candidate model selection.

Do not use test data during any of these steps.

## 14.3 Test partition

Protect test data from:

- Hyperparameter tuning.
- Feature selection.
- Model family selection.
- Preprocessing fitting.
- Resampling.
- Threshold optimization.
- Calibration method selection.
- Feature importance-based model changes.

## 14.4 Final model comparison

Create a validation leaderboard.

Select a candidate using the predefined selection objective and the full validation results.

Do not select a model by an unsupported single metric.

## 14.5 Final refit policy

Support a configurable finalization approach.

Preferred approach:

1. Train candidate models on the training partition.
2. Tune parameters using training-only temporal folds where supported.
3. Select the candidate using validation results.
4. Lock the model family and hyperparameters.
5. Determine training duration or number of boosting rounds without using test labels.
6. Optionally refit the selected model on training plus validation data, if its label-maturity and historical timing policy permits it.
7. Refit any preprocessing transformations on the combined permitted training data.
8. Freeze the final model artifact.
9. Evaluate that final artifact on the test partition once.
10. Save the test evaluation report as the final holdout result.

If refitting on training plus validation is not suitable for the dataset timeline, retain the training-only candidate and document why.

## 14.6 No test-driven iteration

After final test evaluation:

- Do not adjust model parameters based on test results.
- Do not change feature selection based on test results.
- Do not optimize the threshold using test outcomes.
- Do not repeat test-driven experimentation and present the final result as an untouched holdout.

If a substantive model change is necessary after examining the test results, declare the original test set consumed and require a new later-period holdout dataset version for a new confirmatory evaluation.

## 14.7 Evaluation modes

Respect both Phase 11 evaluation modes:

- FORWARD_TEMPORAL.
- STRICT_ENTITY_DISJOINT_CHRONOLOGICAL.

Do not combine their results into one leaderboard.

They answer different generalization questions.

---

# PART 15 — TASK 12: PROBABILITY CALIBRATION

A churn-risk system must distinguish ranking ability from probability reliability.

Implement a separate calibration workflow.

## 15.1 Purpose

A model may rank higher-risk customers correctly while producing inaccurate probability estimates.

Calibration checks whether a predicted probability is consistent with the observed event frequency.

## 15.2 Calibration methods

Where justified, support:

- Uncalibrated model.
- Sigmoid/Platt scaling.
- Isotonic regression.

Select methods only with adequate data.

Do not automatically select isotonic regression for small validation populations.

## 15.3 Calibration data rules

Calibration must use a documented permitted calibration procedure.

Options include:

- A separate chronological calibration subset.
- Time-aware cross-fitting within training.
- A carefully documented calibration procedure on validation.

Do not use test labels to fit a calibrator.

Do not calibrate on the same observations and then claim an unbiased calibration result.

## 15.4 Calibration comparison

Compare:

- Uncalibrated model.
- Calibrated model.
- Brier score.
- Log loss.
- Reliability diagram.
- Calibration sample size.

## 15.5 Calibration limitations

Report when a calibration method cannot be trusted because of:

- Small sample size.
- Few positive examples.
- Distribution shift.
- High censoring or incomplete labels.
- Changes in class prevalence.

## 15.6 Output

Persist the calibration method and calibration artifact with the selected model.

---

# PART 16 — TASK 13: DECISION THRESHOLD OPTIMIZATION

A probability model and a business decision threshold are not the same thing.

Build a separate threshold optimization service.

## 16.1 Default threshold

Provide 0.50 as a reference classification threshold.

Do not assume it is automatically the best operational threshold.

## 16.2 Candidate thresholds

Evaluate configurable thresholds using validation probabilities.

For example:

- 0.10.
- 0.20.
- 0.30.
- 0.40.
- 0.50.
- 0.60.
- 0.70.
- 0.80.
- 0.90.

Also support a finer threshold search where justified.

## 16.3 Business constraints

Allow authorized users to define a hypothetical decision objective based on:

- Retention team capacity.
- Maximum customer contact volume.
- Cost of a false positive.
- Cost of a false negative.
- Expected value of a retained customer.
- Intervention cost.

These must be configurable assumptions, not invented real business economics.

## 16.4 Threshold output

Show:

- Threshold.
- Predicted high-risk count.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- False positive count.
- False negative count.
- Potential intervention volume.

## 16.5 Threshold selection

Select thresholds using validation outcomes only.

The chosen threshold must be saved separately from the underlying model.

Do not hardcode a threshold into the model artifact without versioned configuration.

## 16.6 Test evaluation

Evaluate the locked threshold on the final test predictions.

Do not optimize the threshold on test labels.

---

# PART 17 — TASK 14: MODEL COMPARISON AND SELECTION

Build a consistent comparison framework.

## 17.1 Mandatory model leaderboard

Compare:

- Logistic Regression.
- Random Forest.
- XGBoost.
- LightGBM, if successfully implemented.

## 17.2 Comparison columns

Show:

- Model family.
- Configuration.
- Dataset version.
- Feature count.
- Training rows.
- Validation rows.
- Positive label count.
- Negative label count.
- Average Precision.
- ROC-AUC.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- Balanced accuracy.
- MCC.
- Log loss.
- Brier score.
- Calibration status.
- Training time.
- Prediction time.
- Model artifact size.

## 17.3 Primary selection criterion

Default to validation Average Precision for imbalanced binary churn prediction.

However, make the selection criterion configurable and require it to be set before the experiment.

Also consider:

- Recall at a precision constraint.
- Precision at a capacity constraint.
- PR-AUC.
- Probability quality.
- Stability.
- Interpretability.
- Computational requirements.

## 17.4 Model suitability

Do not automatically choose XGBoost or LightGBM because they are more advanced.

A Logistic Regression model may be preferable when:

- Performance is competitive.
- Calibration is better.
- Interpretability is important.
- Complexity is lower.
- Runtime is substantially better.

Select based on evidence.

## 17.5 Model ranking

Produce:

- Best validation candidate.
- Best calibrated candidate.
- Best high-recall candidate.
- Best capacity-constrained candidate.
- Best interpretable baseline.

These should be derived from actual results.

Do not fabricate a winner where models cannot be compared fairly.

---

# PART 18 — TASK 15: FEATURE IMPORTANCE AND MODEL INTERPRETABILITY

Build model-specific interpretability outputs.

These explain learned associations, not causal drivers.

## 18.1 Logistic Regression

Show:

- Coefficients.
- Direction.
- Magnitude.
- Reference categories.
- Regularization configuration.

## 18.2 Random Forest

Show:

- Impurity-based importance.
- Permutation importance.
- Feature ranking.

## 18.3 XGBoost

Show:

- Gain importance.
- Cover importance.
- Weight/frequency importance.
- Permutation importance where appropriate.

## 18.4 LightGBM

Where implemented, show supported feature importance measures.

## 18.5 Permutation importance

Calculate using validation data or a dedicated permitted interpretation dataset.

Do not use test data to repeatedly select features or modify the model.

## 18.6 Optional SHAP

SHAP analysis may be added if:

- The dependency is compatible.
- The model family is supported.
- Calculation cost is acceptable.
- The results are verified.
- The data is authorized.

Provide:

- Global summary.
- Feature dependence.
- Selected local prediction explanations.

Do not make SHAP mandatory if its implementation would destabilize the primary training workflow.

## 18.7 Interpretation safeguards

Display explicit warnings:

- Feature importance is not causality.
- Correlated features can redistribute importance.
- Tree importance is not directly comparable to model coefficients.
- SHAP explanations describe model behavior, not the true cause of customer churn.

---

# PART 19 — TASK 16: CUSTOMER SEGMENT AND COHORT MODEL EVALUATION

Use Phase 9 cohort definitions and the approved Phase 11 dataset metadata.

## 19.1 Segment evaluation

Evaluate performance across available:

- Customer segments.
- Acquisition channels.
- Subscription plans.
- Billing frequencies.
- Contract types.
- Organization-size groups.

Use authorized attributes only.

## 19.2 Cohort evaluation

Report model performance for:

- Earlier acquisition cohorts.
- Later acquisition cohorts.
- Major acquisition periods.
- Customer populations with different follow-up coverage.

## 19.3 Segment metrics

Where sample sizes allow, calculate:

- Number of evaluated observations.
- Positive events.
- Negative observations.
- Average Precision.
- ROC-AUC.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- Brier score.

## 19.4 Low sample sizes

Suppress or mark unreliable comparisons when segments have too few positive examples.

Do not present unstable small-sample metrics as definitive.

## 19.5 Repeated customer records

In forward-temporal mode, multiple snapshots of the same customer may appear.

Report both:

- Observation-level performance.
- Distinct customer counts.

Use suitable entity-aware uncertainty analysis where needed.

## 19.6 Fairness and governance

When authorized and appropriate, evaluate performance disparities across business segments.

Do not infer protected characteristics.

Do not use sensitive personal attributes without legal, organizational and policy approval.

Do not make automated adverse decisions solely from a model score.

# PART 20 — TASK 17: TRAINING RUNS AND EXPERIMENT TRACKING

Create a reliable experiment tracking system.

Reuse any existing tracking infrastructure.

Do not add an external service without justification.

## 20.1 Training run metadata

Store:

- Training run ID.
- Dataset specification.
- Dataset version.
- Dataset checksum.
- Model family.
- Model version.
- Feature schema.
- Target.
- Target horizon.
- Entity scope.
- Evaluation mode.
- Split configuration.
- Preprocessing configuration.
- Hyperparameters.
- Random seed.
- Dependency versions.
- Hardware configuration.
- Execution status.
- Start time.
- Completion time.

## 20.2 Metrics tracking

Store training and validation results separately.

Record:

- Epoch/iteration metrics where supported.
- Best iteration.
- Training time.
- Validation time.
- Prediction time.
- Evaluation metrics.
- Calibration metrics.
- Threshold results.

## 20.3 Experiment history

Allow users to:

- View training runs.
- Compare model runs.
- Inspect failed runs.
- Retrieve configuration.
- View metrics.
- Open artifact references.
- Download authorized reports.

## 20.4 Immutable experiment records

Do not overwrite an earlier run when retraining the same model family.

Every new experiment must have a unique run identity.

## 20.5 Model selection history

Record why a particular model candidate was selected.

Include:

- Selection metric.
- Competing models.
- Validation scores.
- Calibration results.
- Operational constraints.
- Approver where required.

---

# PART 21 — TASK 18: MODEL ARTIFACT MANAGEMENT

Save model artifacts and all information required to reproduce them.

## 21.1 Artifact contents

Each completed training run should store:

- Trained model.
- Preprocessing pipeline.
- Feature schema.
- Target schema.
- Model configuration.
- Hyperparameters.
- Training metrics.
- Validation metrics.
- Threshold configuration.
- Calibration artifact, if used.
- Feature importance.
- Dataset manifest reference.
- Dependency manifest.
- Artifact checksums.

## 21.2 Native model formats

Use appropriate native formats.

Examples:

- Scikit-learn estimators using a controlled and pinned serialization approach.
- XGBoost native JSON or UBJ.
- LightGBM native model text format.

Do not rely on a single generic pickle format for every model family if native formats are more appropriate.

## 21.3 Preprocessing consistency

The saved artifact must include the exact fitted preprocessing pipeline used during inference.

A model must not be distributed separately from the preprocessing rules required to reproduce its inputs.

## 21.4 Feature schema enforcement

Before prediction by the model artifact in a later phase, the input schema must match the recorded schema.

Include:

- Required features.
- Feature order.
- Data types.
- Missing-value rules.
- Unknown-category rules.
- Feature versions.

## 21.5 Artifact validation

After saving:

1. Verify artifact existence.
2. Verify checksum.
3. Reload the model.
4. Reload preprocessing.
5. Run test predictions using a controlled sample.
6. Verify output dimensions.
7. Verify probability range.
8. Verify expected feature schema.
9. Compare reload predictions with in-memory predictions.

## 21.6 Artifact security

- Restrict downloads.
- Validate artifact references.
- Do not load untrusted model files.
- Record artifact provenance.
- Preserve version history.

## 21.7 Publication status

Use statuses such as:

- TRAINING.
- VALIDATING.
- CANDIDATE.
- FINAL_TESTED.
- FAILED.
- BLOCKED.
- ARCHIVED.

Do not label an artifact production-ready merely because it passed local training tests.

Reuse suitable experiment, dataset and artifact tables.

Implement:

# PART 23 — TASK 20: BACKEND MODEL TRAINING ENGINE

Implement modular backend services consistent with the existing architecture.

Suggested logical responsibilities:

**ModelDatasetLoader**

- Load approved Phase 11 artifacts.
- Verify manifests and checksums.
- Validate schemas.

**ModelPreprocessor**

- Fit transformations on training data.
- Reuse fitted transformations.
- Enforce feature order.

**LogisticRegressionTrainer**

- Train and save the baseline model.

**RandomForestTrainer**

- Train and save the forest.

**XGBoostTrainer**

- Train and save the boosted-tree model.

**LightGBMTrainer**

- Train the optional model when enabled.

**HyperparameterSearchService**

- Execute bounded model-specific searches.

**ModelValidationService**

- Calculate validation metrics.

**ModelCalibrationService**

- Fit approved calibrators.

**ThresholdOptimizationService**

- Select validation-based decision thresholds.

**ModelComparisonService**

- Generate the model leaderboard.

**FeatureImportanceService**

- Generate model-specific importance results.

**ModelArtifactService**

- Save and verify trained artifacts.

**ExperimentTrackingService**

- Maintain immutable training run history.

**ModelReportService**

- Generate the complete model training report.

Do not create separate independent pipelines for each model family when they can safely use shared services.

Each trainer must still preserve the model-specific requirements.

# PART 24 — TASK 21: BACKEND API IMPLEMENTATION

Extend the existing backend API architecture.

All endpoints must use current authentication and authorization.

## 24.1 Model configuration APIs

Support:

- List model families.

## 27.6 Probability correctness

- Output row counts match input observations.

- Prediction output schema is documented.

## 27.7 Reload consistency

Compare predictions before and after model artifact reload.

Use justified numerical tolerances.

## 27.8 Training reproducibility

Repeat selected experiments using identical configuration and random seed.

Measure whether results are reproducible within the documented tolerance.

Where a library, GPU kernel or parallel operation is not deterministic, record the limitation and avoid claiming exact reproducibility.

# PART 28 — TASK 25: TEMPORAL LEAKAGE AND TEST-ISOLATION VERIFICATION

This is mandatory.

## 28.1 Test-label mutation test

1. Train candidate models using the approved training and validation data.
2. Record the model configuration and selected candidate.
3. Change only test labels in an isolated test fixture.
4. Re-run model selection.
5. Verify that the selected model, hyperparameters and preprocessing artifacts do not change.

The final test metric itself should change in response to changed test labels, proving that evaluation is reading the test targets.

But model selection must remain unaffected.

## 28.2 Test-feature isolation test

Modify test feature values.

Verify that the modification does not affect:

- Preprocessing fit parameters.
- Feature selection.
- Hyperparameter selection.
- Training model parameters.

## 28.3 Training-only imputation test

Mutate validation and test missing values.

Verify that fitted training imputation parameters remain unchanged.

## 28.4 Training-only scaling test

Mutate the validation and test distributions.

Verify the training scaler parameters remain unchanged.

## 28.5 Threshold isolation test

Modify test outcomes.

Verify that the selected threshold remains unchanged.

## 28.6 Calibration isolation test

Modify test outcomes.

Verify that the calibration artifact remains unchanged.

## 28.7 Future-feature mutation test

Use the same principle as Phase 11.

Introduce future business records after a prediction cutoff and verify that the historical features and resulting training input do not change.

## 28.8 Dataset provenance test

Verify that all model inputs link back to the approved Phase 11 dataset version and source lineage.

## 28.9 Repeated customer isolation

Verify behavior separately for:

- Forward-temporal evaluation.
- Strict entity-disjoint evaluation.

Report customer overlap correctly.

Do not silently claim all test customers are unseen when the evaluation mode allows historical customers to recur.

# PART 33 — PHASE 12 IMPLEMENTATION ORDER AND GATES

Follow the steps in order.

## STAGE 1 — Phase 1–11 compatibility audit

Inspect the repository, test reports, dataset manifests and available artifacts.

Verify the actual training datasets.

**Gate 1:** Approved training, validation and test datasets are identified.

## STAGE 2 — Model training specification

Define:

- Prediction target.
- Entity scope.
- Prediction horizon.
- Dataset version.
- Primary metric.
- Model families.
- Search budget.
- Reproducibility configuration.

**Gate 2:** Model training configuration is valid.

## STAGE 3 — Data loading and integrity

Implement:

- Dataset loading.
- Checksum verification.
- Feature validation.
- Target validation.
- Split isolation.

**Gate 3:** All partitions load without schema or integrity errors.

## STAGE 4 — Preprocessing

Implement model-specific pipelines.

**Gate 4:** Training-only preprocessing is verified.

## STAGE 5 — Baseline training

Train Logistic Regression.

**Gate 5:** Baseline training and validation metrics are verified.

## STAGE 6 — Ensemble model training

Train Random Forest.

Train XGBoost.

Train LightGBM if compatible.

**Gate 6:** Each enabled model has a valid trained artifact and recorded validation metrics.

## STAGE 7 — Hyperparameter optimization

Execute bounded, reproducible temporal-safe searches.

**Gate 7:** Search history and selected configurations are preserved.

## STAGE 8 — Evaluation and calibration

Calculate classification, ranking and calibration metrics.

**Gate 8:** All model comparisons use consistent validation data and verified metric calculations.

## STAGE 9 — Threshold selection

Select thresholds using permitted validation data and documented objectives.

**Gate 9:** Thresholds and business assumptions are versioned.

## STAGE 10 — Model comparison

Produce the validation leaderboard.

**Gate 10:** A model candidate is selected using the predefined validation objective.

## STAGE 11 — Final model and test evaluation

Freeze the selected candidate.

Optionally refit on permitted training plus validation data.

Evaluate the final model on the untouched test set once.

**Gate 11:** Final test evaluation is complete and its evidence is stored.

## STAGE 12 — Model artifacts and reports

Save and reload the model, preprocessing, metadata and evaluation results.

**Gate 12:** All published artifacts pass integrity and prediction consistency tests.

## STAGE 13 — Frontend and API

Complete the actual Model Training workspace.

**Gate 13:** All advertised workflows work through backend operations.

## STAGE 14 — Full verification

Run all model, statistical, temporal, artifact, API, UI, performance and regression tests.

**Gate 14:** Final engineering report is produced.

Do not skip failed gates.

# PART 36 — NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES

1. Never train on unapproved raw data.
2. Never ignore Phase 11 dataset manifests.
3. Never replace chronological splitting with random splitting.
4. Never train on unresolved labels.
5. Never use future customer features.
6. Never fit preprocessing on validation or test data.
7. Never use test data for hyperparameter selection.
8. Never use test data for early stopping.
9. Never optimize thresholds on test labels.
10. Never fit a calibrator using test labels.
11. Never resample validation or test data.
12. Never calculate class weights using validation or test labels.
13. Never compare models on different evaluation populations without disclosure.
14. Never use accuracy as the only selection metric.
15. Never ignore the effect of class imbalance on probability calibration.
16. Never report uncalibrated scores as guaranteed churn probabilities.
17. Never fabricate training results.
18. Never fabricate accuracy.
19. Never invent feature importance values.
20. Never claim GPU support without verified hardware execution.
21. Never report optional LightGBM as implemented when it is not verified.
22. Never interpret feature importance as causality.
23. Never use the test set repeatedly to improve the model.
24. Never hide failed model runs.
25. Never overwrite old model artifacts.
26. Never claim the model is production-ready just because training succeeded.
27. Never claim predictive performance on real companies using synthetic-only data.
28. Never break Phases 1–11.
29. Never automatically implement production deployment.
30. Never start Phase 13 automatically.

---

# PART 37 — FINAL EXECUTION COMMAND

Begin by inspecting the complete existing repository and verifying all Phase 1–11 outputs.

Identify the exact approved Phase 11 dataset version to use.

Inspect its training, validation and test manifests, target schema, feature schema, leakage audit, maturity status and checksums.

Do not train on an arbitrary CSV.

Do not build a new dataset if the approved Phase 11 version already exists.

First verify the data, feature types, class distributions and training readiness.

Implement a reproducible Model Training Engine.

## The critical model evaluation rule

## Correct evaluation sequence

1. Training dataset

   Fit Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and optional LightGBM. Fit preprocessing transformations here.
2. Validation dataset

   Compare models, tune hyperparameters, select the calibration method and choose the decision threshold.
3. Freeze the selected candidate

   Lock model configuration, preprocessing, calibration and threshold.
4. Test dataset

   Perform the final independent evaluation. Do not use test results to improve the model and still describe that same test as untouched.

Important: Do not select the winner based only on accuracy. For an imbalanced churn dataset, validation Average Precision is a sensible default primary selection metric, supported by recall, precision, calibration and business intervention capacity.

The implementation should also use proper preprocessing pipelines so that fitted transformations cannot learn from held-out data. The official scikit-learn documentation explains this leakage-prevention role of pipelines and column transformers.&#x20;

# Phase 13 — Model Evaluation & Financial Impact Analysis



Model verification and business evaluation

Step 13 of 20



Phase 13 builds directly on Phase 12's trained Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and optional LightGBM models.

Its purpose is not simply to calculate accuracy. It must establish whether the selected model reliably identifies customers at risk of churn, produces trustworthy probabilities, performs consistently across different customer populations, and offers a measurable potential financial benefit.

This phase introduces an especially important distinction: predicting churn correctly and proving that a retention intervention saves money are two different things. The financial evaluation must therefore use transparent, configurable assumptions and must never present hypothetical intervention savings as actual achieved revenue.

## 3.1 Main evaluation workflow

`Phase 12 Model Artifacts → Artifact Verification → Phase 11 Dataset Verification → Predictions → Classification Metrics → Ranking Metrics → Calibration → Threshold Analysis → Financial Cost Analysis → Cohort and Segment Evaluation → Stability Analysis → Model Comparison → Evaluation Report`

## 3.2 Separate evaluation layers

Maintain four separate analytical layers:

**Layer A — Model prediction quality**

Measures how effectively the model identifies future churn.

**Layer B — Probability quality**

Measures whether predicted churn probabilities reflect observed event frequencies.

**Layer C — Decision quality**

Measures the consequences of choosing different risk thresholds and intervention policies.

**Layer D — Financial assessment**

Estimates potential costs and benefits using documented economic inputs.

Do not collapse all four into one arbitrary model score.

# PART 6 — TASK 3: IMPLEMENT THE CONFUSION MATRIX ENGINE

Generate a mathematically correct confusion matrix for binary churn classification.

Use:

- Positive class: churn.
- Negative class: no qualifying churn.

At a selected threshold:

- True Positive (TP): Actual churn and predicted churn.
- False Positive (FP): Actual non-churn and predicted churn.
- True Negative (TN): Actual non-churn and predicted non-churn.
- False Negative (FN): Actual churn and predicted non-churn.

## 6.1 Required output

Return:

- TP.
- FP.
- TN.
- FN.
- Total observations.
- Correct predictions.
- Incorrect predictions.
- Classification threshold.

## 6.2 Matrix visualization

Create an interactive confusion matrix.

Each cell should support:

- Count.
- Percentage.
- Row percentage.
- Column percentage.
- Click-through to authorized aggregate diagnostics.

Do not expose sensitive customer records to unauthorized users.

## 6.3 Matrix consistency

Verify:

`Total = TP + FP + TN + FN`

Confirm all metric denominators are consistent with the same evaluated observation population.

## 6.4 Threshold dependence

Explain that the confusion matrix changes when the threshold changes.

Do not display a confusion matrix without stating its threshold.

---

# PART 7 — TASK 4: CALCULATE PRECISION

Implement standard positive-class precision.

`Precision = TP / (TP + FP)`

Precision answers:

Of the customers predicted to churn, what proportion actually experienced qualifying churn?

## 7.1 Required outputs

Calculate:

- Precision.
- TP.
- FP.
- Predicted positive count.
- Threshold.

## 7.2 Edge cases

If the model predicts no positive customers:

- Do not divide by zero.
- Return an explicitly undefined or conventionally zero metric with its zero-division policy documented.
- Flag the absence of predicted positive cases.

## 7.3 Interpretation

Higher precision generally means fewer non-churning customers are incorrectly flagged.

However, it does not automatically mean higher retention value.

A model with high precision but very low recall may miss many customers who eventually churn.

---

# PART 8 — TASK 5: CALCULATE RECALL

Implement:

`Recall = TP / (TP + FN)`

Recall answers:

Of all customers who actually churned, what proportion did the model identify?

## 8.1 Required outputs

Calculate:

- Recall.
- TP.
- FN.
- Actual positive count.
- Threshold.

## 8.2 Edge cases

If there are no actual positive observations:

- Do not silently report a meaningful recall estimate.
- Report it as undefined for that evaluation population.
- Flag the insufficient positive-event sample.

## 8.3 Interpretation

Higher recall means fewer actual churn events were missed.

A high-recall model can still be operationally expensive if it flags too many non-churning customers.

---

# PART 9 — TASK 6: CALCULATE F1 SCORE AND ADDITIONAL CLASSIFICATION METRICS

## 9.1 F1 score

Calculate:

`F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall)`

When precision and recall are both zero, handle the result using a documented zero-division policy.

## 9.2 Additional mandatory metrics

Calculate:

- Accuracy.
- Specificity.
- Balanced accuracy.
- F-beta score where configured.
- Matthews correlation coefficient.
- Negative predictive value.
- False positive rate.
- False negative rate.
- Positive prediction rate.
- Actual churn prevalence.
- Predicted churn prevalence.

## 9.3 Formula validation

Use independently tested metric utilities.

Verify each metric against known confusion matrix examples.

## 9.4 Class imbalance warning

Accuracy must not be the sole assessment metric.

A model could classify almost everyone as non-churning and achieve high accuracy while missing most actual churn events.

Display class prevalence next to accuracy.

## 9.5 F-beta

Allow F-beta to be calculated for alternative precision/recall trade-offs.

Use the configured beta value.

Explain that:

- Beta greater than 1 emphasizes recall.
- Beta less than 1 emphasizes precision.
- Beta equal to 1 gives the standard F1 score.

Do not select beta solely to create a more impressive reported number.

---

# PART 10 — TASK 7: IMPLEMENT ROC-AUC

Calculate the Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve.

## 10.1 ROC curve

Use predicted probabilities or continuous prediction scores.

For different score thresholds, calculate:

- True positive rate.
- False positive rate.

Plot:

- False positive rate on the X-axis.
- True positive rate on the Y-axis.
- Random-ranking reference line.
- Model ROC curve.

## 10.2 ROC-AUC

Calculate ROC-AUC using a validated statistical library or a verified internal implementation.

Check numerical results against known examples.

## 10.3 Interpretation

Explain that ROC-AUC measures the model's ranking ability across thresholds.

It does not directly specify:

- The selected operating threshold.
- The number of customers contacted.
- Financial costs.
- Probability calibration.
- Business value.

## 10.4 Edge cases

If the evaluated population contains only one actual class:

- ROC-AUC is not defined.
- Do not fabricate a value.
- Display a clear diagnostic.

## 10.5 ROC comparison

Compare the trained models on the same evaluation population.

Use consistent positive-class and sample definitions.

---

# PART 11 — TASK 8: IMPLEMENT PRECISION–RECALL CURVE AND PR-AUC

This is a major evaluation requirement for imbalanced churn data.

## 11.1 Precision–recall curve

Calculate precision and recall across prediction thresholds.

Display:

- Precision.
- Recall.
- Thresholds.
- Baseline prevalence.

## 11.2 Average Precision

Calculate Average Precision as a ranking metric.

Document the implementation and formula.

Do not incorrectly assume all implementations of the term PR-AUC use the same numerical integration method.

## 11.3 PR-AUC terminology

When using the non-interpolated Average Precision metric, label it:

`Average Precision (AP)`

When using a numerical area integral over the precision–recall curve, label the method and interpolation convention explicitly.

Do not mix these results under one ambiguous label.

## 11.4 Baseline

Show the positive-class prevalence as the no-skill reference level for the precision–recall analysis.

## 11.5 Model comparison

Compare:

- Logistic Regression.
- Random Forest.
- XGBoost.
- LightGBM where trained.

Use the same evaluation observations.

## 11.6 Business interpretation

PR-AUC can be more informative than ROC-AUC when the churn class is substantially imbalanced.

However, it does not directly calculate intervention cost or the financial benefit of retention campaigns.

---

# PART 12 — TASK 9: PROBABILITY CALIBRATION EVALUATION

A churn prediction model must not merely rank customers. Its probability estimates should also be trustworthy.

## 12.1 Purpose

Calibration asks whether customers assigned a predicted probability have an approximately corresponding observed event frequency over the evaluated population.

For example, among observations receiving approximately 0.70 predicted churn risk, a well-calibrated model should experience a churn frequency reasonably close to 70%, subject to sample uncertainty and the evaluation definition.

## 12.2 Reliability diagram

Create a probability reliability diagram.

Display:

- Predicted probability bins.
- Mean predicted probability.
- Observed positive-event frequency.
- Sample count per bin.
- Confidence interval where suitable.
- Perfect-calibration reference line.

## 12.3 Calibration bins

Support configurable:

- Uniform-width bins.
- Quantile-based bins.

Select the appropriate binning method for the dataset size and distribution.

Do not use extremely small bins that produce unstable observed rates.

## 12.4 Brier score

Calculate:

`Brier Score = Mean((predicted_probability - actual_label)^2)`

Lower values indicate better probability accuracy for the evaluated binary outcome.

Interpret the score alongside outcome prevalence.

## 12.5 Log loss

Calculate binary logarithmic loss.

Ensure numerical stability when predictions approach 0 or 1.

Document clipping behavior if the chosen implementation requires it.

## 12.6 Expected Calibration Error

Optionally calculate Expected Calibration Error.

Document:

- Binning method.
- Number of bins.
- Weighting.
- Sample counts.

Do not present ECE as a universally sufficient calibration measure. It can depend significantly on binning choices.

## 12.7 Calibration slope and intercept

Where statistically appropriate, estimate calibration slope and intercept.

Interpret them carefully.

Do not report them as reliable when sample size or class representation is insufficient.

## 12.8 Calibration comparison

Compare:

- Original probabilities.
- Sigmoid-calibrated probabilities.
- Isotonic-calibrated probabilities, where supported.

Use only calibrators legitimately fitted in Phase 12 or another approved training/validation-only procedure.

Do not fit or select calibrators using test labels.

## 12.9 Calibration uncertainty

Show:

- Evaluation sample size.
- Positive count.
- Negative count.
- Bin sizes.
- Confidence information.
- Dataset observation period.

## 12.10 Calibration output

For every model, report:

- Brier score.
- Log loss.
- Calibration method.
- Reliability diagram.
- ECE if supported.
- Calibration sample size.
- Known limitations.

# PART 14 — TASK 11: CUSTOMER RISK RANKING AND LIFT ANALYSIS

A retention team may only be able to contact a limited fraction of customers.

Evaluate the model's ability to rank customers by predicted risk.

## 11.1 Risk ranking

Sort evaluation observations using predicted churn probabilities in descending order.

Do not expose personal information in aggregate ranking outputs.

## 11.2 Population bands

Calculate performance at configurable top-risk groups, such as:

- Top 1%.
- Top 5%.
- Top 10%.
- Top 15%.
- Top 20%.
- Top 25%.

## 11.3 Required metrics

For each group calculate:

- Contacted population.
- Actual churn events captured.
- Precision within the group.
- Recall of total churn events captured.
- Churn prevalence.
- Lift over baseline prevalence.

## 11.4 Lift

Calculate:

`Lift = Precision in selected risk group / Overall churn prevalence`

Handle zero baseline prevalence without division errors.

## 11.5 Cumulative gains

Calculate the percentage of all actual churn events captured as a function of the population contacted.

## 11.6 Capacity analysis

Provide a curve showing:

- Percentage of customers contacted.
- Percentage of churn events captured.
- Expected campaign expenditure under configured costs.

This helps determine whether a model is useful for constrained intervention capacity.

## 11.7 Repeated customer observations

If the evaluation population contains multiple snapshots of the same customer:

- Preserve the observation-level metric.
- Report unique customer counts.
- Avoid presenting repeated snapshots as distinct customers.
- Provide a customer-level summary when the business intervention is customer-based.

---

# PART 15 — TASK 12: FINANCIAL COST MODELING ARCHITECTURE

Implement a proper financial decision analysis engine.

This is one of the most important parts of Phase 13.

Do not limit financial evaluation to a simple confusion matrix.

The system must estimate the financial consequences of:

- Correctly identifying an at-risk customer.
- Incorrectly targeting a customer who would not churn.
- Missing a customer who eventually churns.
- Correctly leaving a stable customer without intervention.
- Selecting different intervention thresholds.
- Running retention campaigns at different capacities.

However, predictions alone cannot prove that an intervention prevents churn.

Separate three concepts:

1. **Observed predictive outcome:** Whether the customer actually churned in the evaluation dataset.
2. **Financial exposure:** The economic value potentially at risk if the customer churns.
3. **Intervention effectiveness:** The proportion of that risk a retention action may actually prevent, which requires causal evidence or an explicitly labelled scenario assumption.

Never present hypothetical treatment effectiveness as experimentally proven.

---

# PART 16 — TASK 13: CREATE THE FINANCIAL INPUT CONFIGURATION

Create a versioned Financial Evaluation Scenario.

Do not hardcode economic assumptions throughout the application.

## 16.1 Required financial parameters

Support:

**Customer economics**

- Monthly recurring revenue (MRR).
- Annual recurring revenue (ARR), when relevant.
- Average revenue per customer.
- Contribution margin.
- Variable service cost.
- Expected relationship duration.
- Historical customer value.
- Discount rate.
- Currency.

**Retention costs**

- Cost per customer contact.
- Cost per retention call.
- Cost per email or campaign message, if applicable.
- Discount amount.
- Promotional offer cost.
- Retention service cost.
- Account management effort.
- Campaign operating cost.

**Churn exposure**

- Expected contribution margin lost.
- Defined financial exposure horizon.
- Remaining contractual value where relevant.
- Expected replacement acquisition cost where supported.
- Expected recovery or collection amounts where applicable.

**Intervention assumptions**

- Assumed intervention effectiveness.
- Expected retention uplift.
- Probability that a customer accepts the retention offer.
- Offer cost when accepted.
- Expected incremental retained duration.
- Incremental operating cost.

Every parameter must identify its source or provenance.

## 16.2 Financial assumption types

Classify each input as:

- ACTUAL_RECORDED_COST.
- ACTUAL_RECORDED_REVENUE.
- VERIFIED_ACCOUNTING_VALUE.
- HISTORICAL_ESTIMATE.
- BUSINESS_PROVIDED_ASSUMPTION.
- SCENARIO_ASSUMPTION.
- UNKNOWN.

Do not present scenario assumptions as actual financial records.

## 16.3 Financial scenario metadata

Store:

- Scenario ID.
- Scenario name.
- Scenario version.
- Currency.
- Financial period.
- Contribution margin methodology.
- Discount rate.
- Intervention assumptions.
- Source references.
- Author.
- Approval status.
- Creation timestamp.

## 16.4 Currency handling

Preserve source currencies.

If a calculation requires conversion:

- Use an approved exchange-rate source.
- Store the exchange-rate date.
- Store the exchange-rate version.
- Preserve original amount and currency.
- Preserve converted amount and reporting currency.

Never combine INR, USD, EUR or other currencies without documented conversion.

Where reliable exchange-rate information is unavailable, report separate currency totals.

## 16.5 Financial precision

Use appropriate decimal precision for financial calculations.

Use Decimal-based calculations for monetary quantities.

Do not perform financial accounting calculations using uncontrolled binary floating-point rounding.

---

# PART 17 — TASK 14: CREATE THE CLASSIFICATION COST MATRIX

Build a configurable classification cost matrix.

Use the actual churn outcome and the model's selected classification decision.

## 17.1 Cost categories

Define four cells:

- True Positive cost.
- False Positive cost.
- True Negative cost.
- False Negative cost.

## 17.2 True Positive

A customer is predicted to churn and the customer actually experiences qualifying churn.

Potential costs may include:

- Retention campaign cost.
- Contact cost.
- Retention offer cost.
- Residual churn-related economic exposure.

Do not assume that a true-positive prediction means the intervention successfully prevented churn.

The historical label generally describes observed churn under the historical treatment conditions.

## 17.3 False Positive

A customer is predicted to churn but does not experience qualifying churn.

Potential costs may include:

- Unnecessary contact cost.
- Campaign operating cost.
- Discount or offer expense.
- Sales or retention team capacity consumption.
- Customer annoyance or relationship friction where measurable.

Do not assume the entire customer's revenue was lost.

## 17.4 True Negative

A customer is predicted not to churn and does not churn.

Potential baseline costs may include:

- Ordinary monitoring.
- Routine customer servicing.
- Standard operating expenditure.

Only include incremental model-related costs if they are supported.

## 17.5 False Negative

A customer is predicted not to churn but actually churns.

Potential economic consequences may include:

- Avoidable contribution margin exposure.
- Expected lost customer value.
- Replacement acquisition cost where relevant.
- Contractual or service-related loss where verified.

Do not automatically equate missed churn with lost gross revenue.

## 17.6 Configurable cell costs

Store configurable costs for each cell:

- C_TP.
- C_FP.
- C_TN.
- C_FN.

The system must show the composition of each value.

## 17.7 Total estimated classification cost

Calculate:

`Total classification cost = TP × C_TP + FP × C_FP + TN × C_TN + FN × C_FN`

The calculation must use the same:

- Evaluation population.
- Threshold.
- Financial scenario.
- Currency.
- Cost policy.

## 17.8 Baseline comparison

Compare the model policy against configurable baseline policies:

- No proactive intervention.
- Contact everyone.
- Contact no one.
- Contact a fixed percentage.
- Use a simple baseline rule.
- Use a historical approved risk policy.

Clearly define each baseline.

Do not claim a financial improvement without calculating the same scenario for the baseline and model-driven policy.

## 17.9 Cost interpretation

Label these results as estimated scenario costs unless they originate from actual recorded intervention and accounting data.

---

# PART 18 — TASK 15: ESTIMATE CUSTOMER CONTRIBUTION MARGIN AT RISK

Build a more realistic financial exposure model.

## 18.1 Revenue versus contribution margin

Distinguish:

- Gross revenue.
- Net revenue.
- Recurring revenue.
- Variable service cost.
- Contribution margin.
- Customer lifetime value.

Do not describe gross MRR as profit.

## 18.2 Customer contribution margin

Where sufficient information exists:

`Contribution margin = Net revenue - Relevant variable service costs`

Use the company's approved accounting definition where available.

If only revenue is available:

- Report revenue exposure.
- Label it revenue, not profit or contribution margin.
- Mark the contribution margin estimate unavailable.

## 18.3 Contribution margin horizon

Allow a configurable evaluation horizon, such as:

- 30 days.
- 60 days.
- 90 days.
- 180 days.
- 365 days.
- Custom period.

Do not automatically multiply one month's revenue by an arbitrary number of months without checking customer contract, retention assumptions and payment behavior.

## 18.4 Expected contribution margin at risk

For an entity with an estimated churn probability p and an approved forecast of contribution margin exposure M:

`Expected contribution margin at risk = p × M`

This is a forecasted economic exposure, not an amount already lost.

## 18.5 Discounting

Where the exposure horizon is longer than the immediate period, support discounted expected contribution margin.

Use the approved discounting convention and record:

- Discount rate.
- Time unit.
- Cash-flow timing.
- Forecast horizon.

## 18.6 Customer-level exposure

Where actual financial data exists, calculate the estimated contribution margin at risk for an individual customer.

Restrict access to authorized users.

## 18.7 Aggregate exposure

Calculate:

- Total expected revenue exposure.
- Total expected contribution margin at risk.
- Average exposure per customer.
- Exposure among the highest-risk group.
- Exposure by acquisition cohort.
- Exposure by customer segment.
- Exposure by subscription plan.

Do not count the same financial relationship twice because a customer has multiple subscription rows.

---

# PART 19 — TASK 16: MODEL RETENTION INTERVENTION ECONOMICS

Build an intervention scenario engine.

This must be clearly separated from ordinary predictive metrics.

## 19.1 The core decision

For each customer, compare:

**Option A — No proactive intervention**

The model provides an estimated probability of churn.

The business incurs the expected economic exposure associated with that probability under the approved scenario.

**Option B — Retention intervention**

The business incurs an intervention cost and may reduce the customer's probability of churn.

The amount of reduction is an intervention-effectiveness assumption that requires independent evidence.

## 19.2 Define intervention effectiveness

Possible sources:

- Randomized controlled experiment.
- Valid quasi-experimental analysis.
- Approved historical retention experiment.
- Business-provided scenario assumption.

If no credible estimate exists:

- Do not claim proven intervention effectiveness.
- Allow a scenario sensitivity input.
- Label all results hypothetical.
- Mark intervention impact as unverified.

## 19.3 Illustrative mathematical structure

For an estimated churn probability p:

- M = Forecast contribution margin exposed over the approved horizon.
- e = Assumed relative reduction in churn probability from the intervention.
- C = Total intervention cost.

Estimated expected economic benefit:

`Expected benefit = p × e × M - C`

This is a scenario calculation, not proof that the intervention caused the benefit.

## 19.4 Expected decision cost

No-intervention scenario:

`Expected cost_no_action = p × M`

Intervention scenario under the assumed relative risk reduction:

`Expected cost_intervention = C + p × (1 - e) × M`

The intervention becomes economically attractive under these simplified assumptions when:

`p × e × M > C`

If M and C are fixed and e is positive:

`Break-even churn probability = C / (e × M)`

Use this only when the stated assumptions are valid.

If the break-even probability exceeds 1, the intervention cannot break even under the specified scenario.

## 19.5 Variable intervention costs

Allow intervention cost to depend on:

- Customer segment.
- Account size.
- Retention channel.
- Offer type.
- Customer plan.
- Required staff effort.
- Discount amount.

Calculate customer-specific expected economics where supporting data exists.

## 19.6 Retention offers

Distinguish:

- Offer offered.
- Offer accepted.
- Offer redeemed.
- Incremental discount actually applied.
- Customer retained.
- Actual contribution margin after discount.

Do not treat the nominal value of a promotional offer as the same as its actual economic cost without documenting the calculation.

## 19.7 Customer contact policy

Support scenario analysis for:

- No intervention.
- Contact customers above a risk threshold.
- Contact top 5%.
- Contact top 10%.
- Contact top 20%.
- Contact within a fixed team capacity.
- Contact only when expected net benefit is positive.

## 19.8 Output

For each policy, calculate:

- Customers targeted.
- Total intervention expenditure.
- Expected churn events before intervention.
- Scenario-adjusted expected churn events.
- Expected retained customers under assumptions.
- Estimated contribution margin preserved.
- Expected net benefit.
- Return on intervention spending where defined.
- Break-even requirements.

Clearly label estimated retained customers and retained value as scenario outputs.

Do not call these actual saved customers.

---

# PART 20 — TASK 17: FINANCIAL COST SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS

Financial inputs are uncertain.

A single assumed intervention effect or contribution margin should not produce a false sense of certainty.

## 20.1 Scenario types

Support:

**Conservative scenario**

- Lower assumed intervention effectiveness.
- Higher intervention cost.
- Lower contribution margin.
- Shorter retention horizon.

**Base scenario**

- Approved central business assumptions.

**Optimistic scenario**

- Higher assumed intervention effectiveness.
- Lower intervention cost.
- Higher contribution margin.

All three must be configurable.

## 20.2 Sensitivity ranges

Allow sensitivity testing for:

- Intervention effectiveness.
- Cost per contact.
- Retention discount.
- Contribution margin.
- Churn forecast horizon.
- Expected retained duration.
- Customer acquisition replacement cost.

## 20.3 Sensitivity output

Display:

- Expected net benefit.
- Estimated total cost.
- Break-even threshold.
- Expected retained value.
- Intervention volume.

Show which scenarios become financially unattractive.

## 20.4 Assumption uncertainty

Show:

- Source of each parameter.
- Confidence or evidence classification.
- Approval status.
- Scenario range.

Do not treat a broad sensitivity range as a statistical confidence interval.

## 20.5 No fabricated economics

If financial inputs are unavailable:

- Report predictive metrics normally.
- Display financial results as NOT AVAILABLE.
- Provide an optional scenario-configuration workflow.
- Do not substitute arbitrary INR values.
- Do not manufacture actual return on investment.

---

# PART 21 — TASK 18: THRESHOLD-BASED FINANCIAL COST OPTIMIZATION

Create a financial threshold analysis engine.

## 21.1 Purpose

Identify how the predicted churn probability threshold changes:

- Customers selected.
- Churn customers captured.
- False positive contacts.
- False negative missed customers.
- Campaign expenditure.
- Estimated financial exposure.
- Expected scenario net benefit.

## 21.2 Threshold evaluation

For each validation-selected threshold, calculate the classification and financial outcomes.

Do not optimize using test labels.

## 21.3 Cost curves

Generate:

- Total estimated cost versus threshold.
- False negative cost versus threshold.
- False positive cost versus threshold.
- Intervention expense versus threshold.
- Expected net benefit versus threshold.

## 21.4 Capacity-constrained decision

Identify thresholds satisfying a configured intervention capacity.

For example:

- 100 customers per week.
- 500 customers per month.
- 10% of the eligible customer base.

These are configurable examples, not hardcoded assumptions.

## 21.5 Optimal policy

A threshold can be reported as scenario-optimal only under its defined assumptions.

Store:

- Financial scenario ID.
- Cost matrix version.
- Intervention assumptions.
- Threshold.
- Dataset version.
- Evaluation period.

## 21.6 Decision comparison

Compare:

- Default 0.50 threshold.
- Phase 12 selected threshold.
- Financial break-even threshold.
- Capacity-constrained threshold.

Do not assume all four should be identical.

# PART 22 — TASK 19: MODEL PERFORMANCE ACROSS COHORTS AND CUSTOMER SEGMENTS

Integrate Phase 9.

## 22.1 Acquisition cohorts

Evaluate:

- Historical acquisition cohorts.
- Monthly cohorts.
- Quarterly cohorts.
- Earlier versus later cohorts.

Preserve exact cohort membership.

## 22.2 Customer segments

Evaluate where supported:

- Customer size.
- Business category.
- Acquisition channel.
- Plan.
- Contract type.
- Billing frequency.
- Engagement group.

Use approved, historically available attributes.

## 22.3 Segment metrics

For each group:

- Sample count.
- Distinct customer count.
- Positive count.
- Negative count.
- Churn prevalence.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- PR-AUC.
- ROC-AUC.
- Brier score.
- Calibration status.
- Threshold.
- Expected financial exposure where available.

## 22.4 Financial segment analysis

Calculate:

- Contribution margin exposure by segment.
- Expected intervention volume.
- Estimated campaign cost.
- Expected net benefit under each scenario.

## 22.5 Small samples

When a group has too few positive or negative examples:

- Mark metrics unreliable or unavailable.
- Display sample size.
- Avoid confident rankings.
- Do not merge unrelated segments solely to produce attractive charts.

## 22.6 Group performance differences

Evaluate disparities in:

- Recall.
- Precision.
- False positive rate.
- Calibration.
- Prediction rate.
- Financial intervention exposure.

Do not infer sensitive personal attributes.

Do not make automatic adverse customer decisions based solely on model scores.

# PART 23 — TASK 20: TEMPORAL MODEL STABILITY AND DRIFT EVALUATION

A model with strong historical metrics can become less reliable over time.

Create a temporal stability assessment.

## 23.1 Monthly evaluation windows

Where data permits, calculate performance by:

- Month.
- Quarter.
- Rolling 30-day window.
- Rolling 90-day window.

Preserve target maturity requirements for each historical evaluation window.

## 23.2 Required metrics per window

Report:

- Sample size.
- Positive count.
- Negative count.
- Churn prevalence.
- PR-AUC.
- ROC-AUC.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- Brier score.
- Calibration error.
- Expected financial exposure.

## 23.3 Performance drift

Detect:

- Declining recall.
- Declining precision.
- PR-AUC deterioration.
- ROC-AUC changes.
- Calibration deterioration.
- Increasing false-positive rate.
- Increasing false-negative rate.

## 23.4 Feature distribution drift

Where historical feature snapshots are available, evaluate changes in feature distributions.

Use suitable diagnostic measures.

Do not claim concept drift solely because feature distributions change.

## 23.5 Prediction distribution drift

Monitor:

- Average predicted probability.
- Median predicted probability.
- Risk-score distribution.
- High-risk customer proportion.
- Threshold crossing volume.

## 23.6 Calibration drift

Evaluate whether the relationship between predicted and actual churn changes over time.

## 23.7 Cohort versus calendar-time differences

Distinguish acquisition-cohort differences from calendar-time model performance drift.

Do not confuse these separate dimensions.

## 23.8 Drift report

For each detected issue, provide:

- Metric.
- Baseline period.
- Comparison period.
- Magnitude.
- Sample size.
- Severity.
- Evidence.
- Recommended review.

Do not automatically retrain the model.

Retraining belongs to an explicitly authorized later workflow.

# PART 24 — TASK 21: UNCERTAINTY AND STATISTICAL CONFIDENCE

Point estimates can be misleading, especially when positive churn examples are limited.

Implement uncertainty analysis.

## 24.1 Metric confidence intervals

Where appropriate, estimate confidence intervals for:

- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- ROC-AUC.
- Average Precision.
- Brier score.
- Expected financial exposure.

Use statistical methods appropriate to each metric.

## 24.2 Repeated customers

If observations contain repeated snapshots of the same customer, do not automatically bootstrap rows independently.

Consider customer-level clustered bootstrap or another appropriate entity-aware method.

## 24.3 Temporal dependence

If observations are serially correlated over time:

- Avoid claiming that ordinary independent-row confidence intervals account for this dependence.
- Use suitable grouped or time-aware methods where justified.
- Document limitations.

## 24.4 Sample adequacy

Display:

- Positive count.
- Negative count.
- Distinct customer count.
- Evaluation time range.
- Effective sample-size limitations where estimable.

## 24.5 Statistical significance

Do not treat small metric differences as meaningful simply because their point estimates differ.

Where models are evaluated on the same observations, use appropriate paired comparison methods when supported.

## 24.6 Comparison methodology

Potential methods include:

- Paired bootstrap for metric differences.
- DeLong's method for comparing ROC-AUC where assumptions are appropriate.
- Entity-clustered bootstrap for repeated customer observations.
- Appropriate uncertainty estimation for Average Precision and calibration metrics.

Do not select a statistical test without checking its assumptions.

## 24.7 Multiple comparisons

When comparing several models or many segments:

- Document the number of comparisons.
- Use suitable multiplicity controls where inferential claims are made.
- Report adjusted results where necessary.

# PART 25 — TASK 22: CUSTOMER LIFETIME VALUE AND RETENTION VALUE INTEGRATION

Integrate with the existing billing, customer and cohort data.

Do not create a second independent customer lifetime value engine if one already exists.

## 25.1 CLV inputs

Potential inputs:

- Net revenue.
- Contribution margin.
- Historical customer duration.
- Subscription status.
- Contract terms.
- Renewal history.
- Discounts.
- Variable costs.
- Approved discount rate.
- Expected future relationship duration.

## 25.2 Financial methodology

Document the distinction between:

- Historical realized customer value.
- Forecast customer lifetime value.
- Contribution margin at risk.
- Expected retention value.
- Potential campaign benefit.

## 25.3 Customer-level prioritization

Where financial inputs and access permissions allow, rank customers using:

- Predicted churn probability.
- Contribution margin exposure.
- Estimated net intervention value.
- Intervention cost.
- Confidence of the financial estimate.

## 25.4 Avoid score multiplication errors

A high churn probability does not necessarily imply high financial value.

A lower-risk customer with much higher contribution margin may have greater expected exposure.

Ensure financial calculations correctly combine:

- Probability.
- Economic exposure.
- Intervention effectiveness.
- Intervention cost.

## 25.5 CLV uncertainty

Do not treat estimated lifetime value as verified accounting value.

Record methodology and assumptions.

- Best interpretable model.

The same model may not win every category.
