Create a central registry for external providers.
4.1 Provider metadata
Every provider definition must include:
- Provider ID.
- Provider name.
- Provider category.
- Adapter name.
- Supported API version.
- Authentication method.
- Supported operations.
- Webhook support.
- Campaign capability.
- CRM capability.
- Customer messaging capability.
- Current implementation status.
- Documentation reference.
- Dependency version.
- Configuration schema.
4.2 Integration categories
Support:
- CRM.
- Customer support.
- Marketing automation.
- Email communication.
- Customer messaging.
- Campaign management.
- Analytics and engagement.
4.3 Provider statuses
Use clear states:
- NOT_CONFIGURED.
- CONFIGURED.
- AUTHORIZATION_PENDING.
- CONNECTED.
- VALIDATING.
- HEALTHY.
- DEGRADED.
- AUTH_EXPIRED.
- RATE_LIMITED.
- ERROR.
- DISCONNECTED.
- REVOKED.
4.4 Implementation versus connection status
Maintain two separate concepts.

Implementation status:
- Implemented.
- Partially implemented.
- Not implemented.
- Blocked.
Connection status:
- Not configured.
- Connected.
- Authentication expired.
- Error.
- Disconnected.
Do not display a provider as connected merely because the adapter exists.
4.5 Multiple accounts
Support multiple authorized provider accounts if the existing tenant model permits them.

For example:
- Two separate Salesforce organizations.
- Multiple HubSpot portals.
- Multiple Intercom workspaces.
Each connection must have independent:
- Credentials.
- Permissions.
- External account identity.
- Mapping rules.
- Sync state.
- Audit history.
4.6 Provider discovery
Provide a capability discovery workflow.

For every connected account:
1. Verify authentication.
2. Retrieve account identity.
3. Retrieve permitted capabilities.
4. Check required scopes.
5. Check API access.
6. Check account configuration.
7. Store capability results.
8. Set connection health.

PART 5 — TASK 2: IMPLEMENT SECURE AUTHENTICATION AND CREDENTIAL MANAGEMENT
Implement secure provider authentication.

Do not store credentials in frontend code, source code, logs or ordinary configuration files.
5.1 Authentication architecture
Use provider-supported secure authentication.

Support where appropriate:
- OAuth 2.0 authorization code.
- PKCE for applicable public-client flows.
- OAuth refresh-token rotation where supported.
- Provider-specific service credentials where explicitly supported.
- Provider-specific app authentication.
- Supported server-to-server authentication where appropriate.
Do not force an identical authentication method onto every provider.
5.2 Salesforce authentication
Verify the currently supported Salesforce authentication approach and application configuration.

Build support for the appropriate approved flow, preferably a secure OAuth-based integration suited to the deployment architecture.

The developer must verify the current Salesforce requirements for external client applications, OAuth flows, scopes and API versions.

Do not rely on deprecated username-password authentication flows.

Do not assume that legacy Connected App creation and configuration procedures remain universally available.
5.3 HubSpot authentication
Verify the latest supported HubSpot developer platform authentication options.

Support the appropriate method for the required capabilities.

Distinguish:
- OAuth-based integrations.
- Supported system-to-system credential options.
- Legacy authentication methods.
- Webhook-capable application configurations.
Do not assume that an API credential type supports webhooks merely because it supports ordinary REST API requests.
5.4 Intercom authentication
Verify the latest Intercom developer application requirements.

Support appropriate authorized app authentication and workspace connection.

Do not assume that every Intercom account exposes every messaging or campaign capability.
5.5 OAuth workflow
Implement:
1. User requests provider connection.
2. Backend generates state and PKCE values where appropriate.
3. Browser redirects to provider.
4. User authorizes requested scopes.
5. Provider returns authorization response.
6. Backend validates state.
7. Backend exchanges the authorization code securely.
8. Backend stores credentials in the encrypted credential store.
9. Backend retrieves external account identity.
10. Backend validates connection.
11. Backend discovers capabilities.
12. Backend displays connection status.
5.6 OAuth security
Implement:
- Cryptographically secure state.
- PKCE where supported and required.
- Exact redirect URI validation.
- HTTPS for production callbacks.
- Scope minimization.
- CSRF prevention.
- Authorization code one-time handling.
- Token expiry tracking.
- Refresh-token rotation handling.
- Token revocation where supported.
- Secure disconnect.
5.7 Credential storage
Use:
- Existing secret manager, if available.
- Encrypted application secret storage where an external vault is unavailable.
- Strong encryption at rest.
- Key rotation.
- Restricted decryption access.
Never:
- Store client secrets in frontend environment variables.
- Store access tokens in browser local storage.
- Include tokens in API responses.
- Log authorization headers.
- Commit actual credentials.
- Store secrets in test fixtures.
5.8 Credential lifecycle
Support:
- Token expiration.
- Automatic authorized refresh.
- Refresh-token rotation.
- Revocation.
- Credential replacement.
- Connection reauthorization.
- Disconnect.
- Credential rotation audit.
5.9 Authorization scopes
Use the minimum required scopes.

Do not request write permissions for a read-only connection.

Separate permissions for:
- Read customer records.
- Read support records.
- Write CRM activities.
- Create tasks.
- Manage audiences.
- Create campaigns.
- Send communications.
5.10 Connection health
Periodically verify provider authentication without unnecessarily consuming rate limits.

A connection is healthy only when the actual credential and required capabilities work.

PART 6 — TASK 3: IMPLEMENT THE SALESFORCE CONNECTOR
Build a functional Salesforce provider adapter.

Do not implement a fake Salesforce connector.
6.1 Official documentation audit
Before implementation, inspect the current Salesforce developer documentation.

Verify:
- OAuth authorization.
- External client app configuration.
- Supported authentication flows.
- REST API version.
- API limits.
- Object permissions.
- Webhook or event capabilities.
- Bulk API availability.
- Campaign object capabilities.
- Task and activity APIs.
Pin and document the supported API version.

Do not depend on retired or unsupported endpoints.
6.2 Connection information
Store:
- Salesforce organization identifier.
- Instance or base URL.
- External account identity.
- API version.
- Connected user reference where available.
- Granted scopes.
- Token expiry metadata.
- Connection health.
Do not hardcode Salesforce production domains.

Resolve the instance using the authorized provider response.
6.3 Supported CRM objects
Implement appropriate support for available objects, including:
- Account.
- Contact.
- Lead.
- Opportunity.
- Campaign.
- Campaign Member.
- Task.
- Event.
- Case.
- Custom objects when explicitly configured and accessible.
Do not assume every organization uses the same object configuration.
6.4 Customer synchronization
Map canonical entities to appropriate Salesforce records.

Potential mappings:
- Customer → Account or Contact according to the customer's business entity model.
- Organization → Account.
- Person/contact → Contact.
- Lead → Lead only when the lifecycle and ownership model supports it.
Do not map all customers to Salesforce Leads without checking the target data model.
6.5 Read operations
Support configured operations:
- Retrieve record.
- Search record.
- List records.
- Retrieve changes.
- Query permitted fields.
- Retrieve record relationships.
Use current supported REST or Bulk API methods where appropriate.
6.6 Write operations
Where permission and approval exist, support:
- Create account.
- Update account.
- Create contact.
- Update contact.
- Create task.
- Create event.
- Add approved note or activity.
- Create campaign membership.
- Update explicitly approved fields.
Do not overwrite owner-managed fields without an approved field mapping.
6.7 Campaign operations
Where the connected organization and API support them, investigate:
- Campaign creation.
- Campaign member management.
- Campaign status.
- Campaign member status.
- Campaign result tracking.
Verify actual API support and permissions before enabling these actions.

Do not assume that creating campaign membership sends a customer communication.
6.8 Activity synchronization
Support:
- Internal retention task.
- Customer follow-up task.
- Approved account review.
- Customer meeting record.
- Intervention status.
- Completed CRM activity.
Every created activity must reference the corresponding Phase 17 recommendation or intervention.
6.9 Salesforce custom fields
Support controlled field mapping for custom fields.

Before activating a mapping:
- Retrieve or inspect the external object schema.
- Validate field type.
- Validate field permissions.
- Validate picklist values.
- Validate required fields.
- Record field mapping version.
6.10 Salesforce error handling
Normalize provider responses for:
- Invalid session.
- Insufficient access.
- Invalid field.
- Invalid object.
- Validation failure.
- Record conflict.
- Duplicate record.
- API limit reached.
- Unsupported operation.
Do not discard the original diagnostic information.
6.11 Salesforce webhook and event capabilities
Use an appropriate supported integration mechanism, such as platform events, change-data capture, supported event subscriptions or approved webhook architecture where available.

Document the selected mechanism.

Do not fabricate Salesforce webhook support with an unsupported generic endpoint.

PART 7 — TASK 4: IMPLEMENT THE HUBSPOT CONNECTOR

Inspect current HubSpot documentation and developer changelog.

- Supported authentication.

- Search.

- Write validation.

- Service credential limitations.
- Rate limits.

Store:

7.3 CRM objects
Support authorized operations for:

- Companies.
- Deals.
- Tickets.
- Products.
- Activities.
- Tasks and notes where available.
- Custom objects where supported and configured.
7.4 Customer mapping
Define deterministic mapping rules:
- Canonical person customer → HubSpot Contact where suitable.
- Canonical organization → HubSpot Company.
- Customer retention opportunity → Deal or another approved CRM object if the business process requires it.
- Support issue → Ticket where appropriate.
- Retention action → Task or activity where supported.
Do not create deals for every high-risk customer automatically.
7.5 Read operations
Implement:
- Record lookup.
- Record search.
- Pagination.
- Association retrieval.
- Batch retrieval.

7.6 Write operations
Support authorized:
- Contact creation.
- Contact update.
- Company creation.
- Company update.
- Task creation.
- Note creation.
- Ticket creation where appropriate.
- Approved activity creation.
- Approved property updates.
Handle administrator-configured required-property and validation rules.

When an external provider rejects a write, preserve its validation details.

Do not bypass the provider's record validation rules.
7.7 Association management
Where supported:
- Associate contact and company.
- Associate contact and deal.
- Associate company and deal.

- Associate tasks and activities.
Verify the association type and object compatibility.

7.8 Campaign and automation capabilities
Inspect available account and app capabilities.

Potential operations may include:

7.9 Webhooks
Implement supported webhook subscriptions.

Support:
- Relevant contact changes.
- Company changes.
- Deal changes.
- Ticket changes.
- Approved property changes.
- Subscription and communication preference events where available.
Acknowledge webhook delivery quickly and process the work asynchronously.
7.10 HubSpot error handling
Handle:
- Authorization errors.
- Missing scopes.
- Validation failures.
- Duplicate records.
- Conflict responses.
- Rate limiting.
- API-version errors.
- Association failures.
- Account permission restrictions.
7.11 Account configuration compatibility
Where APIs enforce account-configured validation rules:

- Allow administrators to configure safe mappings.
Do not suppress provider-side validation errors.

Build a functional Intercom provider adapter.

Do not treat its object model as identical to Salesforce or HubSpot.

- Tags.
- Notes.
- Custom attributes.
- Events.
- Customer interaction history.

Map canonical customers to Intercom contacts using verified external identifiers.

Support organization-to-company relationships where applicable.

8.5 Read operations
Implement supported:
- Contact lookup.
- Contact search.
- Contact list.

Where supported and authorized:

8.7 Intercom messaging
Support only explicitly permitted message operations.

- Customer-visible message.

- Message delivery.
- Customer response.

8.8 Conversation synchronization
Retrieve relevant conversation information where authorized.

- Resolution timestamp.

8.9 Webhook signature verification
Implement the actual provider-specified signature validation for the currently supported Intercom webhook protocol.

Use:
- The exact raw request body.
- The correct app secret.
- The provider-defined signature header.
- Constant-time comparison.
- Correct encoding and digest algorithm.
Do not parse and reserialize the JSON payload before verifying the signature.
8.10 Webhook duplicate handling
Intercom may retry deliveries.

Implement event-level idempotency.

A duplicate delivery must not:
- Duplicate a customer record.
- Duplicate a message.
- Create another intervention.

8.11 Intercom rate limits
Implement response-aware throttling.

Respect documented rate-limit headers and retry signals.

8.12 Intercom error handling
Normalize:
- Expired token.
- Invalid workspace.
- Missing permission.
- Invalid contact.
- Invalid conversation.
- Message validation.
- Rate limiting.
- API version mismatch.
- Webhook verification failure.

- Other approved business engagement platforms.

Define a common interface supporting:

9.5 Connector development guide

PART 10 — TASK 7: BUILD THE CANONICAL CRM DATA MAPPING ENGINE
Different providers use different data models.

Create a stable mapping layer between the canonical platform and each provider.
10.1 Canonical objects
Define or reuse canonical representations for:
- Customer.
- Organization.
- Customer contact.
- Subscription.
- CRM account.
- CRM contact.
- Deal.
- Ticket.
- Task.
- Note.
- Activity.
- Campaign.
- Campaign membership.
- Audience.
- Message.
- Communication event.
Do not force every provider object into an inappropriate canonical entity.
10.2 Customer mapping
Map:
- Canonical customer ID.
- Canonical organization ID.
- External provider.
- External account.
- External object type.
- External object ID.
- Mapping status.
- Mapping method.
- Verification status.
10.3 Field mapping configuration
Allow authorized administrators to configure mappings.

Examples:
- Canonical customer name → provider name property.
- Customer segment → provider segment field.
- Acquisition channel → source field.
- Latest churn risk → approved custom risk field.
- Latest prediction timestamp → approved timestamp field.
- Retention recommendation category → approved custom property.
- Internal account owner → external owner mapping.
These are candidate mappings, not compulsory fields.
10.4 Field mapping properties
For every mapping, store:
- Mapping ID.
- Provider.
- Object type.
- Canonical field.
- External field.
- Data type.
- Transformation.
- Direction.
- Permission.
- Validation.
- Version.
- Effective date.
10.5 Mapping directions
Support:
- READ_ONLY.
- OUTBOUND_ONLY.
- INBOUND_ONLY.
- BIDIRECTIONAL.
- DISABLED.
Do not make every field bidirectional by default.
10.6 Field transformations
Support safe transformations:
- Date conversion.
- Timezone normalization.
- Enum mapping.
- Boolean normalization.
- String normalization.
- Numeric validation.
- Currency formatting.
- Null handling.
Do not introduce lossy transformations without explicit configuration.
10.7 Custom fields
Allow approved provider-specific custom fields.

Validate actual external schema.

Do not assume custom field names or IDs across organizations.
10.8 Sensitive fields
Prevent accidental synchronization of:
- Credentials.
- Authentication secrets.
- Payment card data.
- Restricted financial attributes.
- Sensitive personal information.
- Internal SHAP details.
- Restricted customer notes.
Require explicit policy for sensitive data.
10.9 Mapping test
Before activation, preview:
- Source value.
- Target field.
- Transformed value.
- Validation status.
- Permission status.
- Synchronization direction.
Do not activate incompatible mappings.

PART 11 — TASK 8: IMPLEMENT CUSTOMER IDENTITY MAPPING ACROSS PROVIDERS
Provider records must map to the canonical customer identity from Phase 16.
11.1 Unique identity
Use the canonical customer ID internally.
11.2 External identity mapping
Maintain mappings for:
- Salesforce Account ID.
- Salesforce Contact ID.
- HubSpot Contact ID.
- HubSpot Company ID.
- Intercom Contact ID.
- Intercom Company ID.
- Additional provider records.
Only store identifiers that are actually returned and verified.
11.3 Mapping rules
Prioritize:
1. Existing verified mapping.
2. Verified exact external identifier.
3. Approved deterministic business-key mapping.
4. Human-approved mapping.
11.4 Email identity limitations
Do not use email as a universal, immutable customer identity.

Email addresses can change, be shared or be reused.

Use them as a matching attribute only under the approved identity policy.
11.5 Duplicate prevention
Before creating an external contact:
- Search for an existing mapping.
- Search using approved identifiers.
- Check likely duplicates.
- Verify organization relationships.
- Record the decision.
11.6 Ambiguous mapping
If multiple external records match:
- Mark identity as AMBIGUOUS.
- Do not arbitrarily select a record.
- Require review.
- Preserve all candidate references.
11.7 Identity conflict
If two canonical customers map to one external record:
- Block unsafe synchronization.
- Preserve evidence.
- Create an identity conflict record.
- Require authorized resolution.
11.8 Mapping history
Preserve:
- Previous mapping.
- New mapping.
- Source.
- Reviewer.
- Reason.
- Effective timestamp.
Do not silently change mappings.

PART 12 — TASK 9: IMPLEMENT INBOUND CRM DATA SYNCHRONIZATION
External platforms may contain useful customer profile, activity and engagement information.

Implement controlled inbound synchronization.
12.1 Supported inbound records
Where authorized:
- Customer updates.
- Organization updates.
- Contact updates.
- CRM activities.
- Tasks.
- Notes.
- Tickets.
- Deal or account activity.
- Customer communication preferences.
- Campaign membership.
- Campaign delivery events.
- Customer responses.
Only import permitted object types.
12.2 Inbound synchronization methods
Support:
- Initial full synchronization.
- Incremental synchronization.

- Scheduled synchronization.
- Manual refresh.
12.3 Incremental synchronization
Use provider-supported:
- Updated timestamps.
- Cursor pagination.
- Change tracking.
- Webhook events.
- Delta tokens.
- Watermarks.

- Last successful sync.
- Last attempted sync.
- Current cursor.
- Provider timestamp.
- Local processing timestamp.
12.4 Pagination
Implement provider-specific pagination.

Do not assume all providers use page numbers.

Handle:
- Cursor.
- Next URL.
- Offset.
- Page number.
- Provider-specific paging token.
12.5 Initial sync
Support controlled initial synchronization.

Allow selection of:
- Object types.
- Date range where supported.
- Account scope.
- Maximum record count.
- Field allowlist.

12.6 Incremental sync safety
Handle:
- Late-arriving records.
- Duplicate events.
- Updated records.
- Deleted records.
- Archived records.
- Permission changes.
- Missing fields.
12.7 Inbound validation
Imported records must pass appropriate validation and mapping.

12.8 Source ownership
Define field ownership.

For example:
- Provider owns CRM account owner.
- Canonical platform owns churn predictions.
- Retention platform owns generated retention recommendations.
- Provider owns its own communication delivery status.

12.9 Inbound conflict handling
When inbound data conflicts with canonical data:
- Preserve both values.
- Identify authoritative source.
- Apply an approved precedence rule.
- Create a conflict record when necessary.
- Do not silently overwrite.
12.10 Provenance
Every imported field must retain:
- Provider.
- External record ID.
- External timestamp.
- Import time.
- Sync run.
- Field mapping version.

PART 13 — TASK 10: IMPLEMENT OUTBOUND CRM SYNCHRONIZATION
Phase 17 creates approved recommendations and interventions.

Phase 18 must translate those approved internal decisions into supported provider actions.
13.1 Outbound data candidates
Support configured synchronization of:
- Customer reference.
- Organization reference.
- Customer segment.
- Approved churn risk category.

- Ticket.
- Deal or related record if configured and appropriate.

13.4 Intervention synchronization
For a Phase 17 intervention:
1. Verify approval.
2. Verify customer eligibility.
3. Verify current status.
4. Resolve provider mapping.
5. Check provider capability.
6. Check external duplicate.
7. Prepare external payload.
8. Validate field mapping.
9. Execute provider operation.
10. Record provider response.
11. Link external record ID.
12. Update internal intervention state.
13. Audit the operation.

Support:
- READ_ONLY.

- BLOCKED.

13.6 Conflict prevention

13.7 External operation status
Differentiate:
- QUEUED.
- VALIDATING.
- SUBMITTED.
- ACCEPTED.
- COMPLETED.
- FAILED.
- UNKNOWN.
- CANCELLED.

- COMPLETED.

- CANCELLED.
- ARCHIVED.
Map them to provider statuses only when an equivalent provider status exists.

Do not assume exact one-to-one mappings.
15.4 Campaign builder
Allow authorized users to configure:
- Campaign name.
- Target population.
- Eligibility conditions.
- Provider.
- Message template.
- Communication channel.
- Start date.
- End date.
- Follow-up.
- Frequency limits.
- Approval requirements.
15.5 Audience source
Support approved audience creation using:
- Phase 17 approved retention recommendations.
- Customer segment.
- Churn risk category.
- Acquisition cohort.
- Verified issue category.
- Customer owner.
- Renewal window.
15.6 Audience validation
Before campaign creation, validate:
- Canonical customer identity.
- Provider identity mapping.
- Contact availability.
- Permission and consent.
- Opt-out.
- Suppression.
- Duplicate enrollment.
- Existing intervention.
- Campaign eligibility.
15.7 Audience preview
Show:
- Total candidates.
- Eligible candidates.
- Ineligible candidates.
- Missing external mappings.
- Suppressed customers.
- Duplicate customers.
- Customers requiring human review.
15.8 Campaign approval
Require approval before any external campaign enrollment or customer communication.

Commercial campaigns may require additional financial approval.
15.9 Campaign creation
Create a corresponding external campaign only if:
- The provider supports the required operation.
- The connected account has the required scopes.
- The campaign mapping is valid.
- The campaign has been approved.
Otherwise create an internal campaign record and explicitly report the external capability as unavailable.
15.10 Campaign enrollment
Preserve the relationship between:
- Campaign.
- Canonical customer.
- External contact.
- Phase 17 recommendation.
- Intervention.
- Provider campaign membership.
Do not assume creating a contact or list entry means the customer has received a communication.
15.11 Campaign execution modes
Support:
- Internal-only campaign plan.
- External campaign draft.
- Approved external campaign enrollment.
- Approved provider-supported campaign execution.
Execution must be explicitly enabled and authorized.

PART 16 — TASK 13: BUILD CAMPAIGN AND MESSAGE TEMPLATE MANAGEMENT
Create a controlled template registry.
16.1 Template categories
Support:
- Payment assistance.
- Product adoption.
- Customer onboarding.
- Renewal communication.
- Support follow-up.
- Customer success outreach.
- Service recovery.
- Customer health check.
16.2 Template metadata
Store:
- Template ID.
- Name.
- Version.
- Provider.
- Channel.
- Purpose.
- Language.
- Subject where appropriate.
- Body.
- Variable schema.
- Approval state.
- Effective date.
- Owner.
16.3 Variables
Support validated placeholders such as:
- Customer name.
- Organization name.
- Approved subscription name.
- Verified invoice reference.
- Assigned account owner.
- Appointment reference.
- Approved follow-up date.
Do not include unapproved financial or sensitive customer data.
16.4 Template validation
Before execution:
- Confirm variable availability.
- Check required fields.
- Validate maximum lengths.
- Validate formatting.
- Validate provider template requirements.
- Validate consent.
- Validate destination channel.
16.5 Message review
Show the exact rendered message before approval.

Do not silently change the content after approval.

If content changes, create a new message version and require reapproval where configured.
16.6 Localization
Support language and locale fields where configured.

Do not automatically translate regulated or commercial messaging without a review process.
16.7 Communication tone
Messages should be:
- Clear.
- Respectful.
- Professional.
- Helpful.
- Accurate.
- Non-manipulative.
Do not fabricate urgency or claim that customers will lose access when no such condition exists.

PART 17 — TASK 14: IMPLEMENT APPROVED COMMUNICATION EXECUTION
Create a controlled communication execution service.
17.1 Supported channels
Where configured and authorized:
- Email.
- Customer messaging.
- In-app communication.
- Approved provider messaging.
- CRM-supported activity communication.
- Other explicitly configured channels.
Do not claim a provider supports a channel without verifying its current capabilities.
17.2 Execution prerequisites
Before every outbound communication:
1. Identify canonical customer.
2. Resolve provider contact.
3. Check customer eligibility.
4. Check consent and communication preferences.
5. Check opt-out and suppression.
6. Check contact frequency.
7. Check active campaign conflicts.
8. Validate message template.
9. Validate required provider capability.
10. Validate approval.
11. Validate scheduled time.
12. Create idempotency key.
13. Submit the action.
14. Record provider response.
15. Track delivery and response.
17.3 Customer preferences
Respect:
- Marketing opt-out.
- Channel preference.
- Contact limitations.
- Consent records.
- Applicable do-not-contact restrictions.
- Customer-specific suppression.
- Organization-level restrictions where relevant.
17.4 Transactional versus marketing communication
Keep separate policies for:
- Legitimate service-related communication.
- Marketing communication.
- Commercial retention communication.
- Support response.
- Billing-related notifications.
Do not assume one consent type authorizes every communication purpose.
17.5 Suppression list
Maintain an authoritative, auditable communication suppression mechanism.

Synchronize suppression information with relevant providers where supported and authorized.

The central platform must not continue sending a message because one provider's suppression record was unavailable.
17.6 Contact frequency
Configure:
- Per-channel frequency limits.
- Per-customer frequency limits.
- Minimum contact interval.
- Campaign cooling-off period.
- Maximum messages per time window.
- Duplicate communication prevention.
17.7 Sending restrictions
Use configured timezones and appropriate contact windows.

Do not assume the application server timezone equals the customer's timezone.
17.8 External send status
Distinguish:
- Draft created.
- Approved.
- Queued.
- Submitted.
- Provider accepted.
- Sent.
- Delivered.
- Bounced.
- Failed.
- Opened.
- Clicked.
- Responded.
- Unsubscribed.
Only display a status when the provider or an authoritative source confirms it.
17.9 No false delivery claims
A successful HTTP request does not prove message delivery.

Do not mark a message delivered without a provider delivery event or other reliable confirmation.

PART 18 — TASK 15: IMPLEMENT AUDIENCE AND SEGMENT SYNCHRONIZATION
Build an audience management layer.
18.1 Audience sources
Support approved populations from:
- Phase 17 recommendations.
- Customer 360 segments.
- Customer risk categories.
- Subscription categories.
- Acquisition cohorts.
- Renewal windows.
- Verified support issues.
- Payment problems.
- Product adoption gaps.
18.2 Dynamic audiences
Allow configurable audience rules.

Where supported, synchronize dynamic audience membership with the provider.
18.3 Static audiences
Allow versioned snapshots of approved campaign populations.

Record the exact membership at campaign execution time.
18.4 Audience exclusions
Apply:
- Opt-outs.
- Suppression.
- Invalid contact data.
- Duplicate identities.
- Existing active campaigns.
- Ineligible customers.
- Missing consent.
- Customer-requested restrictions.
18.5 Audience deduplication
One canonical customer must not accidentally receive the same campaign multiple times because multiple provider records represent the same customer.

Handle account and organization scope explicitly.
18.6 Audience reconciliation
Report:
- Canonical audience size.
- Provider audience size.
- Successful mappings.
- Missing mappings.
- Duplicate records.
- Suppressed records.
- Failed synchronization.
18.7 Audience versioning
Preserve every approved audience snapshot.

Do not silently change an already approved campaign population.

PART 19 — TASK 16: BUILD BI-DIRECTIONAL WEBHOOK AND EVENT PROCESSING
Implement robust event processing.
19.1 Webhook gateway
Create provider-specific webhook endpoints.

Each endpoint must have:
- Provider identity.
- Connection identity.
- Authentication validation.
- Signature validation.
- Payload size limits.
- Request timestamp checks where supported.
- Event identity.
- Duplicate prevention.
- Rate limiting.
19.2 Provider-specific verification
Use each provider's current official webhook authentication mechanism.

Examples:
- HMAC-based signature validation where specified.
- Exact signed payload verification.
- OAuth or provider-defined webhook authentication where applicable.
Do not assume all providers use the same signature scheme.
19.3 Raw request preservation
Where necessary for signature validation:
- Preserve raw request bytes.
- Verify the signature before altering the body.
- Avoid parsing and reserializing the payload prematurely.
19.4 Acknowledgement
Acknowledge verified webhooks quickly.

Do not perform long CRM synchronization operations in the HTTP request handler.

Persist or queue the event and process it asynchronously.
19.5 Incoming event types
Support available provider events such as:
- Contact created.
- Contact updated.
- Company updated.
- Deal updated.
- Ticket updated.
- CRM task updated.
- Conversation created.
- Conversation updated.
- Message sent.
- Message delivered.
- Customer replied.
- Contact unsubscribed.
- Campaign membership changed.
Only enable actual provider-supported event topics.
19.6 Event normalization
Normalize provider payloads into a shared internal event representation.

Include:
- Internal event ID.
- Provider.
- Provider account.
- External event ID.
- External object ID.
- Canonical customer ID.
- Event type.
- Event timestamp.
- Received timestamp.
- Payload reference.
- Processing status.
19.7 Duplicate webhook handling
Webhook deliveries may be repeated.

Use an idempotency identity based on provider event identity and connection.

Do not generate duplicate:
- Customer responses.
- Intervention completion events.
- Campaign enrollment.
- Customer timeline events.
- CRM updates.
19.8 Event ordering
Handle out-of-order events.

Compare:
- Provider event timestamp.
- Provider object update timestamp.
- Local processing timestamp.
Do not let an older webhook overwrite a newer canonical state.
19.9 Delayed events
Process late events using the appropriate correction and historical lineage policy.

Do not discard an event merely because it arrived later than expected.
19.10 Dead-letter handling
Failed events must be recoverable.

Store:
- Event.
- Failure reason.
- Attempt count.
- Last attempt.
- Provider.
- Next eligible retry.
- Manual resolution status.
Do not silently delete failed events.

PART 20 — TASK 17: IMPLEMENT SYNCHRONIZATION CONFLICT RESOLUTION
Two systems may change the same customer data independently.

Implement a clear ownership and conflict policy.
20.1 Field ownership
Each mapped field must declare:
- AUTHORITATIVE_LOCAL.
- AUTHORITATIVE_PROVIDER.
- PROVIDER_SPECIFIC.
- HUMAN_REVIEW_REQUIRED.
- READ_ONLY.
20.2 Conflict conditions
Detect:
- CRM contact name changed.
- Canonical customer name changed.
- Different organization mapping.
- Different customer owner.
- Conflicting communication preferences.
- External prediction field modified manually.
- Customer record merged externally.
- Conflicting lifecycle state.
20.3 Resolution strategy
Support:
- Local wins.
- Provider wins.
- Latest verified timestamp wins where safe.
- Human review.
- Field-specific custom policy.
Do not use last-write-wins blindly across all fields.
20.4 Human review
Provide a conflict workspace.

Display:
- Canonical value.
- External value.
- Source.
- Timestamp.
- Mapping policy.
- Suggested resolution.
- Reviewer.
- Resolution reason.
20.5 CRM merges
If external records are merged:
- Detect the merge event where supported.
- Preserve previous mappings.
- Map the surviving external record.
- Verify canonical identity.
- Update the mapping history.
- Do not merge unrelated internal customers automatically.
20.6 Prediction field protection
CRM users must not silently modify canonical model predictions.

Where external systems store risk values, treat the central prediction as authoritative unless an explicitly configured override workflow exists.

PART 21 — TASK 18: IMPLEMENT RATE LIMITS, RETRIES AND RESILIENCE
Implement provider-specific reliability.
21.1 Rate-limit management
Track:
- Provider.
- Account.
- Endpoint family.
- Remaining quota where available.
- Reset time.
- Concurrency.
- Throttling status.
21.2 HTTP 429
Handle provider-specific 429 responses.

Respect:
- Retry-After.
- Rate-limit reset headers.
- Provider-specific retry guidance.
Do not repeatedly retry without waiting.
21.3 Exponential backoff
Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter for appropriate transient failures.
21.4 Error classification
Differentiate:
- AUTHENTICATION_ERROR.
- AUTHORIZATION_ERROR.
- VALIDATION_ERROR.
- DUPLICATE_RECORD.
- CONFLICT.
- RATE_LIMITED.
- NETWORK_ERROR.
- TIMEOUT.
- SERVER_ERROR.
- UNSUPPORTED_CAPABILITY.
- PROVIDER_CONFIGURATION_ERROR.
- UNKNOWN_ERROR.
21.5 Retryable errors
Retry only errors that may succeed later.

Do not retry:
- Invalid data.
- Missing required fields.
- Unsupported permissions.
- Invalid customer identity.
- Expired approval.
- Communication opt-out.
21.6 Idempotent outbound operations
For every external write:
- Generate an internal operation ID.
- Use a provider idempotency key where supported.
- Record the exact outbound payload.
- Record the provider response.
- Detect ambiguous timeouts.
- Reconcile before repeating non-idempotent operations.
Do not blindly repeat a message send because a network timeout occurred.
21.7 Circuit breaker
Prevent repeated calls to an unhealthy provider.

Support:
- Open.
- Half-open.
- Closed.
21.8 Retry queue
Use existing background job infrastructure.

Record all attempts.
21.9 Dead-letter queue
Create a controlled failed-operation review workflow.

Allow authorized retry after correcting the underlying problem.

PART 22 — TASK 19: BUILD THE CRM SYNCHRONIZATION JOB MANAGER
Support independently tracked synchronization jobs.
22.1 Sync job metadata
Record:
- Sync job ID.
- Provider.
- Provider account.
- Object type.
- Sync direction.
- Start timestamp.
- End timestamp.
- Cursor or watermark.
- Records discovered.
- Records processed.
- Records created.
- Records updated.
- Records skipped.
- Records failed.
- Status.
22.2 Sync modes
Support:
- INITIAL_FULL_SYNC.
- INCREMENTAL_SYNC.
- WEBHOOK_INCREMENTAL.
- MANUAL_SYNC.
- RETRY_FAILED.
- RECONCILIATION_SYNC.
22.3 Sync status
Support:
- QUEUED.
- RUNNING.
- PARTIALLY_COMPLETED.
- COMPLETED.
- COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS.
- FAILED.
- CANCELLED.
22.4 Checkpointing
Preserve:
- Last successful page or cursor.
- Last processed object.
- Last provider timestamp.
- Last successful record.
- Failed records.
Resume only unfinished work.
22.5 Idempotency
A repeated sync request with identical provider, account, object scope and checkpoint must not duplicate data.
22.6 Concurrent sync prevention
Prevent conflicting jobs for the same object and provider account.
22.7 Sync report
Generate:
- Total records.
- New records.
- Changed records.
- Unchanged records.
- Failed records.
- Duplicate records.
- Conflict count.
- Duration.
- Last successful checkpoint.

Create a capability-driven workflow rather than assuming uniform campaign APIs.
23.1 Salesforce
Investigate supported capabilities for:
- Campaigns.
- Campaign Members.
- CRM activities.
- Tasks.
- Account/contact activities.
- Provider-supported event or automation mechanisms.
Document which actions are actually available through the connected organization.
23.2 HubSpot
Investigate supported capabilities for:
- Contact and company lists.

- CRM activities.
- Workflow-related operations.
- Customer engagement.

- Email or marketing enrollment where authorized.

23.3 Intercom
Investigate supported capabilities for:

- Messages.
- Tags.
- Customer segments.
- Customer engagement.
- Supported campaign or series operations.
- Message delivery events.
Do not assume a conversation reply is equivalent to a campaign enrollment.
23.4 Provider capability matrix
Display an actual matrix per connection.

Customer records	Verify	Verify	Verify
Contact records	Verify	Verify	Verify
Company records	Verify	Verify	Verify

When an operation is unavailable:

- Explain whether the cause is missing app scope, provider account restriction, API limitation or unimplemented adapter.
- Keep other working features operational.

PART 24 — TASK 21: CONNECT CRM AUTOMATION TO PHASE 17 RETENTION INTERVENTIONS
This is the most important business integration.

Every external action must originate from an approved internal retention intervention.
24.1 End-to-end relationship
Maintain:

Customer → Prediction → SHAP Explanation → Retention Recommendation → Approval → Intervention → CRM Record → Campaign Enrollment → Communication → Provider Event → Customer Response → Intervention Outcome
24.2 Recommendation synchronization
When a recommendation is approved:
- Resolve customer identity.
- Check provider connection.
- Check required capability.
- Resolve intervention mapping.
- Check existing CRM activity.
- Create the appropriate task or activity.
- Link external ID.
- Record execution status.
24.3 Campaign selection
Choose an appropriate provider according to:
- Approved campaign purpose.
- Available capabilities.
- Customer contact permissions.
- Existing provider contact.
- Audience availability.
- Account configuration.
Do not default to sending through the first connected provider.
24.4 Approval transfer
Preserve:
- Phase 17 approval ID.
- Approver.
- Approval timestamp.
- Approved intervention.
- Financial approval where required.
The external operation must be linked to this approval.
24.5 Pre-execution revalidation
Immediately before external execution:
1. Revalidate customer identity.
2. Revalidate eligibility.
3. Revalidate customer contact permissions.
4. Check suppression.
5. Check contact frequency.
6. Revalidate intervention approval.
7. Check recommendation expiration.
8. Check relevant customer issue status.
9. Check communication template version.
10. Check provider connection.
11. Check provider capability.
12. Check idempotency.
24.6 Obsolete recommendation
If the customer issue has already been resolved:
- Stop or cancel the outbound action where possible.
- Update internal status.
- Record the reason.
- Do not send obsolete communication.
24.7 External execution status
Maintain separate statuses for:
- Internal recommendation.
- Internal approval.
- External operation.
- Provider delivery.
- Customer response.
- Intervention outcome.
Do not collapse them into one status.

PART 25 — TASK 22: IMPLEMENT CUSTOMER RESPONSE AND EVENT SYNCHRONIZATION
Provider events must flow back into Phase 17.
25.1 Customer response events
Where provider capabilities support it, process:
- Message reply.
- Conversation response.
- Email response.
- Meeting response.
- Campaign interaction.
- Opt-out.
- Unsubscribe.
- Delivery failure.
- Bounce.
- Complaint or suppression event.
Do not assume every provider supplies every event.
25.2 Canonical response model
Create a normalized response event containing:
- Response event ID.
- Customer ID.
- Provider.
- External contact ID.
- External conversation or message ID.
- Campaign ID.
- Intervention ID.
- Response type.
- Event timestamp.
- Received timestamp.
- Content reference where authorized.
- Processing status.
25.3 Response mapping
Map provider events to Phase 17 outcomes.

Examples:
- Customer replied.
- Customer accepted.
- Customer declined.
- Customer requested no contact.
- Customer asked for assistance.
- Customer reported issue unresolved.
- Customer completed onboarding.
Only map to an outcome when the evidence supports it.
25.4 Free-text response
Do not automatically interpret free-text sentiment as an authoritative acceptance or rejection without a validated classification workflow.

If AI-assisted classification is added:
- Preserve the original event.
- Record the classification model/version.
- Show uncertainty.
- Require review for high-impact interpretation.
- Do not overwrite the original communication.
25.5 Response deduplication
Do not record one customer response multiple times when multiple webhooks refer to the same external message.
25.6 Customer timeline
Write external interaction events into the Phase 16 Customer 360 timeline.

Preserve:
- Provider.
- External record.
- Timestamp.
- Campaign.
- Intervention.
- Response type.

PART 26 — TASK 23: IMPLEMENT CONSENT, UNSUBSCRIBE AND SUPPRESSION SYNCHRONIZATION
Communication permissions are mandatory.
26.1 Consent authority
Define the authoritative location for each relevant preference.

Possible sources:
- Central platform consent record.
- Provider consent record.
- Verified customer instruction.
- Legal or business suppression record.
26.2 Consent synchronization
Where authorized and supported:
- Read provider preferences.
- Update central consent state.
- Synchronize approved changes.
- Preserve source timestamp.
- Preserve the original change event.
26.3 Immediate suppression
A verified unsubscribe or opt-out must prevent subsequent communication of the applicable type while the updated permission state is being reconciled.
26.4 Conflicting consent
If consent states conflict:
- Apply the safer approved policy.
- Block the affected outbound communication.
- Create a review record.
- Preserve all sources.
26.5 Consent categories
Keep separate consent categories where required:
- Marketing email.
- Transactional email.
- Customer service communication.
- Phone outreach.
- Messaging.
- In-app engagement.
Do not treat permission for one category as automatic permission for another.
26.6 Suppression testing
Test that an unsubscribe event received by webhook prevents later execution from every configured provider for the relevant communication category.
26.7 Retention policy
Preserve the minimum necessary evidence of consent and suppression according to existing privacy and retention rules.

Create a dedicated frontend module:

CRM & Integrations Center

PART 28 — TASK 25: IMPLEMENT CAMPAIGN REPORTING AND OUTCOME ANALYTICS
28.1 Campaign metrics
Where reliable provider events exist, calculate:
- Audience size.
- Eligible recipients.
- Suppressed recipients.
- Enrollment count.
- Sent count.
- Delivery count.
- Failed count.
- Bounce count.
- Open count.
- Click count.
- Replies.
- Unsubscribes.
- Complaints where available.
Do not claim a metric is available from a provider unless the event is actually supplied.
28.2 Metric definitions
For every metric, record:
- Numerator.
- Denominator.
- Observation window.
- Provider.
- Event definition.
- Attribution method.
28.3 Campaign conversion
A customer converting after receiving a campaign does not automatically prove that the campaign caused the conversion.

Distinguish:
- Attributed outcome.
- Observed subsequent outcome.
- Experimentally estimated incremental outcome.
28.4 Retention outcomes
Connect campaign activity to Phase 17 intervention outcomes.

Track:
- Contacted.
- Replied.
- Accepted.
- Declined.
- Payment recovered.
- Usage recovered.
- Issue resolved.
- Renewal completed.
- Churn observed.
28.5 Attribution windows
Support configurable outcome attribution windows.

The campaign must record which window was applied.

Do not count a churn outcome that occurred before the relevant campaign as a campaign-induced failure.
28.6 Financial performance
Where data exists, compare:
- Campaign spending.
- Actual communication costs.
- Discounts applied.
- Contribution margin.
- Payment recovery.
- Observed retention.
- Experimentally supported incremental effect.
Do not report hypothetical value as actual financial performance.
28.7 Campaign comparison
Compare providers and campaign types only where metric definitions and eligible populations are comparable.

Do not compare provider open rates as equivalent when tracking mechanisms or privacy limitations differ.

PART 38 — IMPLEMENTATION ORDER AND GATES
Implement in this order.
STAGE 1 — Previous-phase compatibility audit
Inspect Phases 1–17.

Identify existing connectors, credentials, identity mappings, communication permissions, intervention approvals and provider dependencies.

Gate 1: The actual repository and provider requirements are understood.
STAGE 2 — Generic integration framework
Implement:
- Registry.
- Adapter contract.
- Capability registry.
- Connection management.
- Provider-specific API client.
- Credential vault.
Gate 2: A reference provider adapter can connect, validate and execute safe test operations.
STAGE 3 — OAuth and security
Implement secure authorization, token storage, refresh, revocation and health.

Gate 3: Authentication and credential security tests pass.
STAGE 4 — Salesforce connector
Implement real Salesforce provider capabilities according to current official documentation.

Gate 4: Supported Salesforce adapter operations pass contract and available sandbox tests.
STAGE 5 — HubSpot connector
Implement real HubSpot provider capabilities according to current official documentation.

Gate 5: Supported HubSpot operations pass contract and available developer-account tests.
STAGE 6 — Intercom connector
Implement real Intercom provider capabilities according to current official documentation.

Gate 6: Supported Intercom operations and webhook tests pass.
STAGE 7 — Canonical identity and mappings
Implement identity resolution, custom field mapping and conflict handling.

Gate 7: External records map to canonical customers reliably.
STAGE 8 — Inbound and outbound synchronization
Implement sync jobs, activities, retries and checkpoint recovery.

Gate 8: Synchronization produces reconciled and auditable results.
STAGE 9 — Campaign and audience management
Implement campaign drafts, audience validation, communication approval, supported provider execution and result tracking.

Gate 9: All outbound actions obey Phase 17 approval and consent rules.
STAGE 10 — Webhooks and event processing
Implement signed webhook verification, asynchronous processing, deduplication and recovery.

Gate 10: Valid external events update the correct internal records exactly once.
STAGE 11 — Frontend integration workspace
Implement provider connections, mappings, synchronization, campaigns, events and error dashboards.

Gate 11: All displayed features are connected to actual backend functions.
STAGE 12 — Customer 360 and retention integration
Connect external activity and responses to Customer 360 and Phase 17 intervention tracking.

Gate 12: Full end-to-end business workflows pass.
STAGE 13 — Full verification
Run all connector, security, API, webhook, campaign, performance and Phase 1–17 regression tests.

Gate 13: Produce the complete Phase 18 engineering report.

Do not skip failed gates.

PART 41 — NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES
1. Never fabricate provider connections.
2. Never claim a provider is connected when credentials are missing.
3. Never hardcode API credentials.
4. Never expose access or refresh tokens.
5. Never bypass OAuth or provider permission requirements.
6. Never use deprecated authentication methods without an explicit approved compatibility requirement.
7. Never assume identical APIs across providers.
8. Never claim unsupported provider capabilities.
9. Never map customers using ambiguous identity matches automatically.
10. Never create duplicate CRM contacts or companies.

Important current provider implementation considerations
The prompt instructs the coding agent to verify current official documentation because provider APIs and authentication rules change.
Provider	Important requirement
Salesforce	Current documentation recommends External Client Apps for new integrations; creation of new Connected Apps has been restricted since Spring '26.  Salesforce Developers+1
HubSpot	Service Keys are intended for certain system-to-system integrations, but do not support webhooks. Webhook-based integrations need an appropriate app configuration.  developers.hubspot.com+1
HubSpot	Its 2026-09 CRM API version introduced enforcement of administrator-configured validation rules on API writes, so write validation must be tested.  developers.hubspot.com
Intercom	Webhook processing needs duplicate-delivery protection, signature validation and correct rate-limit handling.  Intercom Help+2

Official documentation for implementation:
- Salesforce OAuth and REST API.
- HubSpot developer platform.
- HubSpot webhooks.
- Intercom developer documentation.
- Intercom API rate limits.
Three requirements I particularly recommend retaining
1. Make the integration framework provider-independent. Salesforce, HubSpot and Intercom should be separate adapters connected to the same canonical customer and retention workflow. Adding another provider later should not require rewriting Phase 17.

2. Treat customer permission and approval as hard execution gates. An approved retention recommendation must still pass communication consent, suppression, contact-frequency, provider-permission and final eligibility checks before sending.

3. Preserve the complete external action history. The platform should be able to trace a recommendation to its approval, external CRM record, campaign, message, delivery event, customer response and eventual retention outcome.

The final standard: Phase 18 should turn IntelliGuard's retention recommendations into controlled, traceable workflows inside the company's actual CRM and communication platforms—not simply display provider logos or simulate integrations.


# Phase 19 — MLOps and Production Deployment



Model lifecycle and operationalization

Step 19 of 20



Phase 19 turns the existing churn prediction platform into a continuously managed ML system. It connects the work from Phases 1–18 into a governed lifecycle:

Data → Feature Store → Training → Evaluation → Model Registry → Approval → Deployment → Prediction Monitoring → Drift Detection → Controlled Retraining → New Model Release.

This phase must build on the actual model training, evaluation, SHAP, prediction engine, Customer 360, Retention Intelligence and CRM integrations already implemented. It must not create a second prediction engine or silently replace the existing production model.

The architecture will use:

- MLflow for experiment tracking, artifact management, model versioning and registry. Its tracking system records parameters, code versions, metrics and artifacts; its registry supports model lineage, versioning and aliases. A self-hosted registry requires a database-backed backend store.&#x20;

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://mlflow.org\&sz=32)

  MLflow AI Platform+2

- Apache Airflow for scheduled and dependency-managed ML workflows. The implementation must follow the currently supported Airflow architecture and task execution model.&#x20;

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://airflow.apache.org\&sz=32)

  Airflow 3.3.2 Documentation+2

- Evidently or a compatible monitoring implementation for data quality, feature drift, prediction drift and model-performance monitoring. Performance monitoring must distinguish checks that can run without actual labels from evaluation that requires matured ground truth.&#x20;

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.evidentlyai.com\&sz=32)

  Machine Learning Monitoring and Observability+2

- Existing FastAPI prediction infrastructure for the canonical inference API, unless repository inspection proves a different existing serving architecture is already authoritative.

- Existing Docker, database, security, background workers and CI/CD infrastructure wherever they are suitable.

The central rule is that detecting drift does not automatically mean a model should be retrained or deployed. Every candidate model must pass data, evaluation, governance and approval gates before it can replace the current model.

**Primary objective:** Transform the existing customer churn prediction application into a reproducible, observable, secure and continuously managed machine learning platform. **Required final outcome:** An operational MLOps platform in which every prediction can be traced to a specific deployed model release, every model can be traced to its training data and experiment, every retraining run is reproducible, every deployment is governed, and every production model can be monitored and rolled back safely.

# PART 3 — DEFINE THE COMPLETE MLOPS ARCHITECTURE

Build an integrated MLOps platform with the following logical architecture.

`Canonical Data → Phase 4 Quality → Phase 5 Labels → Phase 6 Features → Phase 7 Feature Store → Phase 11 Dataset Builder → Phase 12 Training → MLflow Tracking → Phase 13 Evaluation → Phase 14 Explainability → MLflow Model Registry → Release Approval → Phase 15 Serving → Prediction Monitoring → Drift Detection → Matured Outcome Evaluation → Retraining Decision → Candidate Pipeline → Registry → Controlled Deployment`

Supporting infrastructure:

- Apache Airflow.
- PostgreSQL.
- MLflow.
- Artifact storage.
- Docker.
- Existing application API.
- Existing Redis/Celery if appropriate.
- Existing metrics and logging.
- Drift monitoring framework.
- CI/CD.

## 3.1 Separate the responsibilities

**MLflow:**

- Experiment tracking.
- Run metadata.
- Parameters.
- Metrics.
- Model artifacts.
- Model versions.
- Model lineage.
- Registry.
- Release metadata.

**Airflow:**

- Scheduled ML workflows.
- Dataset preparation orchestration.
- Label maturity checks.
- Training orchestration.
- Evaluation orchestration.
- Monitoring workflows.
- Retraining workflows.
- Deployment workflow orchestration.

**Phase 15 FastAPI prediction service:**

- Canonical inference.
- Single and batch scoring.
- Model loading.
- Release selection.
- Prediction history.
- Feature retrieval.

**Monitoring subsystem:**

- Input quality.
- Feature drift.
- Prediction drift.
- Data freshness.
- Delayed model performance.
- Calibration.
- Operational reliability.

**Existing Celery/Redis:**

Keep it for appropriate application-level background work already using it.

Do not replace it with Airflow indiscriminately.

## 3.2 Airflow and Celery separation

Airflow should manage multi-step ML and data workflows.

Celery should continue handling suitable application background jobs, such as:

- Existing asynchronous API jobs.
- Application-level work queues.
- Existing batch scoring tasks where appropriate.
- Short-running operational work.

Do not implement competing duplicate schedulers.

Do not run every customer prediction as a separate Airflow task.

## 3.3 Data transfer between orchestration tasks

Pass references, IDs, dates and manifest locations between Airflow tasks.

Do not transfer entire customer datasets or model files through XCom.

Use the existing database and artifact storage for large objects.

- Model version.
- Raw probability.
- Calibrated probability where available.
- Risk classification.
- Threshold policy version.
- Prediction timestamp.
- Feature snapshot reference.

## 7.4 Artifact integrity

Calculate and verify cryptographic checksums for relevant artifacts.

Do not deploy a release if its model or schema artifacts are missing or inconsistent.

## 7.5 Release reproducibility

A release manifest must permit an authorized engineer to reconstruct the runtime environment and identify all relevant source artifacts.

---

# PART 8 — TASK 5: IMPLEMENT APACHE AIRFLOW ORCHESTRATION

Integrate Airflow into the existing infrastructure.

Select a supported Airflow release after compatibility testing.

Do not install an unpinned or untested dependency set.

## 8.1 Deployment architecture

Inspect the current infrastructure and select a suitable Airflow executor and deployment architecture.

Support appropriate components, depending on the selected deployment:

- Airflow API server.
- Scheduler.
- DAG processor.
- Triggerer where needed.
- Worker or executor infrastructure.
- Metadata database.
- Logging.
- Secrets backend.

Do not assume that every local development deployment needs a production-scale distributed topology.

## 8.2 Configuration

Separate:

- Development.
- Testing.
- Staging.
- Production.

Do not mix Airflow metadata with application business data without a documented boundary.

## 8.3 Airflow connections

Use secure connections and a supported secrets backend where available.

Do not store CRM provider tokens or database passwords inside DAG source files.

Do not print secrets in task logs.

## 8.4 DAG structure

Implement modular DAG files.

Suggested DAGs:

1. `churn_data_quality_monitoring`
2. `churn_feature_snapshot_pipeline`
3. `churn_label_maturity_check`
4. `churn_training_dataset_builder`
5. `churn_model_training_pipeline`
6. `churn_candidate_evaluation_pipeline`
7. `churn_model_registration_pipeline`
8. `churn_production_scoring_pipeline`
9. `churn_drift_monitoring_pipeline`
10. `churn_model_performance_monitoring`
11. `churn_retraining_orchestration`
12. `churn_deployment_validation_pipeline`
13. `churn_backup_and_integrity_checks`

Reuse existing DAGs if equivalent functionality already exists.

Do not create a separate DAG for every insignificant subtask.

## 8.5 DAG task design

Every task must have:

- Defined input.
- Defined output.
- Validation.
- Execution timeout.
- Retry policy.
- Error handling.
- Logs.
- Idempotency behavior.

## 8.6 Workflow parameters

Use explicit, validated parameters.

Examples:

- Dataset version.
- Prediction date.
- Training cutoff.
- Model version.
- Feature schema.
- Execution mode.
- Retraining reason.
- Backfill range.

Do not permit arbitrary runtime paths or unsafe executable input.

## 8.7 Scheduling

Support schedules for:

- Daily data quality checks.
- Feature freshness checks.
- Prediction monitoring.
- Weekly monitoring summaries where appropriate.
- Label maturity checks.
- Performance monitoring.
- Periodic retraining eligibility assessment.

Make schedules configurable.

Use the correct timezone.

Use Asia/Kolkata when this application requires Indian operational scheduling.

Do not confuse UTC data timestamps with local business schedules.

## 8.8 Backfills

Support controlled historical backfills.

A backfill must:

- Use valid historical data.
- Respect original feature availability.
- Respect label maturity.
- Avoid overwriting production predictions.
- Preserve historical dataset lineage.
- Require appropriate authorization.

## 8.9 Airflow monitoring

Record:

- DAG run ID.
- Task instance ID.
- Execution date.
- Data interval.
- Start and end.
- Duration.
- Status.
- Retry count.
- Error information.
- Related dataset/model/release ID.

# PART 9 — TASK 6: IMPLEMENT THE END-TO-END TRAINING DAG

Create a complete orchestrated training workflow.

The DAG must call the existing Phase 11 and Phase 12 implementations.

## 9.1 Training workflow

Recommended sequence:

1. Validate execution parameters.
2. Verify source data freshness.
3. Check Phase 4 data quality.
4. Check label maturity.
5. Validate Phase 6 feature availability.
6. Materialize or retrieve Phase 7 feature snapshots.
7. Build Phase 11 training dataset.
8. Validate dataset manifest.
9. Validate chronological splits.
10. Check leakage constraints.
11. Verify target maturity.
12. Start MLflow run.
13. Execute Phase 12 training.
14. Log parameters.
15. Log training metrics.
16. Log candidate artifacts.
17. Run validation evaluation.
18. Run applicable explainability checks.
19. Register candidate model.
20. Record completion report.

## 9.2 Training preconditions

Block training when:

- No valid data exists.
- Labels are not mature.
- Dataset manifest is missing.
- Feature schema is incompatible.
- Training split is invalid.
- Required features are missing.
- Data quality is below configured limits.
- Leakage checks fail.
- Required dependencies are unavailable.

## 9.3 Training reproducibility

Reuse exact Phase 11 split definitions.

Do not introduce random shuffling into the primary temporal evaluation process.

## 9.4 Training failure

A failed task must:

- Record the failed run.
- Preserve diagnostics.
- Avoid partial production registration.
- Permit safe retry.
- Avoid corrupting the previous model release.

# PART 10 — TASK 7: BUILD AUTOMATED MODEL EVALUATION GATES

Every retrained model must pass the same authoritative evaluation process.

## 10.1 Candidate evaluation

Call Phase 13.

Do not duplicate metrics in a new implementation.

## 10.2 Required evaluation

Evaluate:

- Accuracy.
- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- Specificity.
- Balanced accuracy.
- MCC.
- ROC-AUC.
- Average Precision.
- Brier score.
- Log loss.
- Calibration.
- Confusion matrix.
- Threshold behavior.
- Ranking quality.
- Top-risk population performance.
- Segment performance.
- Temporal stability.

## 10.3 Baseline comparisons

Compare a candidate against:

- Existing champion.
- Prior production release.
- Approved baseline.
- Appropriate simple model.

## 10.4 Evaluation gates

Make gates configurable and version-controlled.

Potential gates:

- Minimum performance.
- Maximum acceptable performance degradation.
- Minimum recall.
- Calibration tolerance.
- Segment-level safeguards.
- Data quality thresholds.
- Feature compatibility.
- Fairness or policy checks where relevant.
- Explainability validity.

Do not choose arbitrary thresholds merely to make tests pass.

Use approved Phase 13 evaluation requirements.

## 10.5 Test-set protection

Preserve Phase 11 and Phase 13 test-isolation rules.

Do not repeatedly use the final test set as an optimization tool.

A retraining process must distinguish:

- Training.
- Validation.
- Candidate comparison.
- Untouched final test evidence.
- Production monitoring.

## 10.6 Failed candidate

A failed candidate may be registered for audit as rejected, but must never become the production model.

## 10.7 Human approval

Require authorized approval for production release unless an explicitly documented deployment policy has been approved.

Do not automatically promote a model simply because a scheduled retraining task completed.

# PART 11 — TASK 8: IMPLEMENT DATA AND FEATURE DRIFT MONITORING

Use an appropriate compatible monitoring library, such as Evidently, or a validated equivalent.

Retain the monitoring interface independent of a single library.

## 11.1 Establish reference datasets

Define reference data from approved training or evaluation datasets.

Record:

- Dataset version.
- Reference period.
- Feature version.
- Model version.
- Population.
- Sample count.
- Cohort composition.

Never compare arbitrary populations without documenting differences.

## 11.2 Feature drift

Monitor changes in:

- Customer tenure.
- Subscription age.
- Plan category.
- Usage frequency.
- Active days.
- Engagement.
- Support ticket frequency.
- Payment delay.
- Overdue balance.
- Renewal window.
- Usage trend.
- Other approved production features.

## 11.3 Drift techniques

Support suitable methods for numeric and categorical variables.

Examples:

- Population Stability Index.
- Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.
- Jensen–Shannon divergence.
- Wasserstein distance.
- Chi-square or appropriate categorical tests.
- Other suitable statistical tests.

Select methods based on the feature distribution, sample size and data characteristics.

Document the method per feature.

## 11.4 Practical significance

Do not flag a business-critical issue solely because a very large sample produces a statistically significant difference.

Evaluate:

- Magnitude.
- Statistical evidence.
- Practical impact.
- Data volume.
- Segment context.
- Baseline variability.

## 11.5 Multiple comparisons

Account for multiple feature comparisons and false alarms.

Avoid treating every individual feature p-value as an independent proof of model degradation.

## 11.6 Prediction drift

Monitor:

- Churn probability distribution.
- Risk-category distribution.
- Percentage of high-risk customers.
- Prediction volume.
- Probability concentration.
- Prediction changes over time.

## 11.7 Feature quality monitoring

Monitor:

- Missing values.
- New categories.
- Unexpected ranges.
- Duplicate snapshots.
- Invalid types.
- Feature freshness.
- Broken transformations.
- Feature schema mismatch.
- Extreme values.
- Feature availability delay.

## 11.8 Segment drift

Analyze drift by:

- B2B SaaS.
- Telecom.
- Streaming.
- E-commerce subscriptions.
- Plan type.
- Customer tenure.
- Acquisition cohort.
- Customer size.
- Region where authorized.
- Customer versus subscription scope.

Do not report a segment unless sufficient and valid data exists.

## 11.9 Reference stability

Version the reference dataset.

Do not continuously replace the baseline with the latest population; doing so could hide gradual distribution changes.

## 11.10 Monitoring reports

Generate:

- Drift summary.
- Feature-level detail.
- Prediction drift.
- Segment analysis.
- Data quality.
- Alert reasons.
- Comparison period.

---

# PART 12 — TASK 9: IMPLEMENT MODEL PERFORMANCE MONITORING WITH DELAYED LABELS

Data drift is not the same as actual model performance degradation.

Implement both separately.

## 12.1 Prediction logging

Every production prediction must preserve:

- Prediction ID.
- Customer ID.
- Subscription ID where applicable.
- Prediction timestamp.
- Model release.
- Model version.
- Feature snapshot.
- Raw probability.
- Calibrated probability.
- Risk label.
- Threshold version.

## 12.2 Outcome synchronization

Use Phase 5 as the authoritative source for actual churn outcomes.

Customer responses and CRM events from Phase 18 may provide context, but they do not automatically establish churn.

## 12.3 Label maturity

Use the 30-day prediction horizon and existing label-maturity rules.

Only evaluate completed observation windows with valid labels.

## 12.4 Delayed performance metrics

Once outcomes mature, calculate:

- Precision.
- Recall.
- F1.
- Specificity.
- Balanced accuracy.
- MCC.
- ROC-AUC where appropriate.
- Average Precision.
- Brier score.
- Log loss.
- Calibration.
- Confusion matrix.

## 12.5 Evaluation cohorts

Group results by:

- Prediction date.
- Model version.
- Customer segment.
- Customer tenure.
- Product category.
- Subscription type.
- Acquisition cohort.

## 12.6 Cohort maturity

Do not mix immature and mature observation periods.

Clearly display the eligible evaluation population and excluded immature records.

## 12.7 Performance uncertainty

Account for uncertainty and repeated customer snapshots.

Use suitable confidence intervals and cluster-aware approaches where necessary.

## 12.8 Calibration drift

Track:

- Brier score changes.
- Calibration curve.
- Calibration slope.
- Calibration intercept.
- Probability reliability.

Do not silently change calibration or thresholds in production.

## 12.9 Production versus test results

Clearly separate:

- Historical test results.
- Validation results.
- Staging results.
- Production prediction drift.
- Matured production performance.

Never present production monitoring as a newly untouched benchmark test.

Implement a common monitoring service.

## 13.1 Monitoring domains

Monitor at least:

1. Data quality.
2. Data freshness.
3. Feature drift.
4. Prediction drift.
5. Model performance.
6. Calibration.

Use monitoring frequencies appropriate to data volume and operational cost.

## 13.3 Alert levels

Define:

- RECOVERY.

## 13.4 Alert configuration

Each alert requires:

## 13.5 Alert suppression

## 13.7 Monitoring dashboard

# PART 14 — TASK 11: IMPLEMENT RETRAINING DECISION INTELLIGENCE

Retraining should be controlled, evidence-based and reproducible.

Do not retrain simply because a drift alert exists.

## 14.1 Retraining trigger types

Support:

- Scheduled retraining assessment.
- Manual retraining request.
- Feature drift threshold.
- Prediction drift threshold.
- Matured performance degradation.
- Data quality recovery.
- New eligible labeled data.
- Business policy change.
- Model dependency or schema upgrade.

## 14.2 Trigger classification

Classify each trigger:

- IMMEDIATE_INVESTIGATION.
- MONITOR_ONLY.
- RETRAINING_RECOMMENDED.
- RETRAINING_APPROVED.
- RETRAINING_BLOCKED.
- NO_ACTION_REQUIRED.

## 14.3 Trigger evidence

Every retraining decision must contain:

- Trigger source.
- Metric.
- Reference.
- Current value.
- Threshold.
- Observation window.
- Sample size.
- Impact.
- Recommendation.
- Decision maker.
- Timestamp.

## 14.4 Minimum training data

Require sufficient new mature labels.

Do not repeatedly train on an unchanged dataset simply because a schedule runs.

## 14.5 Retraining eligibility

Check:

- Mature labels available.
- Data freshness.
- Feature freshness.
- Data quality.
- Label distribution.
- Churn event coverage.
- Training sample size.
- Temporal coverage.
- Dataset novelty.
- Existing model age.
- Prior retraining result.

## 14.6 No automatic retraining loop

Prevent an alert-triggered infinite training loop.

Use:

- Cooldown.
- Deduplication.
- Minimum dataset change.
- Run-level idempotency.
- Failure backoff.
- Manual approval where required.

## 14.7 Retraining recommendation

Provide a reasoned explanation:

- Why retraining is recommended.
- Which model is affected.
- Which features drifted.
- Whether labels are mature.
- Whether actual performance declined.
- Whether new data is sufficient.
- What risks exist.

## 14.8 Retraining execution

The decision engine may request a retraining DAG.

It must not bypass candidate evaluation or deployment approval.

# PART 15 — TASK 12: BUILD A GOVERNED RETRAINING PIPELINE

Create a complete retraining workflow.

## 15.1 Pipeline

`Retraining Trigger → Eligibility Validation → Label Maturity → Data Quality → Feature Snapshot → Dataset Builder → Candidate Training → Evaluation → SHAP Verification → Model Registry → Human Approval → Staging → Deployment Decision`

## 15.2 Dataset builder

Invoke Phase 11.

Preserve chronological splits.

Never replace the primary temporal evaluation strategy with random splitting.

## 15.3 New training window

Support configurable training windows.

Record:

- Training start.
- Training cutoff.
- Label maturity cutoff.
- Source data cutoff.
- Feature materialization cutoff.

## 15.4 Candidate training

Invoke Phase 12.

Use existing training implementations.

Track all runs in MLflow.

## 15.5 Evaluation

Invoke Phase 13.

Compare with current champion using consistent datasets and definitions.

## 15.6 Explainability

Invoke Phase 14.

Ensure the registered candidate's explanations refer to the exact candidate model and preprocessing pipeline.

## 15.7 Registration

Register only complete artifacts.

## 15.8 Approval

Require required technical and business approvals.

## 15.9 Rejected candidate

Preserve candidate details and rejection reasons.

Do not delete failed model history.

## 15.10 Retraining report

Record:

- Trigger.
- Input data.
- Dataset version.
- Model version.
- Metrics.
- Comparison.
- SHAP status.
- Decision.
- Approval.
- Next action.

# PART 17 — TASK 14: IMPLEMENT STAGING DEPLOYMENT

Before production, deploy to a staging environment where one is configured.

## 17.1 Staging environment

The staging environment must use:

- A separate configuration.
- Isolated credentials.
- Approved staging data.
- The exact candidate artifact.
- The actual inference application.
- Comparable preprocessing.
- Appropriate monitoring.

## 17.2 Staging checks

Verify:

1. Model artifact retrieval.
2. Model integrity.
3. Model loading.
4. Preprocessing compatibility.
5. Feature schema.
6. Missing-value handling.
7. Output schema.
8. Probability range.
9. Calibration application.

11. Prediction latency.
12. Batch scoring.
13. Error handling.
14. SHAP compatibility.
15. Model metadata.
16. Logging.
17. Health checks.
18. Release identification.

## 17.3 Golden test examples

Use versioned, non-sensitive fixture observations.

Compare inference output with approved expected outputs within justified numeric tolerances.

## 17.4 Shadow deployment

Where infrastructure permits, support shadow scoring.

A candidate receives eligible inputs but does not replace the champion or alter customer-facing behavior.

- Prediction probability.
- Risk category.
- Latency.

- Segment differences.

## 17.5 Canary deployment

Where an appropriate routing infrastructure exists, support controlled canary rollout.

- Monitoring window.
- Failure conditions.
- Rollback conditions.

## 17.6 Approval gate

Staging success is not automatic production approval.

Support deployment according to the actual environment:

- Local Docker deployment.
- Staging Docker deployment.
- Production VM deployment.
- Managed container deployment.
- Kubernetes deployment when genuinely required and available.

Do not require Kubernetes for a small deployment without a justified need.

## 18.2 Production model loading

The Phase 15 prediction service must load an explicitly approved model release.

Use exact registry version or resolved, audited champion release.

Never use:

- Arbitrary latest model path.
- Unverified local model file.
- Partially downloaded model.
- Candidate not yet approved.

## 18.3 Atomic release change

Model release changes must be controlled.

## 18.4 Model release manifest

- Current release.

- Model version.

- Threshold.

Do not reclassify historical predictions using the new model.

## 18.7 Prediction model lineage

Every new prediction must record the actual active release.

Verify this through API tests and database records.

# PART 19 — TASK 16: IMPLEMENT SAFE MODEL ROLLBACK

Rollback is a mandatory production capability.

## 19.1 Rollback triggers

Examples:

- Model load failure.
- Inference error increase.
- Unexpected prediction distribution.
- Performance degradation.
- Feature schema failure.
- Critical data quality issue.
- Latency regression.
- Calibration failure.
- Release integrity issue.

## 19.2 Rollback procedure

1. Detect rollback condition.
2. Create rollback incident.
3. Identify current release.
4. Identify last approved healthy release.
5. Validate previous artifact availability.
6. Validate its schema and dependencies.
7. Obtain required authorization.
8. Switch serving configuration atomically.
9. Verify readiness.
10. Verify test predictions.
11. Record rollback.
12. Notify authorized operators.

For an explicitly approved emergency policy, define whether rollback may be automatically triggered by a severe technical-health condition. Do not silently automate a business-model decision.

## 19.3 Rollback preservation

Keep:

- Failed release.
- Previous release.
- Error diagnostics.
- Deployment ID.
- Rollback reason.
- Approval.
- Timestamp.

## 19.4 Rollback testing

Test rollback without corrupting the active production model.

## 19.5 Rollback safety

Do not delete old model versions that are required for recovery.

Allow an authorized user to compare candidate and champion models.

Display:

- Metrics.
- Calibration.
- Segment performance.
- Data version.
- Model version.
- Feature schema.
- Explainability verification.

## 23.5 Airflow workflow dashboard

Display:

- DAGs.
- Last execution.
- Next scheduled run.
- Running tasks.
- Failed tasks.
- Retry count.
- Execution duration.
- Logs where authorized.

Use actual Airflow integration or APIs.

Do not fabricate workflow executions.

## 23.6 Drift monitoring dashboard

Display:

- Feature drift.
- Prediction drift.
- Data quality.
- Feature freshness.
- Segment drift.
- Reference period.
- Current period.
- Monitoring status.

## 23.7 Performance dashboard

Display matured-label metrics separately from unlabeled drift indicators.

Show sample counts and observation maturity.

## 23.8 Retraining dashboard

Display:

- Retraining requests.
- Trigger reasons.
- Eligibility checks.
- Candidate training.
- Evaluation.
- Approval.
- Final decision.

## 23.9 Deployment dashboard

Display:

- Release.
- Environment.
- Model version.
- Approval.
- Deployment time.
- Health.
- Previous release.
- Rollback availability.

## 23.10 Alert center

Display:

- Alert type.
- Severity.
- Model version.
- Metric.
- Observation period.
- Trigger.
- Owner.
- Resolution status.

## 23.11 UI interaction requirements

Every control must be functional.

Implement:

- Trigger monitoring.
- Request retraining.
- View experiment.
- Compare models.
- Approve candidate.
- Deploy approved release.
- View deployment history.
- Roll back with authorization.
- Inspect workflow history.
- Open monitoring reports.

No decorative buttons that do nothing.

Enforce:

Store artifact references and checksums.
