# PART 26 — TASK 23: IMPLEMENT MODEL GOVERNANCE AND SECURITY

Security must apply to the full MLOps lifecycle.

## 26.1 Access control

Reuse existing authentication and RBAC.

Enforce role-based permissions for:

- Experiment viewing.
- Model registration.
- Model approval.
- Production deployment.
- Rollback.
- Retraining.
- Monitoring configuration.
- Workflow execution.

## 26.2 Environment segregation

Separate development, staging and production credentials.

Do not permit development users to modify the production model without authorization.

## 26.3 Secret management

Use the existing secure credential architecture or a compatible secrets backend.

Do not hardcode:

- MLflow credentials.
- Database passwords.
- Storage credentials.
- Deployment credentials.
- Airflow connections.
- API tokens.

## 26.4 Airflow security

Restrict:

- DAG modification.
- DAG execution.
- Connection access.
- Variable access.
- Log access.
- Administrative operations.

Use a secrets backend where supported.

## 26.5 MLflow security

Protect:

- Tracking server.
- Registry operations.
- Artifact storage.
- Model download.
- Release promotion.

## 26.6 Artifact security

Validate uploaded or retrieved model artifacts.

Do not load arbitrary untrusted serialized model files.

Restrict the approved model artifact format and provenance.

## 26.7 Data privacy

Production monitoring should avoid storing unnecessary personally identifiable information.

Use canonical IDs or protected references.

Do not put customer message content, CRM credentials or full sensitive customer profiles into MLflow parameters or Airflow logs.

## 26.8 Audit events

Audit:

- Training started.
- Training completed.
- Candidate registered.
- Candidate rejected.
- Model approved.
- Deployment requested.
- Deployment approved.
- Deployment started.
- Deployment completed.
- Rollback requested.
- Rollback completed.
- Monitoring threshold modified.
- Retraining policy modified.

## 26.9 Model integrity

Verify checksums before model loading and before deployment.

---

# PART 27 — TASK 24: MONITOR DATA AND MODEL QUALITY SEPARATELY

Create explicit dashboards and separate metrics.

## 27.1 Data quality

Monitor:

- Missing records.
- Missing features.
- Invalid types.
- Invalid ranges.
- Duplicate observations.
- Invalid labels.
- Late arrivals.
- Source coverage.
- Feature freshness.

## 27.2 Data drift

Monitor changes in incoming feature distributions.

No churn ground truth is required for these checks.

## 27.3 Prediction drift

Monitor changes in predicted probability and risk-category distributions.

No churn ground truth is required for these checks.

## 27.4 Model performance degradation

Monitor only after actual outcomes have matured and been validated.

## 27.5 Business performance

Keep retention and business outcomes separate from ML quality.

Examples:

- Renewal rate.
- Payment recovery.
- Product engagement.
- Customer lifetime value.

These measurements do not independently prove model quality.

## 27.6 Campaign influence

Do not claim that a model caused better retention merely because CRM campaign metrics improved.

Campaign effectiveness requires appropriate experimental or causal evidence.

Generate a model card for each registered release.

## 28.1 Model identity

Include:

- Model name.

- Model type.
- Intended use.

- Prediction horizon.

## 28.2 Training information

Include:

- Training metrics.
- Validation metrics.
- Test metrics.
- Temporal metrics.
- Segment metrics.
- Calibration.
- Uncertainty.
- Evaluation limitations.

## 28.4 Explainability

Include:

- Global SHAP.
- Feature attribution.
- Known limitations.
- Correlation caveats.
- Explanation verification.

## 28.5 Operational details

Include:

- Artifact location.
- Dependency versions.
- Serving schema.
- Deployment environments.
- Active release.
- Monitoring requirements.
- Rollback reference.

## 28.6 Data limitations

Clearly state whether the evidence is based on:

- Synthetic data.
- Public data.
- Authorized company data.
- Mixed-source data.

Do not claim synthetic benchmark results prove production performance.

# PART 29 — TASK 26: IMPLEMENT BACKUP AND DISASTER RECOVERY

Design a recovery process for MLOps infrastructure.

## 29.1 Required backup targets

Back up:

- MLflow metadata.
- Model registry records.
- Model artifacts.
- Application deployment manifests.
- Model release metadata.
- Required Airflow metadata.
- Relevant configuration.
- Monitoring and audit records.

## 29.2 Backup schedule

Configure a backup schedule appropriate to data volume and infrastructure.

## 29.3 Backup integrity

Verify:

- File integrity.
- Database consistency.
- Artifact availability.
- Model checksum.
- Restore compatibility.

## 29.4 Recovery tests

Perform an actual restoration in an isolated test environment.

## 29.5 Recovery documentation

Document:

- Backup location.
- Recovery order.
- Required credentials.
- Database restoration.
- Artifact restoration.
- Registry verification.
- Model deployment recovery.
- Service validation.

Do not report a backup as verified merely because the backup command succeeded.

# PART 30 — TASK 27: BUILD END-TO-END MLOPS WORKFLOWS

Implement and verify these complete workflows.

## WORKFLOW A — New training run

`Phase 11 Dataset → Phase 12 Training → MLflow Run → Phase 13 Evaluation → Phase 14 SHAP → Registry Candidate`

Expected result:

- Run tracked.
- Artifacts stored.
- Dataset lineage preserved.
- Candidate registered.
- Candidate not automatically deployed.

## WORKFLOW B — Scheduled monitoring

`Airflow Scheduler → Input Quality → Feature Drift → Prediction Drift → Report → Alert`

Expected result:

- Actual observation windows.
- Actual monitoring results.
- Alert evidence.
- No invented model degradation.

## WORKFLOW C — Matured model performance

`Prediction Records → Phase 5 Matured Labels → Performance Evaluation → Segment Analysis → Monitoring Report`

Expected result:

- Only eligible observations evaluated.
- Matured and immature observations distinguished.
- Model version linked.

## WORKFLOW D — Retraining assessment

`Drift/Performance Alert → Eligibility Validation → Mature Labels Check → Retraining Recommendation`

Expected result:

- Explainable retraining decision.
- No repeated duplicate retraining.
- No automatic production promotion.

## WORKFLOW E — Controlled retraining

`Approved Retraining → Dataset Builder → Training → Evaluation → SHAP → Model Registry`

Expected result:

- Complete candidate package.
- Model comparison.
- Approval required.

## WORKFLOW F — Model staging

`Approved Candidate → Staging Deployment → Golden Tests → Shadow Evaluation → Deployment Readiness`

Expected result:

- Valid artifact.
- Inference compatibility.
- Operational health.
- Release evidence.

## WORKFLOW G — Production deployment

`Approval → Deployment Request → Release Verification → Serving Switch → Health Check → Active Model`

Expected result:

- Exact version deployed.
- Existing serving API preserved.
- New predictions carry the new model release ID.

## WORKFLOW H — Rollback

`Monitoring Alert → Rollback Decision → Previous Release Validation → Serving Reversion → Health Check → Audit`

Expected result:

- Previous release restored.
- Historical predictions preserved.
- Full rollback record.

## WORKFLOW I — Full MLOps lifecycle

Verify the entire lifecycle from a valid dataset snapshot to a deployed, monitored, rollback-ready model.

# PART 31 — TASK 28: BUILD OBSERVABILITY AND ALERT NOTIFICATIONS

Reuse existing notification infrastructure.

Do not send customer-facing retention communications from MLOps monitoring.

## 31.1 Operational alerts

Support:

- Training failure.
- Airflow DAG failure.
- MLflow unavailable.
- Artifact storage unavailable.
- Data quality failure.
- Feature drift.
- Prediction drift.
- Matured model-performance degradation.
- Model loading failure.
- Prediction API unavailable.
- Deployment failure.
- Rollback completed.
- Retraining blocked.

## 31.2 Notification destinations

Use existing authorized internal notification channels.

Optional provider integrations must be explicitly configured and tested.

## 31.3 Alert evidence

Every alert must link to:

- Monitoring run.
- Model version.
- Dataset version.
- Affected features.
- Relevant logs.
- Suggested investigation.

## 31.4 Notification deduplication

Prevent repeated notifications for the same unresolved incident.

# PART 32 — TASK 29: TESTING AND VERIFICATION

Testing must cover real working components, not only syntax or mocked method calls.

Mocking is acceptable for isolated unit and provider-independent tests.

It does not prove production deployment.

## 32.1 MLflow tests

Verify:

- Tracking server starts.
- Experiment creation.
- Run creation.
- Parameter logging.
- Metric logging.
- Artifact logging.
- Run retrieval.
- Database persistence.
- Model registration.
- Model version retrieval.
- Alias resolution.
- Artifact download.
- Model load.
- Restart persistence.

## 32.2 Airflow tests

Verify:

- Airflow services start.
- DAG import.
- DAG parsing.
- Dependency graph.
- Scheduling.
- Task execution.
- Task retry.
- Failure propagation.
- Idempotency.
- Run history.
- Recovery after failure.

## 32.3 Dataset tests

Verify:

- Phase 11 integration.
- Dataset checksum.
- Mature labels.
- Chronological splits.
- Feature schema.
- Leakage tests.
- Training manifest.

## 32.4 Training tests

Verify:

- All configured models.
- MLflow run logging.
- Model artifacts.
- Dependency consistency.
- Repeatable run configuration.
- Candidate registration.

## 32.5 Evaluation tests

Verify:

- Phase 13 is invoked.
- Metrics are correctly recorded.
- Test isolation remains intact.
- Segment performance is available.
- Candidate gates reject unacceptable models.

## 32.6 Explainability tests

Verify:

- Exact candidate model.
- Correct feature mapping.
- SHAP calculation.
- Artifact storage.
- Prediction match.
- Explanation reproducibility where expected.

## 32.7 Drift tests

Create controlled test distributions.

Test:

- Stable feature distribution.
- Numeric feature shift.
- Categorical feature shift.
- Missing-value increase.
- New category.
- Feature schema change.
- Sample-size effects.
- Prediction shift.

Do not use random synthetic variation as evidence of an actual production drift event.

## 32.8 Performance monitoring tests

Verify:

- Matured labels included.
- Immature labels excluded.
- Unknown labels excluded.
- Metrics calculated correctly.
- Model version grouping.
- Temporal grouping.
- Customer overlap treatment.

## 32.9 Retraining tests

Verify:

- Scheduled eligibility.
- Drift-triggered eligibility.
- Performance-triggered eligibility.
- Insufficient labels block.
- Duplicate trigger prevention.
- Failed run recovery.
- Rejected model preservation.

## 32.10 Staging deployment tests

Verify:

- Correct model version.
- Artifact checksum.
- Model loading.
- Feature schema.
- Input validation.
- Output contract.
- Batch inference.
- Latency.
- Readiness.

## 32.11 Production deployment tests

Where production infrastructure is available, verify:

- Release approval.
- Deployment.
- Correct active version.
- Prediction lineage.
- Health.
- Monitoring.
- Rollback.

When production infrastructure is unavailable, report BLOCKED and complete the local equivalent.

## 32.12 Rollback tests

Verify restoration of a previous approved release.

Test that the new failed release does not corrupt prior model metadata.

## 32.13 Security tests

Verify:

- Authentication.
- RBAC.
- Secrets.
- Artifact access.
- Tenant separation.
- Deployment approval.
- Unauthorized rollback rejection.
- Log privacy.

## 32.14 Full regression tests

Rerun all relevant previous phase tests:

- Phase 1 foundation.
- Phase 2 datasets.
- Phase 3 ingestion.
- Phase 4 validation.
- Phase 5 labels.
- Phase 6 features.
- Phase 7 Feature Store.
- Phase 8 EDA.
- Phase 9 cohorts.
- Phase 10 survival.
- Phase 11 dataset preparation.
- Phase 12 training.
- Phase 13 evaluation.
- Phase 14 SHAP.
- Phase 15 prediction.
- Phase 16 Customer 360.
- Phase 17 Retention Intelligence.
- Phase 18 CRM and campaigns.

No existing functionality may silently regress.

# PART 33 — TASK 30: PERFORMANCE, RELIABILITY AND SCALABILITY

Benchmark actual behavior.

## 33.1 Training performance

Measure:

- Training time.
- Dataset build time.
- Model load time.
- Memory use.
- Artifact size.

## 33.2 Airflow performance

Measure:

- DAG scheduling delay.
- Task execution time.
- Retry duration.
- Queue backlog.
- Worker utilization.

## 33.3 MLflow performance

Measure:

- Run creation.
- Metric logging.
- Artifact upload.
- Artifact retrieval.
- Registry lookup.
- Model version loading.

## 33.4 Prediction performance

Use Phase 15.

Measure:

- Single-record inference.
- Batch inference.
- Concurrent requests.
- P50/P95/P99 latency.
- Error rate.
- Model-loading overhead.

## 33.5 Monitoring performance

Measure:

- Dataset profiling.
- Drift comparison.
- Segment monitoring.
- Performance evaluation.
- Report generation.

## 33.6 Resilience

Test:

- Database restart.
- MLflow restart.
- Artifact storage interruption.
- Airflow scheduler restart.
- Worker restart.
- API restart.
- Model-load failure.

## 33.7 Graceful degradation

The main prediction service should not become unavailable merely because an optional dashboard or monitoring report service is temporarily unavailable.

Where a required dependency is unavailable, display an explicit degraded state rather than silently returning misleading predictions.

## Three critical decisions for your implementation

1\. Keep MLflow and Airflow separate. MLflow manages models and experiments; Airflow coordinates workflows. The existing FastAPI prediction engine continues serving predictions. This prevents three competing systems from managing the same model lifecycle.

2\. Do not confuse drift with model accuracy. The platform can detect feature and prediction distribution changes before actual churn labels are available. Actual performance assessment must wait for sufficiently mature churn outcomes.

3\. Build local deployment first, then verify remote deployment. Since the earlier project scope allows synthetic or public data until company data and infrastructure are available, the agent should finish a reproducible local stack and label real-company validation and production hosting as blocked when those resources are unavailable.

The official technical references for the agent to follow are [MLflow](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Apache Airflow](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [Evidently](https://docs.evidentlyai.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). This keeps the implementation tied to their current supported interfaces rather than outdated tutorials.

## 4.1 Traceability rules

A requirement cannot receive PASS simply because a source file exists.

Evidence must demonstrate that the functionality is implemented and works.

For example:

Requirement: Import a customer CSV file.

Insufficient evidence:

- The upload page exists.
- A CSV parser function exists.
- The upload endpoint returns HTTP 200.

Sufficient evidence should demonstrate:

1. User uploads a valid CSV.
2. Backend receives and validates it.
3. Canonical field mapping is applied.
4. Data quality checks execute.
5. Records are staged and persisted.
6. Batch status is correct.
7. Import summary is generated.
8. Records can be retrieved.
9. Provenance is preserved.
10. Invalid records are accounted for.

## 4.2 Create the master manifest

`docs/verification/REQUIREMENT_TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`

`reports/phase-20/requirement_traceability.json`

- Pause.
- Suspension.
- Reactivation.
- Failed payments.
- Payment retry.
- Grace periods.
- Expiration.
- Multi-subscription customer behavior.
- Mature and immature observation windows.

Primary target:

`churn_30d`

Preserve the approved target interval:

`T < churn_event_at <= T + 30 days`

Test:

1. Valid positive label.
2. Mature negative label.
3. Immature label.
4. Unknown label.
5. Censored observation.
6. Cancellation request without effective churn.
7. Failed payment without confirmed churn.
8. Retry followed by successful payment.
9. Reactivation.
10. Paused subscription.
11. Multiple subscriptions.
12. One churned subscription with another active subscription.
13. Missing event timestamp.
14. Conflicting source events.
15. Late-arriving churn event.
16. Correct label revision behavior.

Never silently convert unknown labels to zero.

Never treat a payment failure as confirmed churn by itself.

## PHASE 6 — FEATURE ENGINEERING

Verify:

- RFM.
- Usage.
- Engagement.
- Payment reliability.
- Support activity.
- Subscription lifecycle.
- Tenure.
- Inactivity.
- 7-day trends.
- 30-day trends.
- Missingness.
- Feature aggregation.
- Customer scope.
- Subscription scope.

Critical leakage checks:

- Event time must precede prediction cutoff.
- Feature availability time must not exceed prediction cutoff.
- Future information must never enter historical predictions.
- Target-derived fields must never become predictor features.
- Post-churn fields must not be used to predict earlier churn.

Test time-zone boundaries, late-arriving events, duplicate events and partial observation windows.

## PHASE 7 — FEATURE STORE

Verify:

- Feature registry.
- Feature definitions.
- Offline storage.
- Historical snapshots.
- Point-in-time retrieval.
- Materialization.
- Backfill.
- Feature versioning.
- Schema compatibility.
- Lineage.
- Snapshot immutability.
- Retrieval APIs.

Test that historical snapshots cannot be silently changed by later source updates.

Test correct feature retrieval for a historical prediction cutoff.

## PHASE 8 — EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS

- Missingness analysis.
- Distribution analysis.
- Correlations.
- Appropriate statistical testing.
- Effect sizes.
- Confidence intervals.
- Multiple-testing controls.
- Segment analysis.
- Churn analysis.
- Visualizations.
- Report exports.

Verify calculations against independently computed fixtures.

Do not interpret correlation as causation.

Do not report unsupported statistical significance.

- Cohort period.
- Retention calculation.

- Immature cohort periods.

- Subscription retention.
- Engagement retention.

- Reactivation.
- Churn breakdown.
- Heatmaps.
- Cohort curves.

Check that acquisition dates are based on the authoritative acquisition event and do not silently fall back to subscription start dates.

Verify immature periods are censored rather than treated as zero retention.

## PHASE 10 — SURVIVAL ANALYSIS

- Censoring.
- At-risk population.

- Group comparisons.

- Visualization.

Test the calculation with small datasets for which the expected survival curve can be independently calculated.

Keep survival probability distinct from binary churn probability.

- Zero denominators.

- Exact feature snapshot.

## PHASE 15 — PREDICTION ENGINE

- Single predictions.
- Batch predictions.
- Scheduling.
- Feature retrieval.
- Schema validation.
- Threshold handling.

- Risk classification.
- Prediction history.
- Model release lineage.
- Idempotency.
- Chunking.
- Retry.
- Partial failure handling.
- Freshness validation.
- Inference health.

Critical checks:

1. The service must use the exact approved model version.
2. No arbitrary latest artifact may be selected.
3. Invalid input must produce a controlled error.
4. One failed batch row must not corrupt all successful rows.
5. Repeated idempotent operations must not create uncontrolled duplicate predictions.
6. Historical predictions must retain the model version that created them.
7. Prediction outputs must conform to the established API schema.

Testing individual functions is not sufficient.

- Review.

- Dataset accounting.

## E2E-007 — Training dataset creation

Train a supported model.

Track it.

Evaluate it.

Verify stored artifacts.

Generate explainability evidence.

Verify candidate approval status.

## E2E-009 — Customer prediction

Score a customer.

Verify probability, threshold, risk category, prediction record and lineage.

## E2E-010 — Customer 360

Verify that the prediction, profile, subscriptions, billing, usage, support and SHAP information refer to the correct entity and model version.

## E2E-011 — Retention recommendation

Verify evidence, prioritization, eligibility, consent and approval.

Do not execute an external communication.

## E2E-014 — Drift monitoring

Verify actual metrics and exclusion of immature labels.

## E2E-016 — Controlled retraining

Trigger retraining assessment.

Verify eligibility and candidate generation.

Do not promote the candidate automatically.

## E2E-017 — Staging deployment

Deploy an approved candidate to a test or staging environment.

Verify model loading, schemas, inference, health and rollback availability.

Using browser automation:

2. Open main dashboard.
3. Import datasets.
4. Review quality.
5. Inspect churn cohorts.
6. Open model evaluation.
7. View SHAP explanation.

9. Open Customer 360.
10. Generate retention recommendation.
11. Review integration status.
12. Open MLOps dashboard.
13. Inspect model release.
14. Review monitoring report.
15. Sign out.

Every step must perform a real supported action.

# SECTION 11 — COMPLETE DATA QUALITY AND STATISTICAL VERIFICATION

The platform is an ML system, so statistical correctness matters as much as software correctness.

## 11.1 Independent calculation tests

Create small hand-calculated datasets.

Independently verify:

- Churn labels.
- RFM.
- Feature trends.
- Retention rates.
- Cohort denominators.
- Kaplan–Meier estimates.
- Confusion matrices.
- Performance metrics.
- Calibration.
- SHAP aggregation.
- Drift statistics.

Compare application output with independently calculated expected values.

## 11.2 Boundary conditions

Test:

- Empty dataset.
- One record.
- One customer.
- No churn events.
- All churn events.
- Only unknown labels.
- Mixed mature and immature records.
- Single-class prediction labels.
- Missing features.
- Constant features.
- Extreme numeric values.
- Duplicate events.
- Late events.
- Conflicting records.

## 11.3 Statistical correctness

Verify:

- Correct target definition.
- Correct event cutoff.
- Correct time windows.
- Correct censoring.
- Correct confidence intervals.
- Suitable hypothesis tests.
- Multiple-testing safeguards.
- Correct metric denominator.
- Correct probability interpretation.

## 11.4 Class imbalance

Verify that:

- Metrics remain meaningful under imbalance.
- Precision and recall are not interchanged.
- Average Precision is not mislabeled as trapezoidal PR-AUC.
- ROC-AUC does not replace precision-recall analysis.
- Baseline performance is reported correctly.
- Thresholds are selected with the correct split.

## 11.5 No leakage

Run specific tests for:

- Future events.
- Post-churn records.
- Future financial outcomes.
- Data availability timestamps.
- Target-derived fields.
- Global preprocessing fitted using test data.
- Feature selection leakage.
- Test-set tuning.

Any confirmed material leakage is a critical defect.

# SECTION 12 — MODEL AND ML PIPELINE VALIDATION

Build a comprehensive ML verification suite.

## 12.1 Model serialization

For every supported model:

1. Train using a controlled fixture.
2. Serialize.
3. Store artifact.
4. Load from stored artifact.
5. Generate predictions.
6. Compare with pre-serialization predictions.

Use documented numeric tolerances.

## 12.2 Preprocessing consistency

Verify:

- Missing-value imputation.
- Numeric scaling.
- Categorical encoding.
- Feature ordering.
- Unknown categories.
- Column selection.
- Data type conversion.

The same fitted preprocessing must be used during the corresponding inference process.

## 12.3 Model probability integrity

Verify:

- Probability is finite.
- Probability is between 0 and 1.
- Probability mapping is correct.
- Positive class is correct.
- Calibration configuration is applied correctly.
- Risk categorization uses the correct threshold.

## 12.4 Model comparison integrity

Confirm that candidate and champion comparison uses:

- The same evaluation definition.
- Comparable data.
- The same target.
- Consistent horizon.
- Appropriate temporal splits.

## 12.5 Production prediction integrity

Every prediction must retain:

- Customer or subscription scope.
- Prediction timestamp.
- Model release.
- Model version.
- Feature snapshot.
- Threshold policy.
- Probability.
- Risk classification.

## 12.6 SHAP consistency

Verify that the SHAP artifact used for a prediction refers to the correct exact model version and feature snapshot.

## 12.7 No fabricated ML performance

Every reported metric must have an identifiable:

- Dataset.
- Dataset version.
- Split.
- Model version.
- Evaluation code.
- Run ID.
- Metric definition.

If that provenance is missing, report the metric as unverified.

- Database restart.
- Query timeout.
- Transaction rollback.
- Recovery.

## 16.2 Redis and worker failure

Where used:

- Redis restart.
- Worker shutdown.
- Task retry.
- Queue recovery.
- Duplicate execution prevention.

## 16.3 Airflow failure

Test:

- Scheduler restart.
- Task failure.
- Worker loss.
- Retried DAG task.
- Partial pipeline completion.

## 16.4 MLflow failure

Test:

- Tracking server unavailable.
- Artifact storage unavailable.
- Registry retrieval failure.
- Recovery after restart.

## 16.5 API failure

Test:

- Backend unavailable.
- Timeout.
- Invalid response.
- Partial source failure.

The frontend should display controlled errors instead of crashing.

## 16.6 Model failure

Test:

- Missing model file.
- Corrupt artifact.
- Invalid checksum.
- Incompatible schema.
- Model load exception.
- Prediction exception.

The system must not silently substitute an unapproved model.

## 16.7 External provider failure

Test CRM:

- Invalid token.
- Expired token.
- Provider timeout.
- HTTP 429.
- HTTP 5xx.
- Duplicate webhook.
- Invalid signature.
- Event replay.
- Dead-letter recovery.

Use sandbox or test fixtures.

## 16.8 Backup and recovery

Run an actual backup and restore exercise.

Verify restored:

- Application data.
- Model registry metadata.
- Model artifacts.
- Release metadata.
- Required orchestration metadata.

Document recovery gaps.

# SECTION 17 — DEFECT DETECTION, CLASSIFICATION AND REPAIR

This is a critical requirement of Phase 20.

Do not stop after identifying defects.

Fix all defects that can safely be fixed within the project scope.

## 17.1 Defect severity

Classify findings as:

### CRITICAL

Examples:

- Authentication bypass.
- Unauthorized customer data access.
- Cross-tenant data leakage.
- Silent financial corruption.
- Incorrect churn labels affecting the target.
- Confirmed future-data leakage.
- Production model replaced without approval.
- Model corruption.
- Data loss.
- Unsafe external communication execution.

### HIGH

Examples:

- Core workflow unavailable.
- Incorrect predictions caused by preprocessing mismatch.
- Broken ingestion.
- Incorrect feature snapshots.
- Invalid evaluation.
- Broken Customer 360 relationships.
- Airflow pipeline corruption.
- Failed model rollback.
- Missing database constraints causing inconsistent records.

### MEDIUM

Examples:

- Incorrect filters.
- Broken report download.
- Partial dashboard data.
- Noncritical API errors.
- Retry inconsistencies.
- Poor error messages.
- Monitoring dashboard failures.

### LOW

Examples:

- Minor visual defects.
- Text errors.
- Nonessential layout inconsistencies.
- Documentation formatting defects.

## 17.2 Defect record

Every defect must contain:

- Defect ID.
- Title.
- Severity.
- Discovery date.
- Phase affected.
- Environment.
- Reproduction steps.
- Expected behavior.
- Actual behavior.
- Root cause.
- Affected files.
- Corrective action.
- Test added.
- Fix commit.
- Retest result.
- Regression result.
- Final status.

## 17.3 Root-cause analysis

Do not implement a superficial workaround when the underlying issue can be corrected.

Investigate:

- Data contract mismatch.
- Incorrect business logic.
- Schema mismatch.
- Time-zone error.
- Race condition.
- Missing transaction.
- Missing permission.
- Incorrect model artifact.
- Incorrect environment variable.
- Dependency conflict.
- Frontend state error.
- API response mismatch.
- Migration problem.

## 17.4 Repair sequence

Prioritize:

1. Critical security and data integrity defects.
2. Critical churn-label and leakage defects.
3. Backend startup defects.
4. Database and migration defects.
5. Data ingestion and validation defects.
6. Feature and dataset defects.
7. Model training and evaluation defects.
8. Prediction defects.
9. Customer 360 and retention workflow defects.
10. CRM and integration defects.
11. MLOps and deployment defects.
12. UI functionality defects.
13. Performance and reliability defects.
14. Documentation defects.

## 17.5 Repair constraints

- Make the smallest safe change.
- Reuse existing services.
- Preserve established API contracts unless correction requires a versioned change.
- Write a regression test for each fixed defect.
- Avoid broad refactoring during defect stabilization.
- Never delete test evidence.
- Never suppress failing tests to get a green result.
- Never change expected outputs merely to make incorrect code pass.
- Never weaken validation without a documented reason.

## 17.6 Defect closure

A defect may be marked FIXED only when:

1. The correction exists.
2. A test reproducing the original issue exists.
3. The test passes after the correction.
4. Related regression tests pass.
5. The source change is recorded.

Otherwise classify it as OPEN, BLOCKED or ACCEPTED_RISK with justification.

## 21.4 Allowed statuses

Use only the following statuses:

**PASS:** The requirement is implemented and supported by actual passing evidence.

**FAIL:** The requirement is implemented but does not meet acceptance criteria.

**BLOCKED:** Verification cannot be completed because a required external dependency, account, authorized dataset, credential or environment is unavailable.

**NOT IMPLEMENTED:** The required functionality does not exist.

**NOT TESTED:** The requirement exists, but no adequate test was executed.

**NOT APPLICABLE:** The requirement is genuinely outside the approved project scope, with an explanation.

**ACCEPTED_RISK:** A known issue is explicitly accepted by an authorized decision maker. This is not equivalent to PASS.

Do not mark blocked or untested requirements as passed.

## 21.5 Final release gate

The application must not receive an unconditional final PASS when:

- A critical defect remains open.
- A high-severity defect affecting core functionality remains unresolved.
- A critical security vulnerability remains unaddressed.
- Churn labels are materially incorrect.
- Confirmed leakage exists.
- Model inference is incompatible with the approved artifact.
- Database migrations destroy required data.
- Production release governance can be bypassed.
- A core business workflow is broken.
- A required verification is falsely reported as complete.

The report may still establish that the local application is substantially verified while clearly identifying external production blockers.

These commands are desired interfaces, not permission to create a Makefile with commands that do nothing.

Implement the commands using actual test execution scripts and documented prerequisites.

If the project uses another task runner, integrate the same capabilities into the existing system.

## 24.1 Fail-fast behavior

The verification gate must return a non-zero exit code when:

- A required test fails.
- A critical defect exists.
- An invalid migration is detected.
- Required artifacts are missing.
- Evidence cannot be generated.
- The final acceptance policy is violated.

A blocked external deployment may be represented separately from a failed local test suite.

Do not silently return success because a test was skipped.

# SECTION 25 — FINAL TEST REPORT CALCULATIONS

All totals must be calculated from actual test result records.

Produce:

- Total requirements.
- Passed requirements.
- Failed requirements.
- Blocked requirements.
- Not implemented requirements.
- Not tested requirements.
- Not applicable requirements.
- Accepted risks.
- Total executed tests.
- Passed tests.
- Failed tests.
- Skipped tests.
- Test execution duration.
- Critical open defects.
- High open defects.
- Medium open defects.
- Low open defects.

Ensure the following relationships are valid:

`Passed + Failed + Blocked + Not Implemented + Not Tested + Not Applicable + Accepted Risk = Total requirements`

For executed tests:

`Passed tests + Failed tests + Skipped tests = Total test results`

Only include categories supported by actual result data.

Do not mix test counts with requirement counts.

Do not calculate a single misleading "system accuracy percentage" from unrelated acceptance criteria.

The final system may have a fully implemented technical workflow while still lacking real company-level evidence.

Make this distinction explicit.

## 27.1 Synthetic data

- Dataset generator.
- Dataset version.
- Record count.
- Label-generation logic.
- Known artificial patterns.
- Train/validation/test boundaries.

Do not report synthetic results as real subscription-company performance.

## 27.2 Public datasets

- Dataset name.
- Source.
- License.
- Data dictionary.
- Download date.
- Transformation.
- Known limitations.

Verify the actual dataset license before redistribution.

## 27.3 Real company data

When company data is not available, report:

`BLOCKED — Authorized company data and confirmed business outcomes were not supplied.`

Do not invent company data.

## 27.4 Provider integrations

Distinguish:

- Provider adapter code exists.
- Configuration exists.
- Credentials missing.
- Authentication successful.
- Sandbox tested.
- Production integration verified.

## 27.5 Production infrastructure

Distinguish:

- Local.
- Docker local.
- Staging.
- Production.

Never describe local container verification as hosted production verification.

## 27.6 Model accuracy

State the exact dataset and evaluation conditions.

Report no unsupported claim such as:

- 99% accurate in production.
- 100% churn detection.
- Guaranteed retention improvements.
- Guaranteed MRR increase.

## 27.7 Business impact

A technically correct prediction does not prove that a retention campaign causes a customer to stay.

Separate predictive performance from measured intervention effectiveness.

Run the documented setup in a fresh isolated environment.

When packaging tools are available, create one clean final release archive.

The package should include:

- Source code.

# SECTION 30 — NON-NEGOTIABLE FINAL RULES

1. Verify the actual application, not only its documentation.
2. Test all 20 phases.
3. Preserve existing working architecture.
4. Do not create another application.
5. Do not create duplicate modules or databases.
6. Do not delete useful user data.
7. Do not destroy migration history.
8. Do not bypass validation.
9. Do not weaken security to make tests pass.
10. Do not weaken ML evaluation to approve a candidate.
11. Do not use immature churn labels as negative outcomes.
12. Do not allow future-data leakage.
13. Do not tune on the final test set.
14. Do not fabricate metrics.
15. Do not hardcode dashboard statistics.
16. Do not label synthetic results as real-world results.
17. Do not claim a provider is connected without verifying it.
18. Do not claim a production deployment without testing the actual environment.
19. Do not claim backup recovery without a real restoration test.
20. Do not mark tests as passed when they were skipped.
21. Do not suppress errors.
22. Do not remove failing tests without a valid replacement and documented reason.
23. Do not change expected results to hide a defect.
24. Do not hide broken frontend actions.
25. Do not ignore browser console errors.
26. Do not ignore database transaction failures.
27. Do not ignore background job failures.
28. Do not ignore monitoring blind spots.
29. Do not allow unapproved model promotion.
30. Do not change historical predictions during model release updates.
31. Do not execute real CRM campaigns during automated testing.
32. Do not execute payments or external financial actions.
33. Do not expose private customer data in reports.
34. Do not expose secrets in logs.
35. Do not report all requirements as passed simply because the build succeeded.
36. Do not report a percentage of completion that is not derived from the acceptance matrix.
37. Do not mark BLOCKED requirements as PASS.
38. Do not hide unresolved critical or high defects.
39. Do not create fake screenshots or fabricated test logs.
40. Do not claim human UAT approval without actual approval.
41. Do not start unrelated feature development.
42. Do not automatically begin another phase after Phase 20.
43. Do not claim the project is fully production-ready when external evidence is missing.
44. Preserve an honest history of baseline failures and subsequent repairs.
45. Generate all final reports from actual test and verification results.

# SECTION 31 — FINAL ACCEPTANCE AND PROJECT COMPLETION DEFINITION

The project can receive a strong final verification result only when the following conditions are satisfied.

## Technical completion

- The application builds.
- The application starts.
- Database migrations work.
- APIs function.
- Frontend routes work.
- Core workflows work.
- Data pipelines work.
- ML pipelines work.
- Predictions work.
- MLOps workflows work.
- Deployment procedures work.
- Recovery procedures work.

## Data correctness

- Canonical data contracts are respected.
- Ingestion accounting is correct.
- Churn labels are correct.
- Label maturity is respected.
- Feature leakage is prevented.
- Dataset snapshots are reproducible.

## ML correctness

- Training is reproducible.
- Evaluation is independent.
- Model artifacts are valid.
- SHAP lineage is correct.
- Inference uses the approved model.
- Prediction history is traceable.
- Monitoring uses appropriate outcomes.

## Business workflow correctness

- Customer 360 uses the correct entity.
- Retention suggestions have evidence.
- Communication policies are enforced.
- CRM integration state is truthful.
- Human approval is respected.

## Operational readiness

- MLflow works.
- Airflow works.
- Monitoring works.
- Retraining gates work.
- Model release governance works.
- Deployment and rollback work.
- Security is verified.
- Backup and recovery are tested.

## Evidence completeness

- All phases have a status.
- Every required item has traceability.
- Defects are registered.
- Fixes are retested.
- Regression evidence exists.
- Reports are generated.
- Environmental blockers are documented.
- Release decision is supported by evidence.

A system can be **technically complete for local use** while remaining **blocked for real-company validation or production deployment**. State that distinction clearly.
